items.title: Reduce alert fatigue by customizing threat detection features in Amazon GuardDuty
items.summary: The teams responsible for security today don’t have a problem with the number of alerts they receive; they have a problem turning those alerts into something truly actionable. When an analyst concludes an investigation with “this was caused by our vulnerability scanner” or “this account is configured to share Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) publicly on purpose,” the detection worked as designed, it just wasn’t applicable to the environment. When this happens continuously at scale, alert fatigue sets in. As teams sort through these events, incident response slows down or, worse, teams stop paying attention to the alerts at all. Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors, analyzes, and processes Amazon Web Services (AWS) data sources and logs in your AWS environment for suspicious or potentially malicious activity. GuardDuty then delivers detailed security findings to you for visibility and remediation. GuardDuty accomplishes this by analyzing independent streams of available sources. This includes logging of management events in AWS CloudTrail , information about IP traffic through Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 DNS query logs to name a few. These sources don’t need to be enabled or configured within your accounts for GuardDuty to use them. When GuardDuty observes activity that looks suspicious or anomalous, it produces a finding that’s a detailed security alert naming the behavior, the resources involved, and any supporting evidence. A finding is a signal to investigate, not a final verdict. While the managed detections in GuardDuty work consistently across every AWS customer, personalizing detections for your specific architectures and environments is equally important. Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules. In this post, we walk through those capabilities in three distinct stages. These stages explore how to customize what GuardDuty detects, triage the findings that remain, and accelerate investigations. Throughout this blog post you’ll learn how to: Efficiently detect anomalous behavior that shouldn’t occur in a specific account, without building detection logic yourself Measure if a detection will be noisy before it generates a single finding, flooding security teams Feed your own custom threat intelligence, including file hashes, into GuardDuty Scope a suppression rule narrowly enough to archive expected activity while surfacing the same behavior elsewhere Get an automated analysis of a finding, with a risk level and recommended actions, before the finding is opened manually Prerequisites For the walkthrough in this post, you must have the following prerequisites in place. GuardDuty must be enabled in at least one AWS account and AWS Region. Note that these customization features aren’t currently available in all Regions, for more information, see Region-specific feature availability . Your user or role must have AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to configure these features in GuardDuty. The AmazonGuardDutyFullAccess_v2 managed policy covers the required actions. If you manage multiple accounts through AWS Organizations , AWS recommends administering GuardDuty using the delegated administrator account. By using this method, you can manage lists, suppression rules, and conduct investigations from a centralized location. GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring must be enabled to conduct file hash matching and to use Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring. This protection plan isn’t enabled automatically in GuardDuty. An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket that you control for storage of custom threat entity lists. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed. Stage 1: How to customize what GuardDuty detects An AMI is a pre-configured template that contains the software configurations needed to launch an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance on AWS. Sharing an AMI publicly can be a routine operation in an account whose purpose is distributing images, and a potential security event in any other account. The same might be said for disabling VPC Flow Logs , or signing in without multi-factor authentication for a legacy service account. Until the release of Custom Detection Rules, there was no way to account for these differences in GuardDuty. Custom Detection Rules Custom Detection Rules is a library of prebuilt, opt-in rules that AWS builds and maintains. At launch, it holds 90 rules across AWS CloudTrail management events and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring events, producing 38 finding types mapped to 13 MITRE ATT&CK ® tactics, described using vocabulary from ATT&CK and the Threat Technique Catalog for AWS . The catalog is maintained by the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) and is based on the MITRE ATT&CK Cloud Matrix, documenting threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures specific to AWS as observed by the AWS CIRT during customer engagements. Each entry includes detection guidance and mitigations specific to AWS environments, so a technique ID on a finding points to a public entry that your team can read. Previously, detecting environment-specific behavior meant ingesting your own CloudTrail logs or host telemetry, normalizing them, building the logic, and maintaining that logic as APIs changed. Custom Detection Rules remove that work. You select the rules for GuardDuty to evaluate against the CloudTrail management events it already analyzes and, where Runtime Monitoring is enabled, the runtime events from the GuardDuty security agent, without the undifferentiated heavy lifting of log ingestion, normalization, and storage. Coverage is extended without adding unnecessary alerts that don’t add value to your teams. Each rule runs in one of two modes. In dry run mode, GuardDuty evaluates the rule and publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics showing how often an event matched the rule, but generates no findings. Dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days. In live mode, events that match generate findings, and live mode has no expiration. Custom Detection Rules are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring are available in every region where GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is available. Walkthrough: Measure a rule, then turn it on Start in dry run so you can measure the noise level before receiving a finding. This walkthrough uses the AMIExternalAccess rule, which detects when an AMI is shared with an external AWS account or made public, and applies it from the GuardDuty delegated administrator account. In an organization, the delegated administrator manages Custom Detection Rules for all member accounts through an organization configuration , and accounts that join the organization later inherit it. Using the GuardDuty console Open the AWS Management Console for GuardDuty and choose Custom Detection Rules . Figure 1. The Custom Detection Rules catalog with the detection logic for the AMIExternalAccess rule Select a rule name to see its detection logic on the Details tab. Rules are SQL conditions over CloudTrail fields, so you can review exactly what a rule matches before enabling it. Choose the rule’s Accounts tab, then under Organization configuration , choose Configure . Figure 2. Configuring the AMIExternalAccess rule in dry run mode Under Configuration strategy , select Whole organization . Under Status , select Dry run . Under Accounts , select Apply rule status to all accounts , then choose Save . Watch the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric in CloudWatch. GuardDuty publishes the metric only when the rule matches an event, so a rule with no matching activity shows no data. Because dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days, a full dry-run period is the longest continuous sample GuardDuty collects without you re-enabling the rule. The metric data persists in CloudWatch under its standard retention after the dry run ends, so you can review it shortly before or after expiry and still base your decision on the most complete data available. Volume alone doesn’t tell you whether the activity is benign, so account for what you see before deciding. If a rule matches constantly and someone can point to the process that causes it, that account is a poor candidate for live mode. If nobody can explain the matches, investigate them as they stand, because a dry run measuring real attacker activity looks the same as one measuring routine operations. Figure 3. Dry-run match volume for a rule over one week, shown as hourly totals When you’re satisfied the rule is worth acting on, return to the rule’s organization configuration and change Status to Live to start generating findings. To keep the rule off in accounts where the activity is expected, such as an image-build account, choose Exclude accounts manually under Accounts and select those accounts. Using the AWS CLI From the delegated administrator account, apply the rule in dry run to the whole organization. Omitting account lists targets every member account, including accounts that join later. aws guardduty create-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode DRY_RUN Review the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric over the dry-run period, applying the same judgment described in the preceding console procedure. Move the rule to live mode by updating the existing configuration. Creating a second whole-organization configuration for the same rule fails with a conflict error. To exclude accounts where the activity is expected, add --exclude-account-ids . aws guardduty update-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode LIVE \ --exclude-account-ids Note: In a standalone account that isn’t part of an organization, you enable a rule for that account alone. With the AWS CLI, use create-custom-detection-rule-association with the same --rule-id and --mode parameters. To change the mode later, use update-custom-detection-rule-association with the association ID. Member accounts in an organization can’t enable or change a rule themselves; the delegated administrator manages rules on their behalf. For details, see Managing Custom Detection Rules in multiple-account environments . Threat entity lists If your threat intelligence team already tracks known-bad infrastructure and files, you can pass those indicators to GuardDuty and generate findings when they appear in your AWS account. GuardDuty has two list formats. An IP address list holds IP addresses only. An entity list, the newer format, can hold IP addresses, CIDR ranges, and domain names together in a single file. The difference that matters is coverage: entity list entries apply to CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS query log findings, while IP address lists cover CloudTrail and VPC Flow Log findings only. If you still use IP address lists, the additional DNS coverage is a reason to move. In addition, entity lists now also accept SHA-256 file hashes. Hashes sit alongside network indicators in the same file, and GuardDuty checks them against Runtime Monitoring. When the runtime agent sees an executable whose hash matches an active list, it generates a high severity Execution:Runtime/MaliciousFileExecuted.Custom finding and names the matching list, so your responder knows which intelligence source was used. Note: If the entity list is changed, the list must be reactivated to include the updates. Uploading a new version of the file isn’t sufficient on its own. If this step is automated, build that reactivation step into the same process that refreshes the file. Entity lists are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions, but not in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Stage 2: How to triage the findings that remain Customizing detection reduces findings at the source, but the work is rarely finished there. New workloads appear, teams change how they operate, and some findings still describe activity that’s expected in your environment. You also need a precise way to route those events away from the queue your analysts work from. A filter selects findings. A suppression rule is a filter that automatically archives a GuardDuty finding it matches. Archiving isn’t deletion: the finding is retained for 90 days and stays viewable, but the finding isn’t forwarded to AWS Security Hub , Amazon S3, Amazon Detective , or Amazon EventBridge , so it stays out of your security information and event management (SIEM) system and ticket queue. Two changes have made that routing more customizable. Wildcards Filter criteria now support the Matches and NotMatches operators, where * matches any number of characters and ? matches one. Criteria used to be exact-match only, so suppressing findings from every AWS Lambda function in a service meant listing each name and updating it on every deployment. One pattern now covers the naming convention, including functions that don’t exist yet, so the rule stops going stale. Additional property filter fields You can now use over 1,000 supported fields from a finding as suppression criteria, including runtime process details, Kubernetes workload metadata, network connection information, and attack sequence signals. Take a vulnerability scanner in one Kubernetes namespace generating expected findings. With no namespace criterion available, you previously either suppressed the finding type more broadly than you wanted or wrote downstream logic to strip them. Now you scope the rule to that specific namespace and leave detection intact everywhere else in the cluster. This expanded field set is available in the aws partition; other partitions continue to use the console-supported fields only. See Filtering findings in GuardDuty for the full list of supported fields. The recommended method is to assemble your criteria on the Findings page first, confirm the filtered list contains only findings you’re willing to archive, then choose Create suppression rule . The console and CLI procedures are detailed in the user guide. Figure 4. Findings filtered by finding type and Kubernetes namespace, before creating a suppression rule Before you write wildcard criteria, know that they can’t be validated with ListFindings or GetFindingsStatistics , the testing workflow AWS recommends for ordinary filters. Instead, start from a filter that takes no action and watch the suppression rule metrics to see how much it would match before you rely on it. Nothing is lost if the pattern is too broad, matched findings are archived rather than deleted, so you can lift the suppression rule and return them to your queue. Stage 3: How to accelerate investigations What remains consumes analyst hours. To decide whether a finding is a real event, an analyst pivots into CloudTrail for the operations that identity performed, lines up timestamps, checks IPs and domains against intelligence, and looks for a change ticket that explains the work. That can take hours, and most such investigations end in expected . When one doesn’t, all that time was spent before any actual containment could begin. GuardDuty Investigation , also called AI-powered investigations performs that correlation automatically. GuardDuty Investigation analyzes the finding alongside related activity from the past 90 days, affected resources, threat intelligence, and threat indicators, and returns a structured summary in minutes: a risk level, a confidence rating, a written summary, supporting detail, MITRE ATT&CK classification, and recommended actions including the CLI commands to carry them out. Note: Read the confidence rating as carefully as the risk level. High risk with low confidence is a very different indicator to an analyst than high risk with high confidence. You can investigate a single finding, an account, or a whole organization, from the console, the AWS CLI, the API, or an AWS MCP Server . To turn on AI-powered investigations, go to Settings , find AI powered investigations – Preview , and choose Enable . Figure 5. A completed account investigation with risk level, confidence, analysis summary, and recommended actions The preview runs in 10 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). It allows 10 investigations per account per day and 100 per account in total, and can only be started from an administrator account, member accounts can’t create investigations from their own accounts. The feature uses Amazon Bedrock models with Cross-Region Inference (CRIS) , which automatically selects a Region within your geography to process the analysis and generate the report. Your data remains stored only in the Region where the investigation request originates, but investigation data and summary results might be processed outside that Region. Review that routing if you have data residency commitments. For GuardDuty Region-specific differences more broadly, see Region-specific feature availability in the user guide. Putting it all together Consider a team running containerized workloads on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) across a handful of accounts in one organization. The threat intelligence team uploads SHA-256 hashes from a recent brief as a threat entity list. Security engineering enables Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode and finds after 2 weeks that AMI sharing fires constantly in the image-build account and nowhere else, so they promote the rule to live across the organization and exclude the build account. The team’s vulnerability scanner runs in a dedicated Kubernetes namespace, so they suppress that namespace and finding type while leaving the same behavior detected elsewhere. A second rule uses a wildcard on their Lambda naming convention, replacing a hand-maintained list. Suppressed findings are archived instead of being sent to Security Hub, Amazon S3, EventBridge, or the SIEM, so they never reach the analyst queue. When a finding does warrant attention, an analyst starts an investigation and gets a disposition before manual work begins. Each stage reduces the work of the next. Customizing detection means less to triage, effective triage means less to investigate, and automated investigation means the findings that reach a human get a decision faster. Next steps If you haven’t enabled GuardDuty, start with the 30-day free trial . Most protection plans enable automatically and are included, so you can evaluate them. Turn on Runtime Monitoring separately if you want to test hash matching or Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring.. If you’re already using GuardDuty: Enable two or three Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode. Choose behavior that shouldn’t occur in specific accounts, measure across the dry-run period, then promote selectively. Revisit existing suppression rules. Any rule written before the April 2026 field expansion might be broader than you intended, because the field you wanted wasn’t available then; narrow it to that field now. Audit filters for wildcard opportunities. Any filter with a growing list of exact-match names is maintenance a single pattern can replace. Migrate IP address lists to entity lists for the DNS query log coverage. Conclusion GuardDuty’s managed detections keep expanding, driven by AWS threat intelligence, security research, and customer feedback. These capabilities enable you to decide which activity is worth alerting on in which accounts, and which findings never need to be delivered to a human at all. Learn more Custom Detection Rules in GuardDuty Managing Custom Detection Rules in multiple-account environments Customizing threat detection with entity lists and IP address lists Creating suppression rules in GuardDuty Suppression rule metrics Introducing the Amazon GuardDuty investigation agent: on-demand AI-powered threat assessment Amazon GuardDuty Regions and endpoints Amazon GuardDuty quotas Threat Technique Catalog for AWS Welcoming the AWS Customer Incident Response Team What the March 2026 Threat Technique Catalog update means for your AWS environment Amazon GuardDuty adds optional threat detection rules Allan Holmes Allan brings over 20 years of experience spanning security & compliance, networking, and DevOps to his current role as a Security Specialist. Giving him a uniquely holistic view of cloud security challenges. Allan holds multiple technical certifications from AWS, ISC2, CompTIA, and an MBA, enabling him to bridge deep technical expertise with business strategy. Outside of work, Allan is an avid gardener and electronics enthusiast who enjoys exploring innovative technologies hands-on. Austin Buettner Austin is a Senior Technical Account Manager (TAM) at AWS, where he helps enterprise companies build and operate secure, resilient workloads at scale. A former architect with over 15 years of experience in IT, he focuses on security, networking, and cloud operations, turning AWS capabilities into practical guidance customers can put to work. Outside of work, Austin enjoys golfing, hitting the gym, and spending time with his family. Zhuo Zhang Zhuo is a Technical Lead at AWS GuardDuty, where he builds the software and systems behind the service’s threat detection mission. Since 2016, he has been part of GuardDuty from concept through many expansions. Zhuo uses his background in software engineering and cybersecurity to develop the capabilities of GuardDuty. Outside of work, Zhuo enjoys trying new technologies and spending time with his family.

Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). The feature uses Amazon Bedrock models with Cross-Region Inference (CRIS), which automatically selects a Region within your geography to process the analysis and generate the report. Your data remains stored only in the Region where the investigation request originates, but investigation data and summary results might be processed outside that Region. Review that routing if you have data residency commitments. For GuardDuty Region-specific differences more broadly, see Region-specific feature availability in the user guide.

Putting it all together

Consider a team running containerized workloads on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) across a handful of accounts in one organization.

The threat intelligence team uploads SHA-256 hashes from a recent brief as a threat entity list. Security engineering enables Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode and finds after 2 weeks that AMI sharing fires constantly in the image-build account and nowhere else, so they promote the rule to live across the organization and exclude the build account.

The team’s vulnerability scanner runs in a dedicated Kubernetes namespace, so they suppress that namespace and finding type while leaving the same behavior detected elsewhere. A second rule uses a wildcard on their Lambda naming convention, replacing a hand-maintained list.

Suppressed findings are archived instead of being sent to Security Hub, Amazon S3, EventBridge, or the SIEM, so they never reach the analyst queue. When a finding does warrant attention, an analyst starts an investigation and gets a disposition before manual work begins.

Each stage reduces the work of the next. Customizing detection means less to triage, effective triage means less to investigate, and automated investigation means the findings that reach a human get a decision faster.

Next steps

If you haven’t enabled GuardDuty, start with the 30-day free trial. Most protection plans enable automatically and are included, so you can evaluate them. Turn on Runtime Monitoring separately if you want to test hash matching or Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring..

If you’re already using GuardDuty:

  • Enable two or three Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode. Choose behavior that shouldn’t occur in specific accounts, measure across the dry-run period, then promote selectively.
  • Revisit existing suppression rules. Any rule written before the April 2026 field expansion might be broader than you intended, because the field you wanted wasn’t available then; narrow it to that field now.
  • Audit filters for wildcard opportunities. Any filter with a growing list of exact-match names is maintenance a single pattern can replace.
  • Migrate IP address lists to entity lists for the DNS query log coverage.
Conclusion

GuardDuty’s managed detections keep expanding, driven by AWS threat intelligence, security research, and customer feedback. These capabilities enable you to decide which activity is worth alerting on in which accounts, and which findings never need to be delivered to a human at all.

items.title: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons
items.summary: Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons to inject a short payload. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker’s command. And because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party models and internally developed models. Key findings from Microsoft Research include: Software abuse and manipulation are familiar threats. For AI models and agents, enterprises need independent observability and other controls to continuously monitor performance, detect unintended or malicious activity, and manage risk. Satya Nadella recently outlined this approach in a blog post . A backdoored model can pass evaluations. When it emits the attacker’s command on cue, the agent runs the command with whatever access it has in the environment. The attack needs inference-only compute. If a machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it. Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously. Microsoft has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. However, this research aligns with similar recent research by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively, highlighting the need to audit open weights like code. Notably, Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. Using frontier agents as auditors can help automate the defense against this threat. More broadly, Microsoft Research’s approach demonstrates an adaptable process for securing AI agents: agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. Learn more from the Microsoft Research Blog: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents . Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to defend against this threat as part of a broader defense-in-depth approach. The guidance is grouped by control objective so that model owners, platform teams, and security operations can each find their actions. Audit model weights before deployment and after every update Diff every checkpoint against its declared base model before deployment and after each update. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly and diffusely, while implanted neurons tend to change a few weight vectors by a large amount. Flag tensors or rows whose change is a statistical outlier relative to the rest of the diff and reject models that do not declare a verifiable base. Use frontier AI agents as auditors in the model intake pipeline. Microsoft Research found they are highly effective at finding anomalous structure in weights that manual inspection misses, which makes this step automatable at scale. Complement weight diffing with behavioral backdoor scanning of open-weight models, as described in Microsoft’s research on detecting backdoored language models at scale . Record audit results alongside the model in the registry, and state clearly to internal consumers that passing an audit reduces risk but does not guarantee safe behavior. Secure model hubs and publishers Display provenance and audit status publicly before a checkpoint can be downloaded or served through an API. Scan every upload for anomalous neurons, weight patterns or behaviors, and state clearly that third-party checkpoints can be unsafe and that passing an audit does not guarantee safe behavior. Treat every third-party model as untrusted until audited Source checkpoints only from the original publisher, verify the publisher’s published file hashes, and treat all third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantizations, and adapters as untrusted until they pass an audit. Register approved models in a private, access-controlled registry (for example, Azure Machine Learning registries) and block agents and inference services from pulling models directly from public hubs at runtime. Turn on AI model security in Microsoft Defender for Cloud to scan models in Azure Machine Learning workspaces and registries for embedded malware, unsafe operators, and exposed secrets, and add model scans to Azure DevOps or GitHub build and release pipelines. Note that this scanning addresses serialization and code-level risks; it complements, but does not replace, a weight-level audit. Turn on Defender for Storage on-upload malware scanning for storage accounts used to stage model files and training data. Red team for hidden triggers Add trigger-hunting and backdoor scenarios to your AI red team plan. Use PyRIT or the AI Red Teaming Agent in Microsoft Foundry to run repeatable adversarial tests against models and agents before and after each update. Contain what an agent can do if its model is compromised Run agents with least privilege. Give each agent its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID, scope its permissions to the minimum set of resources it needs, and use Conditional Access for agents to l block unapproved or high-risk agent identities . Execute agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, such as Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions , and never expose host-side file write or shell tools to the model. Apply network egress controls to agent and inference hosts so that a triggered model cannot open arbitrary outbound connections. Allow only the endpoints the agent requires and turn on network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. Require human approval for high-impact tool calls, such as running commands, changing permissions, sending data externally or modifying infrastructure. Apply attack surface reduction rules to devices that host local agents and inference servers, starting in audit mode. Detect and block malicious agent behavior at runtime Turn on Microsoft Defender security for AI agents and configure real-time protection rules so Defender can audit and block risky tool invocations, secret exfiltration, and evasion techniques for Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio and Agent 365 agents, and runtime protection for local agents through Defender for Endpoint. Turn on threat protection for AI services in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, including suspicious prompt evidence, so the security operations center (SOC) receives alerts for jailbreak attempts, credential leakage in model responses and malicious URLs in AI interactions. Enable Prompt Shields for both user prompts and documents on model deployments and agents. Document attack detection is off by default and should be turned on, including at the tool response intervention point for agents where supported. Onboard every device and server that runs agents or local inference to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint in active mode so that suspicious child processes, persistence and outbound connections from agent host processes are detected. Maintain inventory and governance of models and agents Use the AI agent inventory in the Microsoft Defender portal to discover agents, their tools, identities, and risk indicators. Use AI security posture management in Defender for Cloud to build an AI bill of materials (AI BOM) across Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), so you know which models are deployed where. Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps and Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI to discover, sanction or block generative AI apps, and to monitor sensitive data in AI interactions. Map controls to the Microsoft catalog of AI defense capabilities , which groups supply-chain provenance, model hardening, runtime isolation and monitoring into a single framework aligned to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Learn more For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog . To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn , X (formerly Twitter) , and Bluesky . To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast .

items.title: AWS refreshes ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment to enhance customer’s third-party due diligence
items.summary: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce renewal of the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment . This validated assessment report helps customers perform effective cloud supplier due diligence on AWS and enhances their third-party risk management process. What is the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment Many customers use third-party cyber risk management (TPCRM) services such as ProcessUnity to better manage risks from their evolving third-party environments and to drive operational efficiencies. To help with such efforts, AWS has completed the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment of its security posture. ProcessUnity’s assessors perform the review of Global Risk Exchange assessment and validate the results annually. This assessment approach replaces static spreadsheets with a dynamic system that combines advanced analytics, threat intelligence, and risk models with vendor input. Vendor profiles continuously update as cloud provider risk levels and AWS security posture evolve, keeping risk matrices current in near real time. Additionally, customers can also use Framework View which maps AWS assessment controls to threat profiles, MITRE ATT&CK scenarios, and global compliance standards and frameworks including National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 27001, Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), significantly reducing customers’ third-party due diligence burden. How can you access the assessment? Customers can request access to the report by completing an access request form, available on the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange page . If you are an existing ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange member, you can request access from within ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange portal. To learn more about our compliance and security programs, see AWS Compliance Programs . As always, we value your feedback and questions; reach out to the AWS Compliance team through the Contact Us page . Naranjan Goklani Naranjan is an WS Compliance, Security Assurance and Privacy (CAPS) Lead for Canada. He has experience leading audits, attestations, certifications, and assessments across the Americas. Naranjan has more than 16 years of experience in technology risk management, customer security assurance, and technology audits. He previously worked in the Big 4 accounting firms and supported clients from the financial services, technology, retail, and utilities industries.

Microsoft and Adobe Patch Tuesday, November 2026 Security Update Review
items.summary: As the year approaches its final stretch, Microsoft’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday highlights the continued importance of proactive vulnerability management. This month’s security updates address vulnerabilities across the Microsoft ecosystem, reinforcing the need for organizations to promptly identify, prioritize, and remediate security risks. In this month’s updates, Microsoft addressed 1235 vulnerabilities, including 63 critical and 1029 important-severity vulnerabilities. In the updates, Microsoft has addressed 142 vulnerabilities impacting Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based). In this month’s updates, Microsoft has addressed only one vulnerability that has been exploited in the wild. This Patch Tuesday, Qualys InstaScan showed customers their November findings 40 minutes before Microsoft’s own advisory page was updated. Find out more about InstaScan This month’s release includes fixes for several vulnerabilities that could potentially enable remote code execution, privilege escalation, or denial-of-service attacks. As always, timely patch deployment is crucial to reduce exposure and ensure systems remain resilient against exploitation attempts. The November 2026 Microsoft vulnerabilities are classified as follows: Adobe Patch for November 2026 Adobe has released nine advisories addressing 63 vulnerabilities across Adobe After Effects, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Premiere, Adobe Audition, Adobe Experience Manager (AEM), and Adobe Dimension. Four of these vulnerabilities are rated critical. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities may lead to arbitrary code execution. Zero-day Vulnerability Patched in November Patch Tuesday Edition CVE-2026-124194: Microsoft Outlook Spoofing Vulnerability An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook. Opening the file may cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning. Successful exploitation of the vulnerability may lead to disclosure of authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. items.summary_html:
As the year approaches its final stretch, Microsoft’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday highlights the continued importance of proactive vulnerability management. This month’s security updates address vulnerabilities across the Microsoft ecosystem, reinforcing the need for organizations to promptly identify, prioritize, and remediate security risks.

In this month’s updates, Microsoft addressed 1235 vulnerabilities, including 63 critical and 1029 important-severity vulnerabilities. In the updates, Microsoft has addressed 142 vulnerabilities impacting Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based).

In this month’s updates, Microsoft has addressed only one vulnerability that has been exploited in the wild.

This Patch Tuesday, Qualys InstaScan showed customers their November findings 40 minutes before Microsoft’s own advisory page was updated.

Find out more about InstaScan

This month’s release includes fixes for several vulnerabilities that could potentially enable remote code execution, privilege escalation, or denial-of-service attacks. As always, timely patch deployment is crucial to reduce exposure and ensure systems remain resilient against exploitation attempts. 

The November 2026 Microsoft vulnerabilities are classified as follows:

Adobe Patch for November 2026

Adobe has released nine advisories addressing 63 vulnerabilities across Adobe After Effects, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Premiere, Adobe Audition, Adobe Experience Manager (AEM), and Adobe Dimension. Four of these vulnerabilities are rated critical. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities may lead to arbitrary code execution. 

Zero-day Vulnerability Patched in November Patch Tuesday Edition  CVE-2026-124194: Microsoft Outlook Spoofing Vulnerability 

An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook. Opening the file may cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning. Successful exploitation of the vulnerability may lead to disclosure of authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user.

CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, urging users to patch it before November 24, 2026.

items.summary: This is simultaneously the most boring yet exciting blog title I've written in a long time. How you pay for services isn't exactly a sexy topic, but it solves a problem that's been a massive bugbear for a long time. Here's a brief history of the issue: many organisations have policies that make it extremely hard to purchase goods and services with a credit card. I wrote about this more than two years ago now , where I referred to "Neville" in the procurement department who, because "reasons", demanded an invoice in advance and payment via electronic funds transfer (EFT) only. That ultimately means the world's most popular way to make online payments is out of reach for them. Unfortunately, until today, that was the only way we could take payment via Stripe, which processes all our online HIBP purchases. That left only two options for orgs in this situation: Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢 Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢 The problem with the first option is obvious. The second option "solved" the first problem by allowing a company to pay a reseller by EFT, who then paid us by card. The reseller would then mark the price up ( often significantly), slow the whole process down, log countless tickets with us (despite the existence of a dedicated portal for them), and frankly, just be a pain in the arse for everyone. It's hard to express the level of disdain I have for most resellers, and I even still have a 1,381-word draft blog post titled "That's it - Resellers are now Banned from Have I Been Pwned", which I held back from posting. Why? Because I've walked in the shoes of the folks trying to purchase our services who are just trying to get their job done, and Neville has told them they can't pay by card. That was me in a previous life, and it sucked. We kept resellers solely to support those people. But today, HIBP's subscription page has something all new on it: Stripe has given us early access to EFT payments in Australia. They've been available in the US for a while, but as an Aussie company and with global financial systems being what they are (i.e. not always the most flexible), we just didn't have that option. Until now. So, we've added EFT as a payment method to our Pro and High RPM plans and kept the entry-level Core ones on card only, as there's some additional overhead on our end. You'll see these every time you go to purchase an eligible subscription: When you choose to pay by bank transfer, you're given a form for your company details (this is how we calculate any applicable taxes), then a Stripe payment link which loads something similar to the following: The first thing is that, being an Aussie company with an Aussie bank account, we need to reflect EFT payments in AUD rather than USD. It makes sense when you think about it: we do USD for all the existing products paid for by card, and whatever the FX conversion gods decide is the corresponding Aussie amount eventually lands on our end. But that's a model where the card is charged, and access is granted immediately. For EFT, funds flow through the wires, do FX conversion for non-Aussie purchasers, land in the target account and then Stripe webhook magic enables the service. We need that exact amount to land on our end, so we can't be rolling the dice on what exchange rate we're going to get; hence, Stripe requires us to charge in the target currency. The products are exactly the same price based on the rate we currently see via Stripe purchases today (about 69 American cents per Aussie dollar), we'll just have to see if that's revised in the future with any major currency fluctuations. Next are the banking details. Pretty straightforward, and I'm sure we've all made payments to an account like this before. The main thing is that the account number is a virtual one, which is how Stripe reconciles money that comes in from a previously raised invoice. When you sell a very limited number of products and a bunch of customers are buying the same one, this is how Stripe is then able to reconcile who has paid for what. If you really want to geek out on bank payments, Stripe has a dedicated EFT explainer page . And finally, subscriptions in HIBP begin as soon as the invoice is raised, but access to the service only begins when payment is made. You can see the problem if we didn't do it this way: bad guy spins up the service and immediately starts using it then just never pays. But this all ties into the quote ecosystem in the existing HIBP dashboard, so it's easy to generate a quote, go flick it to Neville, get it approved, then raise and pay the invoice straight away. As I said in the opening, it's not the most exciting topic, but it's a major thing for us and the customers who were left with only bad options if they genuinely couldn't pay by card. In the aforementioned draft blog post on binning resellers, I'd written about how we'd seen markups of up to 131% (so yes, more than double the price!), with absolutely zero value add (i.e. they don't do any product support, that remains entirely on us). But the burden resellers really put on us is the support they require to make purchases; in that same draft post, I calculated that resellers accounted for 0.86% of all sales but 43% of all support tickets. That's just nuts, especially for such a small team (although Bruce has helped enormously ). We hope this makes life easier for a bunch of people who were previously stuck between a rock and a hard place, and that includes all the "Nevilles" out there too. This is all now live and accessible via the pricing page . If you run into any issues, Bruce is standing by in the support portal .

items.title: Microsoft November 2026 Patch Tuesday Fixes 1,093 Vulnerabilities, Including Outlook Zero-Day
items.summary: Microsoft has released its November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates, fixing 1,093 newly released vulnerabilities across Windows, Office, SQL Server, SharePoint, Exchange Server, Azure services, and developer tools. The release includes one actively exploited zero-day in Microsoft Outlook that can leak a user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash to an attacker. This update addresses 63 critical vulnerabilities, 1,029 important issues, and one moderate flaw among the newly released entries. Vulnerability Type Count Elevation of Privilege 535 Remote Code Execution 296 Information Disclosure 156 Denial of Service 46 Security Feature Bypass 27 Spoofing 22 Tampering 11 Total 1,093 Note: For our Patch Tuesday coverage, we count only vulnerabilities released by Microsoft on Patch Tuesday itself, excluding fixes issued earlier in the month. Outlook 0-Day Vulnerability CVE-2026-124194 is an actively exploited Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability that can expose a user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash. Microsoft rates it Moderate, with a CVSS score of 6.5, and identifies the underlying weakness as missing warnings about unsafe actions, tracked as CWE-356. According to Microsoft’s advisory , an unauthenticated attacker can send a specially crafted message file and trick the recipient into opening it in Outlook. Opening the file can make Outlook connect to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning. This connection can disclose authentication information that could be used to impersonate the victim. Exploitation requires the user to open the malicious file and have network connectivity. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector. Microsoft confirms that attacks have occurred, but the advisory does not identify the attackers, victims, or scale of exploitation. Affected products include 32-bit and 64-bit editions of Office LTSC 2021, Office LTSC 2024, and Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise. Administrators should prioritize the applicable security updates because exploitation is already underway, despite the Moderate severity rating. The same release lists CVE-2026-124227 and CVE-2026-124228 as Important-rated Outlook code execution issues, neither of which is marked as exploited. Critical Windows, Office, and Server Flaws Of the 63 Critical flaws, 48 are remote code execution bugs, and 15 are elevation of privilege issues. Excel alone has 12 Critical fixes, while Word has four and PowerPoint has one. Outlook also receives three Critical code execution fixes, tracked as CVE-2026-111309, CVE-2026-110068, and CVE-2026-110043, none of which is marked as exploited. On the Windows side, Hyper-V has eight Critical privilege escalation flaws, which matter for cloud and virtual server hosts. Message Queuing has five Critical code execution bugs across its core and Queue Manager parts. Other key server fixes include CVE-2026-113825 in the SMB Server transport driver, CVE-2026-113859 in TCP/IP, CVE-2026-118207 in Exchange Server, and CVE-2026-119958 in LDAP. Microsoft also patched Critical flaws in Schannel, CredSSP, IIS, Print Spooler, Active Directory Domain Services, and Remote Procedure Call Runtime. Cloud and security products are not left out. Azure OpenAI (CVE-2026-119990) and Azure Managed Grafana (CVE-2026-114160) each received a Critical privilege escalation fix, while Microsoft Defender received a Critical code execution fix tracked as CVE-2026-122194. Microsoft provides a comprehensive Security Update Guide that outlines all identified vulnerabilities, complete with detailed references and resources for further exploration. This guide serves as a crucial tool for understanding potential security risks and implementing necessary updates to protect systems effectively. The exploited Outlook flaw deserves early attention despite its Moderate rating. Earlier reporting on the exploited Windows Shell zero-day provides another example of why exploitation status matters alongside severity. items.summary_html:
Microsoft has released its November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates, fixing 1,093 newly released vulnerabilities across Windows, Office, SQL Server, SharePoint, Exchange Server, Azure services, and developer tools.

The release includes one actively exploited zero-day in Microsoft Outlook that can leak a user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash to an attacker. This update addresses 63 critical vulnerabilities, 1,029 important issues, and one moderate flaw among the newly released entries.

Vulnerability TypeCountElevation of Privilege535Remote Code Execution296Information Disclosure156Denial of Service46Security Feature Bypass27Spoofing22Tampering11Total 1,093

Note: For our Patch Tuesday coverage, we count only vulnerabilities released by Microsoft on Patch Tuesday itself, excluding fixes issued earlier in the month.

Outlook 0-Day Vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 is an actively exploited Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability that can expose a user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash. Microsoft rates it Moderate, with a CVSS score of 6.5, and identifies the underlying weakness as missing warnings about unsafe actions, tracked as CWE-356.

According to Microsoft’s advisory, an unauthenticated attacker can send a specially crafted message file and trick the recipient into opening it in Outlook. Opening the file can make Outlook connect to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning. This connection can disclose authentication information that could be used to impersonate the victim.

Exploitation requires the user to open the malicious file and have network connectivity. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector. Microsoft confirms that attacks have occurred, but the advisory does not identify the attackers, victims, or scale of exploitation.

Affected products include 32-bit and 64-bit editions of Office LTSC 2021, Office LTSC 2024, and Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise. Administrators should prioritize the applicable security updates because exploitation is already underway, despite the Moderate severity rating.

The same release lists CVE-2026-124227 and CVE-2026-124228 as Important-rated Outlook code execution issues, neither of which is marked as exploited.

Critical Windows, Office, and Server Flaws

Of the 63 Critical flaws, 48 are remote code execution bugs, and 15 are elevation of privilege issues. Excel alone has 12 Critical fixes, while Word has four and PowerPoint has one.

Outlook also receives three Critical code execution fixes, tracked as CVE-2026-111309, CVE-2026-110068, and CVE-2026-110043, none of which is marked as exploited.

On the Windows side, Hyper-V has eight Critical privilege escalation flaws, which matter for cloud and virtual server hosts. Message Queuing has five Critical code execution bugs across its core and Queue Manager parts.

Other key server fixes include CVE-2026-113825 in the SMB Server transport driver, CVE-2026-113859 in TCP/IP, CVE-2026-118207 in Exchange Server, and CVE-2026-119958 in LDAP. Microsoft also patched Critical flaws in Schannel, CredSSP, IIS, Print Spooler, Active Directory Domain Services, and Remote Procedure Call Runtime.

Cloud and security products are not left out. Azure OpenAI (CVE-2026-119990) and Azure Managed Grafana (CVE-2026-114160) each received a Critical privilege escalation fix, while Microsoft Defender received a Critical code execution fix tracked as CVE-2026-122194.

Microsoft provides a comprehensive Security Update Guide that outlines all identified vulnerabilities, complete with detailed references and resources for further exploration. This guide serves as a crucial tool for understanding potential security risks and implementing necessary updates to protect systems effectively.

The exploited Outlook flaw deserves early attention despite its Moderate rating. Earlier reporting on the exploited Windows Shell zero-day provides another example of why exploitation status matters alongside severity.

Other Patch Tuesday Updates

  2. Barracuda Confirms Active Exploitation of Email Gateway Flaws Allowing Root Access
  3. SAP Security Patch Day – Critical SAP NetWeaver, Dispatcher and Gateway Vulnerabilities Patched
  4. Progress WS_FTP Server Fixes 7 Security Flaws Allowing Credential Theft, Path Traversal, and Remote Attacks
  5. Apple Fixes 9 Security Vulnerabilities in iOS 27.2.1, Including Bluetooth Pairing and iMessage Flaws
  6. Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely
  7. Notepad++ 8.9.9 Released With Fixes for 6 Vulnerabilities Allowing Plugin Command Execution

items.title: BYOD Ransomware Group Allegedly Claims Toyota Data Breach
items.summary: The BYOD ransomware group has allegedly claimed a Toyota data breach, saying it obtained personal information and access involving kiosk devices. A supplied screenshot shows a Toyota listing updated on November 10, 2026. The claim remains unverified, and the material does not establish that Toyota’s systems were breached or that files were encrypted. The listing names full names, email addresses, physical addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth among the allegedly exposed information. It also mentions “Kiosk Devices,” but provides no explanation of their location, purpose, or ownership. The screenshot does not show how many people, records, or devices may be affected by the alleged incident. Toyota Data Breach Claim BYOD says much of the environment was isolated but claims it found remaining access paths. Its wording suggests an alleged way around network restrictions, rather than proof of a specific security flaw. No entry point, stolen account, software weakness, or technical evidence supporting that statement appears in the visible portion of the listing. The distinction matters because access to one device does not establish access across an entire company. The screenshot does not identify a Toyota business unit, country, dealer, or service provider. It also does not show whether the claimed kiosk access involved stored records, remote control, or device details alone. These remain important unanswered questions. Toyota has appeared in earlier breach reporting, including Cyber Security News coverage of a separate 240 GB data leak claim in August 2024. That report concerned ZeroSevenGroup, not BYOD. It should not be treated as evidence supporting the latest allegation or used to assign an attack method to this listing. Independent tracking provides some background on the name. Breachsense tracks BYOD as a ransomware group and records activity beginning in October 2026. However, a tracking entry does not verify every victim claim. The supplied Toyota screenshot is evidence of an allegation, not independent confirmation that the listed information was stolen. Toyota’s own disclosures show why incidents must be assessed separately. In a May 2023 notice , the company described potential customer information exposure caused by cloud settings. Toyota said it blocked outside access and introduced ongoing configuration checks. That disclosure described a different incident and offers no confirmation of BYOD’s current claim. The broader technical issue is checking whether security controls work across connected systems. Cyber Security News has examined cloud misconfiguration detection and fixes , a related concern when reviewing exposed services. Still, nothing in the BYOD screenshot establishes that a cloud setting caused the alleged Toyota breach. Naming a likely cause now would be speculation. The visible listing provides no ransom amount, payment deadline, encryption evidence, or clear account of business disruption. It also does not establish whether the information is new, complete, or linked to Toyota directly. Those gaps prevent a reliable estimate of the alleged breach’s size, impact, and relevance to customers or employees. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.summary_html:
Welcome to volume fifty of Scrolls, a newsletter for sharing cool stuff from the IndieWeb, Fediverse & Cybersecurity realms. This week we’re celebrating web communities, not talking to our computers, and I have one final thing to say about the Fediverse.

IndieWeb

I’m always telling readers of this publication to get a website! So it’s important that I continue to explain why it’s a good idea (despite some aspects that might not seem so fun)… It’s a great place to share and reference your own writing. A website can even help motivate you to write more! A site can also help boost your resume. Getting started is as simple as A. getting a domain, B. finding a writing platform, and C. just get started writing and building!

If you’re concerned about not having the technical chops, or not having anything interesting to put on your site — stop right there. Don’t over think it. Your site doesn’t need to be perfect (especially in the beginning), it doesn’t need to have any specific features and it doesn’t need to have perfectly clean writing. Just put some HTML up and be you.

Once your site is up, congrats! You are one of us. You and your site are automagically part of a network of web communities — weird and wonderful places — with so much to see, things to share, people to meet and relationships to grow. Here’s some fun ways to explore and participate: join a webring (like the smallweb subway), add some octothorpes, and/or join the Record-Relay.

For one to invest the time and energy into a site, and into these communities, it’s fair to wonder, what does the future look like? For personal websites, and for an Internet that is hospitable towards them, some suggest that it may all disappear. Maybe. But I think not. Sure, things will change as they always have. But so much has continued to persist, regardless of the tectonics of technology. Set your sights not on the web of the past. Come build the web you want to see, now and into the future. Long live the (indie)web!

On that note, here’s some cool stuff you can do with your site. To make it yours — forever.

  • Back it up
  • Change the color of the hyperlinks
  • Encourage others to explore
  • Answer the webmaster questionnaire
  • Publish some slash pages (like /photo)
  • Make your site cringey
  • Go cookieless
  • Write a novel
  • Add yourself to the Internet Phonebook
  • Create an RSS feed for your site
Small Web Finds and Features

The web is chock-full of interesting, delightful and amazing li’l goodies. Here’s some cool things I’ve found recently… (Make sure to bookmark the web-things you find that you like, otherwise they may slip away — like a dandelion in the wind.)

  • ascii.rest features a huge catalog of beautiful ascii animations
  • growing explores a lot of interesting concepts through interactive visualizations
  • bimb.ooo is a neat, cozy li’l place to put some things of yours on the web
  • NeverStream is a fun parody of Netflix
  • shen has a really neat and colorful site you should check out!
  • 4x down detector is the downdetector for downdetector’s downdetector (I think I got that right?…)
  • Figuring out time zone conversions can be hell 🔥
  • Let Sam know what he’s missing out on with Ram-Altman 🤭
  • piewpiew by Kristofer is an excellent personal site
  • I’m not really sure what to make of the site cloudlord.management, but I’m drawn to it for some reason
  • Destroy any website you want here 💥
Fediverse

Over these 50 issues of writing Scrolls, I think I’ve made it quite clear where I stand on the “Fediverse”, and its importance in the wider social media landscape. Does it now, or will it ever have true mainstream appeal? Who knows. I certainly don’t. It has had, and continues to have certain drawbacks that prevent your “average” social media user from wanting to invest their time and energy here, and that’s ok. The beauty of the Fediverse is that it can survive and be a great place regardless of MAU. The Fediverse is anything but stagnant, even in the absence of steep user adoption, the developer community continues to build and make really neat contributions to this space. It continues to be a really exciting place to watch and write about.

This said, my plan with Scrolls moving forward is to not have a dedicated section for writing about and sharing things that are specifically about the Fediverse. I think a lot of other journalists, bloggers and Fedi personalities do a much better and more thorough job of that. This doesn’t mean I won’t be there though, following along with what everyone is doing as I have been for the last 5 years or so. In fact, I get most of my “interesting-things-to-share” from my social feeds on the Fediverse, and I’m sure to continue writing about and sharing those things as I come across them. ✌️

Cybersecurity

Security is relentless. Security is hard (lol). Conspiracies abound in the infosec world. But does it have to be annoying? Probably… but maybe not. Of course the best advice is maybe to just avoid computers altogether 😄.

For all of us who can’t just disappear into the woods, here’s some interesting sec-related links/resources…

  • 0xrefs: an interactive cheat sheet of offensive-security commands
  • Ever wanted to learn DMARC but found it too dry a subject? DMARC Starfighter may be your answer.

The EU should go big and hard over border IT failure ( permalink ) If the EU has a future as a political project, it will have to be as a living, breathing repudiation of Ronald Reagan's maxim that "The nine most terrifying words are 'I’m from the government and I’m here to help.'" In other words, the EU's future depends on its ability to publicly perform competence and capacity . The EU is a technocratic project, and the one trait technocrats must show is undeniable technical competence. This is the secret of Zohran Mamdani's administration: being seen in public, constantly fixing things that are broken, and making things that work even better: https://www.nyc.gov/content/100days/pages/ This is a goal that is largely incompatible with charismatic megaprojects, and unfortunately, that's the EU's favorite kind of project: something big and splashy and worthy of the extreme effort required to squeeze anything through the Byzantine EU approvals process: https://backofmind.substack.com/p/the-planning-system-system Even more unfortunate is that the EU isn't just a technocratic project, it's a neoliberal technocratic project, so when it does embark on one of these megaprojects, it almost always does so as a "public-private partnership" that sees vast sums transferred to private firms to carry out public works. Since megaprojects are always over-budget and behind schedule, this creates the perfect conditions for absolute banditry, in which private companies overcharge and underdeliver, and before you know it, you're billions poorer and back in Reagan's "most terrifying words" territory. Here's a perfect example: Schengen is a region of (mostly) EU countries who have opened their borders to one another. Once you've crossed into any of the 29 Schengen countries, you can generally stroll into any of the other Schengen countries without showing a passport or having your bags searched: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Area This is an awfully convenient system…once you're inside of Schengen. But the Schengen agreement means that each of the member states is trusting the other states to manage a common border, a task that is made all the more urgent by the fascist international, whose far right parties have whipped millions of otherwise sensible people into a xenophobic frenzy over migration. This has led to a kind of bureaucracy-shifting exercise that removed all the complexity from inter-Schengen borders and concentrated it at the borders between each Schengen country and the rest of the world. Under this system, every Schengen country must accurately log the passage of every non-Schengen person into and out of the region. If you fly into Rome and out of Helsinki, then both the Italian and Finnish border guards must be cognizant of that fact and correctly log it. To make matters even more complex, visa-free access to Schengen is restricted to 90 days in the entire region out of any given 180-day period. For example, last month I was stranded in Frankfurt overnight thanks to a canceled flight. If I had totaled 90 days out of the previous 180 in Schengen, I would not have been allowed out of the airport's secure area until midnight, when the day ticked over and now my total would be 89 days out of 180 (thankfully, I was able to leave the airport and stay in a crummy airport hotel instead of sleeping on the floor of the airport). To manage this system, the EU commissioned several giant IT companies to build a networked, biometric border-crossing system. Under the spec, the system would track those 90-day windows for everyone who passed in and out of Schengen, using fast fingerprint/facial scans to move people swiftly through any border crossing in the 29 Schengen countries. It is a gross understatement to call this system behind schedule and overbudget. The Entry Exit System (EES) was supposed to roll out in 2022, but it didn't go live until October 2025 – whereupon it completely, catastrophically failed, despite having doubled its budget: https://www.theregister.com/security/2025/09/25/eu-to-register-fingerprints-faces-for-short-stay-visitors/1141501 It's been more than a year since EES went live and it is still an absolute disaster. Travelers arriving or leaving Schengen are frequently hit with multi-hour delays. Numerous flights have been canceled, and airlines who fly without waiting for passengers in the immobile, snaking lines must rebook those passengers and endure their wrath. At major airports, it's routine for border guards to simply suspend their use of the EES system, waving through passengers without registering them in the system: https://eesqueue.com/ EES is a disaster for aviation operations and border crossings. Any true reckoning with its costs wouldn't stop at the hundreds of millions of euros paid to private sector partners, but also the hundreds of millions more in costs borne by travelers and airlines, to say nothing of the opportunity costs paid by travelers who made it through the checkpoints through the brute-force expedient of leaving hours of extra time for a broken border formality. Which means that the disaster isn't merely a logistics crisis, it's also a credibility and legitimacy crisis. A year (and counting) of headlines about this dismal failure of an IT system have further eroded public confidence in the EU's technical capabilities. How can the EU claim to be a sound technocratic steward of the vast administrative challenges facing a 27-state transnational entity when it can't make the computers work, and when those failures produce the very visible phenomenon of gigantic queues of fuming passengers? (Not just fuming, either: when I was stuck in Frankfurt last month, there were at least half a dozen travelers who were loudly sobbing as they realized they were going to miss their flights home.) The contractors for this nonfunctional, grossly overbudget, years-late project (IBM, Atos, and Leonardo) are now being sued, but – incredibly – the EU kept the lawsuit a secret. The only reason we know that IBM, Atos, and Leonardo are facing the EU in court is that the FT spotted an inconspicuous note in the annual financial statements for eu-LISA (the European Union Agency for the Operational Management of Large-Scale IT Systems in the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice): https://www.eulisa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/fy2025_eu-lisa_faa.pdf The secrecy of this lawsuit is another mark against the EU's technical competence. Any administrative system that relies on private-sector outsourcing to carry out its essential projects must have a core competency in overseeing those private partners, which includes loudly and mercilessly punishing those partners when they fail. By keeping the suit secret, the eu-LISA telegraphs that the fault lies with the EU, not with IBM, Atos, and Leonardo, who racked up hundreds of millions in fees and delivered a very broken, very late system that ruined the days (and voyages) of millions of travelers: https://www.theregister.com/public-sector/2026/11/10/eus-212m-border-it-project-lands-ibm-and-atos-in-legal-water/5308669 Anyone who's ever watched a large IT consultancy firm run one of these large projects knows that this kind of bungling and gouging is par for the course. The old adage that "no one ever got fired for buying IBM" does not mean that IBM can deliver a functional IT system; it means that when IBM fucks up your project, you can escape any blame because they're the gold standard for fucking up. Every time the EU lets these companies off the hook without a big, splashy public reckoning, they reinforce Reagan's "most terrifying words" maxim. As Voltaire wrote, "Sometimes you must execute an admiral to encourage the others." The EU should be dragging these IT bandits in public, every day, naming the top executives who oversaw the project. They should do this every time there's a problem with a private contractor, but EES is especially ripe for this kind of treatment. That's because EES whacked a ton of rich, powerful people . Those are the sort of people who might otherwise run cover for giant, bungling, wildly profitable IT consulting firms, but who are also the most reliably pissy, vindictive dickheads about anything that affects them personally. These are the sorts of people you definitely want inside your tent, pissing out – but in hiding its lawsuit under a bushel, the EU has invited them to stand outside its tent and piss in. items.title: Hackers Can Exploit SAP PROXYGATE and ICM2SHELL Flaws for Unauthorized Full System Access
items.summary: SAP has released fixes for PROXYGATE and ICM2SHELL, critical security flaws that could let attackers take control of SAP systems without signing in. Disclosed during the November 10, 2026, Security Patch Day , the vulnerabilities carry maximum CVSS scores of 10.0 and affect core components used across business applications. Onapsis Research Labs discovered and reported both issues. The flaws allow attackers with network access to run operating system commands under the adm account, which owns the SAP installation. This gives them control over the affected SAP environment, though it does not automatically mean root access to the underlying server. Business data, stored credentials, application settings, and system availability could all be at risk. PROXYGATE Targets SAP Gateway Trust PROXYGATE, tracked as CVE-2026-89103, affects the SAP Gateway, a component that handles communication between SAP systems and external programs. Unlike problems caused by weak gateway rules, this kernel vulnerability can remain exploitable even when administrators have secured the commonly checked secinfo and reginfo access control lists. The weakness lies in how the gateway decides whether a request comes from a trusted internal server. When its proxy policy allows the connection, crafted requests can make an outside attacker appear internal. The gateway then accepts requests that its existing rules permit for trusted systems, potentially starting commands chosen by the attacker. Exposure depends on the less commonly reviewed prxyinfo proxy access list and related settings. A restrictive policy blocks exploitation from untrusted networks, while permissive or missing rules can leave systems exposed. The affected gateway runs across ABAP, AS Java, dual-stack, and standalone deployments, widening the scope beyond a single application type. ICM2SHELL Affects Web Traffic Handling According to the Onapsis ICM2SHELL advisory , the second flaw involves memory corruption in shared SAP kernel code that processes WebSocket traffic. CVE-2026-76964 affects Internet Communication Manager, while CVE-2026-89126 affects SAP Web Dispatcher, including its SAP HANA XS component. Cybersecurity News’s November SAP patch coverage also identifies the critical ICM issue. Attackers who can reach an affected HTTP or HTTPS port could corrupt process memory, execute commands, or crash the service. WebSocket support is enabled by default, even where organizations do not actively use it. Some SAP S/4HANA services accept WebSocket connections without authentication, removing the need for stolen credentials or user interaction. Onapsis reported no observed exploitation of either vulnerability at publication. That does not establish that all environments are safe. Earlier, unrelated SAP attacks show the potential business impact, including the NetWeaver compromise used to deploy Auto-Color malware . Those incidents are separate from PROXYGATE and ICM2SHELL. The PROXYGATE technical advisory warns that patching alone may not resolve exposure. Most affected kernel releases require the relevant update plus gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1 . Administrators must also restrict permissive prxyinfo rules. Unsupported kernels need an upgrade to a maintained, compatible release, and changes must cover every application server. SAP addresses ICM2SHELL through Security Notes 3778530 and 3778556. Teams should prioritize exposed Web Dispatcher and ICM services, then verify fixes across their SAP estate. Gateway access should be limited to hosts that need it. Network restrictions reduce exposure, but they do not replace complete patching and required configuration changes. The flaws allow attackers with network access to run operating system commands under the adm account, which owns the SAP installation.

This gives them control over the affected SAP environment, though it does not automatically mean root access to the underlying server. Business data, stored credentials, application settings, and system availability could all be at risk.

PROXYGATE, tracked as CVE-2026-89103, affects the SAP Gateway, a component that handles communication between SAP systems and external programs. Unlike problems caused by weak gateway rules, this kernel vulnerability can remain exploitable even when administrators have secured the commonly checked secinfo and reginfo access control lists.

The weakness lies in how the gateway decides whether a request comes from a trusted internal server. When its proxy policy allows the connection, crafted requests can make an outside attacker appear internal. The affected gateway runs across ABAP, AS Java, dual-stack, and standalone deployments, widening the scope beyond a single application type.

ICM2SHELL Affects Web Traffic Handling

According to the Onapsis ICM2SHELL advisory, the second flaw involves memory corruption in shared SAP kernel code that processes WebSocket traffic. CVE-2026-76964 affects Internet Communication Manager, while CVE-2026-89126 affects SAP Web Dispatcher, including its SAP HANA XS component. Cybersecurity News’s November SAP patch coverage also identifies the critical ICM issue.

Attackers who can reach an affected HTTP or HTTPS port could corrupt process memory, execute commands, or crash the service. WebSocket support is enabled by default, even where organizations do not actively use it.

Some SAP S/4HANA services accept WebSocket connections without authentication, removing the need for stolen credentials or user interaction.

Onapsis reported no observed exploitation of either vulnerability at publication. That does not establish that all environments are safe. Earlier, unrelated SAP attacks show the potential business impact, including the NetWeaver compromise used to deploy Auto-Color malware. Those incidents are separate from PROXYGATE and ICM2SHELL.

The PROXYGATE technical advisory warns that patching alone may not resolve exposure. Most affected kernel releases require the relevant update plus gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1. Administrators must also restrict permissive prxyinfo rules. Unsupported kernels need an upgrade to a maintained, compatible release, and changes must cover every application server.

SAP addresses ICM2SHELL through Security Notes 3778530 and 3778556. Teams should prioritize exposed Web Dispatcher and ICM services, then verify fixes across their SAP estate.

Gateway access should be limited to hosts that need it. Network restrictions reduce exposure, but they do not replace complete patching and required configuration changes.
