items.title: Railway Reveals How Hackers Used AI Agents to Steal API Keys and Rack Up $740,000 in Charges
items.summary: Railway has revealed how an attacker used AI agents, a build system flaw, and cloud access mistakes to steal customer secrets and generate an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized charges. Its November 10 report describes an attack that crossed several internal systems while engineers worked to close multiple entry points. The findings expand on the earlier Railway security incident disclosure . Up to 1.85% of workspaces, roughly 100,000, could have had environment variables decrypted. This is an upper limit, not a confirmed count of workspaces with stolen keys, because available logs identify affected environments rather than individual secrets. The first successful exploit occurred at 07:28 UTC on October 20. A previously unknown flaw let the attacker partially escape the build system’s file isolation and read files on its host machine. Those files exposed a credential that build servers used to access internal services and push completed images. That credential carried more trust than intended. Railway’s Temporal task system accepted it, allowing the attacker to read stored histories from 353 builds, including secrets. Access to cached repository snapshots also exposed Railway’s internal codebase, giving AI agents a map to search for weaknesses and test several routes at once. Railway said the attacker used models with safety limits removed through an agent framework similar to ARTEX. Engineers detected unusual registry API calls at 13:58 UTC and later replaced the stolen credential. However, the copied codebase helped the attacker find another route after Railway blocked the initial entry point. Cloud Trust Error Exposed Encrypted Secrets According to Railway’s detailed incident report , an incorrect OpenID Connect, or OIDC, trust configuration exposed a short-lived cloud credential at 03:26 UTC on October 21. The attacker used it to retrieve internal credentials and an SSH private key, then entered a machine responsible for coordinating customer workloads. That machine had network access to the production database and another credential able to authorize secret decryption. The attacker retrieved encrypted variables and used Railway’s key management service to decrypt some values. This was credential abuse, not evidence of broken encryption. Database queries specifically searched for AI provider key names. Railway believes stolen keys reached services that relay or resell AI access, potentially supporting model distillation . However, it has not established whether the intruder operated those services. Wiz’s “Black October” investigation documents the wider credential theft pattern but does not independently attribute the Railway breach. The stolen data included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, which Railway reset. Investigators found no Railway account logins using stolen credentials and no evidence of customer database access. The resulting charges reflect LLMjacking attacks , where criminals use stolen credentials to consume paid AI services at victims’ expense. Railway estimated unauthorized spending reached approximately $740,000. Railway revoked credentials, rebuilt internal systems, and restored builds for every plan by October 22. Its preliminary report outlined immediate recovery steps. Customers should rotate potentially exposed secrets, review provider usage, and report fraudulent charges. Railway says it is working with providers on refunds and will cover breach-related charges where providers decline reimbursement, rather than leaving affected customers to absorb those losses. Sage: AI for Assumed-Breach Operations, Built Into Mythic
items.summary: TL;DR: Sage is an open-source AI assistant that lives inside Mythic. You tell it what you’re trying to accomplish, it works out the commands across whichever Mythic agents you have, and every action waits for your approval before it reaches a target. It keeps the operation’s memory in BloodHound and in an Engagement State Ledger, where a gain counts as achieved only when real Mythic evidence proves it. Install it like any other Mythic agent, start in read-only conversation mode, and move to supervised mode when you’re ready. The Problem Sage is For An offensive operation starts with almost no knowledge of the environment, and every command after is about learning it. As the operation goes on, the amount of returned information grows faster than any one person can hold in their head and we’re usually looking for one specific thing. I suspect we leave a lot on the table when it comes to correlating what we learned in week one with what we see in week three. Then there’s the typing. I tell friends and family that watching me hack would be anticlimactic: a lot of mistyped commands and a lot of help to remember an argument. Many operations also use more than one agent, so you’re remembering which agent has which command, what its arguments are, and what quirks it has, while keeping up with what the rest of the team has already run. A lot of the rest is smaller but frequent maintenance or tasks. Before you can run a tool, someone has to upload it to Mythic and remember what they called it. Sage will automatically check to see if the binary is already uploaded in Mythic. If it isn’t, Sage will auto discover any binaries in its tools folder, upload it to Mythic, and then use it to accomplish the action. Technique knowledge works the same way. Every operator has techniques they know cold and techniques they’ve run twice in their career. Sage ships with over 200 tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) playbooks that describe how each technique is done and what to check first, so the operator who is less familiar with an attack gets a worked plan to review and approve, and learns the technique along the way. Sage takes that load off the operator. With Sage, you tell Mythic what you’re trying to accomplish, Sage writes the commands, and you still approve every step. The operator spends their time on judgment, the AI does the bookkeeping, and the decisions get better because the full picture of the operation is in front of both of them. Why I Built it I learn by building. When I wanted to understand command and control (C2) applications, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3, I wrote Merlin . Shellcode runners became go-shellcode , Windows post-exploitation techniques became oddments , and COFF loading became go-coff (which I never finished). When AI started changing our industry, I took courses on building neural networks from scratch and on working with LLMs, and then I needed to build something real. That became Sage. I made the first commit in April 2025 (five months after Anthropic released the Model Context Protocol (MCP)) and within a week, Sage could connect to any MCP server and use its tools. 18 months and more than 400 commits later, most of that time has gone into the parts that make an AI teammate trustworthy: who holds authority, what counts as proof, and what Sage remembers. The other part was deciding that Go wasn’t the best language, converting to Python, and deciding which framework to use. At SpecterOps, we primarily use Mythic for our operations and I wanted AI to be as frictionless for our team as possible. Nearly all of an operator’s context about an engagement comes to them through Mythic, so I thought that is where the AI should live too. I’ve been advised by others that Sage should be its own application that connects to Mythic. I disagree. Every extra tool is one more thing to install, connect, and switch between, and keeping everything in one cohesive ecosystem has real value. There’s a second reason Sage lives in Mythic and nowhere else. Much of the attention on offensive AI right now is on the perimeter: what happens when someone points an AI agent swarm at your external network. That’s a fair question, and I expect it to become a routine part of vulnerability management in the future. The work SpecterOps has always found most valuable starts after initial access. Assumed-breach operations ask what an adversary can reach from a foothold, and that is where BloodHound earns its keep. Before BloodHound, operators did the credential shuffle by hand and sketched attack paths on whiteboards. After it, they could see Active Directory and they delivered more for it. Sage is built on that same substrate. It needs a live callback to do any work, because it starts where the operator already is: inside the network, with a graph of what is reachable from there. So much of what we do at SpecterOps comes back to demystifying adversary tradecraft and I wanted Sage to do the same for AI in offensive work: built in the open, inside the tool our operators already use, so anyone can see what it does, how it decides, and where it stops. What Sage Is Sage is an AI harness that runs inside Mythic v4 as a native chat container. It sits on the control plane next to Mythic itself, and every action it takes against a target goes through a Mythic payload callback, the same way yours do. The chat looks like the AI chat apps people already know, and the whole team in the Mythic operation can see the conversation and join in. Under the chat is a multi-agent system using the supervisor pattern. A supervisor agent directs six specialist agents that read the same callbacks, tasks, credentials, files, and BloodHound attack paths you do. My goal is simple: whatever you can do in Mythic during an assessment, Sage should be able to help you do. Most of the offensive-security knowledge lives in the harness, in its tools, capabilities, prompts, and tradecraft files. That means Sage works with whichever provider you choose, and a general-purpose model can do the job. In early lab testing, general-purpose models got further using Sage than they did on their own; the next post covers what that testing does and doesn’t show. Working With Sage From Detailed Command to Stated Intent Today, one or more operators issue individual commands to their C2 agents, one task at a time. In military terms, that is detailed command: every task typed by hand. Sage lets you work closer to mission command. You state your intent and the limits on it in your own words, and Sage turns that one intent into the work streams behind it: which agent has the right command, which callback to run it on, what the arguments should be, and how the result fits with everything the operation already knows. You stop managing individual commands and now manage objectives. Sage still proposes one step at a time and you approve it. Mythic still runs every action and keeps the record. Sage issues the commands and you stay in charge. Three Modes Every Sage chat channel runs in one of three modes that decides what Sage is allowed to do: Conversation (the default) is read-only. Ask about the operation, review the graph, or plan, with no risk of Sage acting in the target environment. Supervised is where I expect real operators to spend their time. Every guarded action (issuing a task, running a capability, creating a payload, adding a credential) stops as a native Mythic approval card before it runs. Approval is default-deny, and you have three choices: Accept runs exactly the prepared action Reject skips it Respond sends your own guidance, which Sage takes into account before proposing again. Autonomous works toward an objective without per-action approval. It is experimental; more on that below. A supervised channel can pursue a stated objective across turns. Sage still proposes one guarded action at a time and waits for your approval, but the objective and the evidence gathered so far carry across approvals, rejections, and hand-offs between specialist agents. When BloodHound has data and the question is about an attack path, Sage asks the graph for a path to the objective before it proposes any tasking. This is where stating your intent pays off. The authority modes page covers the details. Sage in supervised mode, autonomous solve off. From a foothold, the operator asks for administrative control of north.sevenkingdoms.local. Sage collects BloodHound data, then turns write access on a GPO into Domain Admin. The operator approves each step. Sage Works With Any Mythic Agent It was important to me from the start that Sage worked with any Mythic agent, because some of the AI tooling I saw being published only worked with one. So Sage learns how to call each agent from Mythic itself. It asks Mythic which payload types are installed, lists each one’s commands, and fetches each command’s parameters, types, and parameter groups from Mythic’s own schema. It confirms the command is loaded on the callback it plans to use. Before anything is tasked, Sage checks the proposed arguments against that schema and repairs what it can, and for registered executables it requires the model to fill in a strict schema. In supervised mode, that prepared action is exactly what you see on the approval card. Memory That Outlasts the Conversation AI is good at correlating what is in front of it, but long, multi-hop, multi-day operations are harder. Published work shows the same thing. PentestGPT ( arXiv:2308.06782 ) found that LLMs handle individual pentest sub-tasks well but struggle to keep an integrated picture of the whole test. Incalmo ( arXiv:2501.16466 ) found that existing LLM offense systems succeeded in three of 40 multi-host networks and reached 37 of 40 once a separate service tracked context and acquired assets. More generally, “Lost in the Middle” ( arXiv:2307.03172 ) shows models use information less reliably when it sits in the middle of a long context. So Sage keeps its memory of the operation outside the model, in two places. BloodHound holds the graph. The Engagement State Ledger records each capability or credential the operation has gained, with the Mythic evidence behind it. Sage reads every task in the Mythic operation, whoever ran it, and adds a row when a verifier finds a new gain. Failed attempts stay in Mythic’s task history. All chats in the operation share one ledger, and the agents that plan and run tasks get a fresh view of it on every model call, so Sage knows what the operation has already proven even in a new conversation. See the Engagement State Ledger . What Else is in the Box The docs cover everything; these are the pieces I’d want you to know about first: BloodHound at the center. Sage connects to BloodHound over MCP using Matthew Nickerson’s project and has a dedicated BloodHound agent for finding attack paths. Conversation and supervised chats work without BloodHound; they’re just less useful. Autonomous mode refuses to run without it. ( BloodHound guide ) Any model provider. Sage is built on LangGraph and LangChain’s model integrations. The channel offers OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Anthropic, and Ollama, and the openai provider means any endpoint that speaks the OpenAI API , from OpenAI or anyone else. At SpecterOps, we point it at an internal LiteLLM instance that fronts many providers. ( Chat configuration ) Your tradecraft, your tools. Sage ships over 200 TTP files covering Active Directory attack paths, ADCS abuse, ACL chains, and more, and you can add your own. Drop tool binaries such as Rubeus or Certify into Sage’s tools folder and Sage stages them into Mythic when the work calls for them, then runs them through a callback. Each agent’s prompt is a Markdown file you can edit as well. Changes will apply to the next new chat, with no restart. ( Tools and capabilities ) Full visibility. Sage keeps its runtime state, including LangGraph checkpoints and every approval decision, in a SQLite database. The Engagement State Ledger lives in the same database and can be exported as JSON, so the whole engagement can be archived at the end. Arize Phoenix is built in, so you can review every agent trace. ( Observability , runtime state ) Also included: a background Sage Watcher that reviews the operation’s Mythic records and posts findings to a #sage-findings channel without ever tasking a callback (still early; I want operators to tell me whether it earns its place) ( findings watcher ); additional control-plane MCP servers such as Nemesis ( MCP servers ); and a Max Steps guardrail (default 200 model calls per chat session, 0 for unlimited) that stops a runaway session and tells you why and how to continue. A handful of slash commands give you direct control without a model call. The ones you’ll use most: /state to show the engagement state ledger, retract a row, or cite Mythic task and credential IDs for Sage to verify, /mode to switch the channel’s mode.. The full list also covers MCP servers, BloodHound, the watcher, and a local sandbox. Three Design Rules You’re in charge. Talk to Sage however you’d talk with your fellow operators, but the decision to act is always yours. Guarded actions default to deny until you approve them, and each guarded tool requires a matching Mythic bot-token scope, so a tool your channel’s token can’t use is disabled before the conversation starts. items.summary_html:
TL;DR: Sage is an open-source AI assistant that lives inside Mythic. You tell it what you’re trying to accomplish, it works out the commands across whichever Mythic agents you have, and every action waits for your approval before it reaches a target. It keeps the operation’s memory in BloodHound and in an Engagement State Ledger, where a gain counts as achieved only when real Mythic evidence proves it. Install it like any other Mythic agent, start in read-only conversation mode, and move to supervised mode when you’re ready.

The Problem Sage is For

An offensive operation starts with almost no knowledge of the environment, and every command after is about learning it. As the operation goes on, the amount of returned information grows faster than any one person can hold in their head and we’re usually looking for one specific thing. I suspect we leave a lot on the table when it comes to correlating what we learned in week one with what we see in week three.

Then there’s the typing. I tell friends and family that watching me hack would be anticlimactic: a lot of mistyped commands and a lot of help to remember an argument. Many operations also use more than one agent, so you’re remembering which agent has which command, what its arguments are, and what quirks it has, while keeping up with what the rest of the team has already run.

A lot of the rest is smaller but frequent maintenance or tasks. Before you can run a tool, someone has to upload it to Mythic and remember what they called it. Sage will automatically check to see if the binary is already uploaded in Mythic. If it isn’t, Sage will auto discover any binaries in its tools folder, upload it to Mythic, and then use it to accomplish the action. 

Technique knowledge works the same way. Every operator has techniques they know cold and techniques they’ve run twice in their career. Sage ships with over 200 tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) playbooks that describe how each technique is done and what to check first, so the operator who is less familiar with an attack gets a worked plan to review and approve, and learns the technique along the way.

Sage takes that load off the operator. With Sage, you tell Mythic what you’re trying to accomplish, Sage writes the commands, and you still approve every step. The operator spends their time on judgment, the AI does the bookkeeping, and the decisions get better because the full picture of the operation is in front of both of them.

Why I Built it

I learn by building. When I wanted to understand command and control (C2) applications, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3, I wrote Merlin. Shellcode runners became go-shellcode, Windows post-exploitation techniques became oddments, and COFF loading became go-coff (which I never finished). When AI started changing our industry, I took courses on building neural networks from scratch and on working with LLMs, and then I needed to build something real. That became Sage. I made the first commit in April 2025 (five months after Anthropic released the Model Context Protocol (MCP)) and within a week, Sage could connect to any MCP server and use its tools. 18 months and more than 400 commits later, most of that time has gone into the parts that make an AI teammate trustworthy: who holds authority, what counts as proof, and what Sage remembers. The other part was deciding that Go wasn’t the best language, converting to Python, and deciding which framework to use.

At SpecterOps, we primarily use Mythic for our operations and I wanted AI to be as frictionless for our team as possible. Nearly all of an operator’s context about an engagement comes to them through Mythic, so I thought that is where the AI should live too. I’ve been advised by others that Sage should be its own application that connects to Mythic. I disagree. Every extra tool is one more thing to install, connect, and switch between, and keeping everything in one cohesive ecosystem has real value.

There’s a second reason Sage lives in Mythic and nowhere else. Much of the attention on offensive AI right now is on the perimeter: what happens when someone points an AI agent swarm at your external network. That’s a fair question, and I expect it to become a routine part of vulnerability management in the future. The work SpecterOps has always found most valuable starts after initial access. Assumed-breach operations ask what an adversary can reach from a foothold, and that is where BloodHound earns its keep. Before BloodHound, operators did the credential shuffle by hand and sketched attack paths on whiteboards. After it, they could see Active Directory and they delivered more for it. Sage is built on that same substrate. It needs a live callback to do any work, because it starts where the operator already is: inside the network, with a graph of what is reachable from there.

So much of what we do at SpecterOps comes back to demystifying adversary tradecraft and I wanted Sage to do the same for AI in offensive work: built in the open, inside the tool our operators already use, so anyone can see what it does, how it decides, and where it stops.

What Sage Is

Sage is an AI harness that runs inside Mythic v4 as a native chat container. It sits on the control plane next to Mythic itself, and every action it takes against a target goes through a Mythic payload callback, the same way yours do. The chat looks like the AI chat apps people already know, and the whole team in the Mythic operation can see the conversation and join in.

Under the chat is a multi-agent system using the supervisor pattern. A supervisor agent directs six specialist agents that read the same callbacks, tasks, credentials, files, and BloodHound attack paths you do. My goal is simple: whatever you can do in Mythic during an assessment, Sage should be able to help you do.

Most of the offensive-security knowledge lives in the harness, in its tools, capabilities, prompts, and tradecraft files. That means Sage works with whichever provider you choose, and a general-purpose model can do the job. In early lab testing, general-purpose models got further using Sage than they did on their own; the next post covers what that testing does and doesn’t show.

Working With Sage From Detailed Command to Stated Intent

Today, one or more operators issue individual commands to their C2 agents, one task at a time. In military terms, that is detailed command: every task typed by hand.

Sage lets you work closer to mission command. You state your intent and the limits on it in your own words, and Sage turns that one intent into the work streams behind it: which agent has the right command, which callback to run it on, what the arguments should be, and how the result fits with everything the operation already knows. You stop managing individual commands and now manage objectives. Sage still proposes one step at a time and you approve it. Mythic still runs every action and keeps the record. Sage issues the commands and you stay in charge.

Three Modes

Every Sage chat channel runs in one of three modes that decides what Sage is allowed to do:

  • Conversation (the default) is read-only. Ask about the operation, review the graph, or plan, with no risk of Sage acting in the target environment.
  • Supervised is where I expect real operators to spend their time. Every guarded action (issuing a task, running a capability, creating a payload, adding a credential) stops as a native Mythic approval card before it runs. Approval is default-deny, and you have three choices:
    • Accept runs exactly the prepared action
    • Reject skips it
    • Respond sends your own guidance, which Sage takes into account before proposing again.
  • Autonomous works toward an objective without per-action approval. It is experimental; more on that below.

A supervised channel can pursue a stated objective across turns. Sage still proposes one guarded action at a time and waits for your approval, but the objective and the evidence gathered so far carry across approvals, rejections, and hand-offs between specialist agents. When BloodHound has data and the question is about an attack path, Sage asks the graph for a path to the objective before it proposes any tasking. This is where stating your intent pays off. The authority modes page covers the details.

Sage in supervised mode, autonomous solve off. From a foothold, the operator asks for administrative control of north.sevenkingdoms.local. Sage collects BloodHound data, then turns write access on a GPO into Domain Admin. The operator approves each step.

Sage Works With Any Mythic Agent

It was important to me from the start that Sage worked with any Mythic agent, because some of the AI tooling I saw being published only worked with one. So Sage learns how to call each agent from Mythic itself. It asks Mythic which payload types are installed, lists each one’s commands, and fetches each command’s parameters, types, and parameter groups from Mythic’s own schema. It confirms the command is loaded on the callback it plans to use. Before anything is tasked, Sage checks the proposed arguments against that schema and repairs what it can, and for registered executables it requires the model to fill in a strict schema. In supervised mode, that prepared action is exactly what you see on the approval card.

Memory That Outlasts the Conversation

AI is good at correlating what is in front of it, but long, multi-hop, multi-day operations are harder. Published work shows the same thing. PentestGPT (arXiv:2308.06782) found that LLMs handle individual pentest sub-tasks well but struggle to keep an integrated picture of the whole test. Incalmo (arXiv:2501.16466) found that existing LLM offense systems succeeded in three of 40 multi-host networks and reached 37 of 40 once a separate service tracked context and acquired assets. More generally, “Lost in the Middle” (arXiv:2307.03172) shows models use information less reliably when it sits in the middle of a long context.

So Sage keeps its memory of the operation outside the model, in two places. BloodHound holds the graph. The Engagement State Ledger records each capability or credential the operation has gained, with the Mythic evidence behind it. Sage reads every task in the Mythic operation, whoever ran it, and adds a row when a verifier finds a new gain. Failed attempts stay in Mythic’s task history. All chats in the operation share one ledger, and the agents that plan and run tasks get a fresh view of it on every model call, so Sage knows what the operation has already proven even in a new conversation. See the Engagement State Ledger.

What Else is in the Box

The docs cover everything; these are the pieces I’d want you to know about first:

  • BloodHound at the center. Sage connects to BloodHound over MCP using Matthew Nickerson’s project and has a dedicated BloodHound agent for finding attack paths. Conversation and supervised chats work without BloodHound; they’re just less useful. Autonomous mode refuses to run without it. (BloodHound guide)
  • Any model provider. Sage is built on LangGraph and LangChain’s model integrations. The channel offers OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Anthropic, and Ollama, and the openai provider means any endpoint that speaks the OpenAI API, from OpenAI or anyone else. At SpecterOps, we point it at an internal LiteLLM instance that fronts many providers. (Chat configuration)
  • Your tradecraft, your tools. Sage ships over 200 TTP files covering Active Directory attack paths, ADCS abuse, ACL chains, and more, and you can add your own. Drop tool binaries such as Rubeus or Certify into Sage’s tools folder and Sage stages them into Mythic when the work calls for them, then runs them through a callback. Each agent’s prompt is a Markdown file you can edit as well. Changes will apply to the next new chat, with no restart. (Tools and capabilities)
  • Full visibility. Sage keeps its runtime state, including LangGraph checkpoints and every approval decision, in a SQLite database. The Engagement State Ledger lives in the same database and can be exported as JSON, so the whole engagement can be archived at the end. Arize Phoenix is built in, so you can review every agent trace. (Observability, runtime state)

Also included: a background Sage Watcher that reviews the operation’s Mythic records and posts findings to a #sage-findings channel without ever tasking a callback (still early; I want operators to tell me whether it earns its place) (findings watcher); additional control-plane MCP servers such as Nemesis (MCP servers); and a Max Steps guardrail (default 200 model calls per chat session, 0 for unlimited) that stops a runaway session and tells you why and how to continue.

A handful of slash commands give you direct control without a model call. The ones you’ll use most: /state to show the engagement state ledger, retract a row, or cite Mythic task and credential IDs for Sage to verify, /mode to switch the channel’s mode.. The full list also covers MCP servers, BloodHound, the watcher, and a local sandbox.

Three Design Rules

You’re in charge. Talk to Sage however you’d talk with your fellow operators, but the decision to act is always yours. Guarded actions default to deny until you approve them, and each guarded tool requires a matching Mythic bot-token scope, so a tool your channel’s token can’t use is disabled before the conversation starts. The one exception is Autonomous mode, where you grant authority once, up front, by binding the objective, and Sage acts without asking again.

Let code do what code does well. AI is great at deciding what to do next, and plain code is better at doing it the same way every time. Where Sage acts on its own, it uses programmed capabilities. Each capability states its intent, the preconditions that must already be proven, the effects it should produce, and a verifier that checks those effects against real Mythic output. The model can choose a capability, but code turns it into concrete Mythic commands, so the command syntax always comes from code. Sage ships 15 of these. A few examples:

  • collect-graph: from a foothold, collect Active Directory data and ingest it into BloodHound
  • gpo-controlled-system-exec: turn write control of a group policy object (GPO) into verified SYSTEM execution
  • adcs-esc-certificate-enroll: follow a graph-proven ADCS escalation path to a certificate
  • dcsync-account: with proven replication rights, retrieve a specific account’s credentials

The rest cover Kerberos tickets and context, managed local admin secrets, and more ADCS abuse. See the full list on GitHub and the tools and capabilities docs. Capabilities are a polish layer on top of Sage’s any-agent tasking. Each one uses a small per-agent adapter, and Apollo and Merlin have adapters today. I tried to keep range-specific strategy out of the code.

Sage only believes what Mythic can prove. A row in the ledger counts as “achieved” only when it traces back to real evidence: a verifier’s check of Mythic task output or files, Mythic’s credential store, Mythic’s callback records, or BloodHound data collected through a payload. Each achieved row carries a proof envelope recording what it rests on, such as the Mythic callback, task, transaction, or credential ID, and hashes of what the verifier checked. A ledger entry looks roughly like this (identifiers generalized):

technique:      capability:gpo-controlled-system-exec
target:         gpo=;domain=
effect:         system-exec:gpo:@
status:         achieved
preconditions:  [generic-write:gpo:, gpo-domain::, live-foothold:]
proof_envelope: {origin: mythic_task, callback_id: 1, task_id: 8, command: shell,
                terminal_status: completed, transaction_id: capability-exec:,
                verifier_id: capability:gpo-controlled-system-exec, verifier_hash: }

You can retract a row, and undo that, but a row only counts as achieved with real proof behind it, whether you or the model cites the evidence.

Next, I want to move Sage towards auto harness improvement where it can take past operations data and determine what capabilities are missing and get them incorporated in the harness. That work is early and not part of this release.

Autonomous Mode

Sage also has an Autonomous mode. In a Mythic chat channel for Sage with autonomous mode enabled, Sage works toward an objective without asking for approval on each action. That carries real risk of leaving scope or affecting a client’s business, so why have it? Two reasons. It lets me run evaluations in safe lab environments such as a GOAD range, and it is a quick way to show what the harness can do.

Under the hood, Autonomous mode sets aside the supervisor-and-specialists conversation and hands control to a deterministic execution kernel. Each cycle observes the current Mythic and BloodHound state, works out which capabilities are admissible right now, picks one, runs it through a Mythic callback, verifies the result, and records any new effects before continuing. The run has hard stops, including a cycle limit, a limit on cycles with no new effect, a token budget, and a wall clock, and the stop button ends a run between cycles. How Sage works has the full loop.

There is also a separate Autonomous Solve switch, and it is easy to confuse with the mode (I plan to clean this up in a future release). In a supervised channel it forces multi-hop objective solving, but every guarded action still waits for your approval and completion still needs objective evidence. Approvals go away only when you set the channel to Autonomous mode.

Autonomous mode is a research capability. It has been exercised only in a GOAD lab, so keep it to labs and out of production engagements.

Limits

Sage is beta software. The full record of what has (and hasn’t) been validated is at docs.mythicsage.ai/understand/limitations. The short version:

  • Authorized use only, and still maturing. Use Sage only for activity you are explicitly authorized to perform. Its behavior in production environments isn’t well understood yet, so prefer labs and authorized engagements for now.
  • Mythic v4 with chat containers. Earlier Mythic versions can’t host Sage. The validated build is Mythic v4.
  • One validated provider route. Sage supports several providers and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, but the live-validated route is through LiteLLM. Other models use the same code paths and haven’t been validated.
  • Apollo is the proven payload. Release validation ran end to end with Apollo. During development I also drove Merlin through Sage. Other agents can be tasked through Mythic’s schema but haven’t been validated, and the built-in capabilities have adapters only for Apollo and Merlin today.
  • The Sage Watcher is a proof of concept. It ships with Sage, but I’ve only run it in a few quick, limited tests, so treat its findings as unvalidated. I think a background watcher could be among Sage’s most valuable features, and I plan to put more work into it.

Development and testing have mostly been limited to me and what I’ve had time for. I’m 100% certain that as you use Sage you’ll spot issues or have feedback. Please share it, and together we’ll improve it. That’s why Sage is still in beta: it will take real operators doing real authorized work to find and fix the rough edges.

Try It!

Sage needs Mythic v4 and credentials for a model provider or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. From your Mythic directory, install it like any other agent:

sudo ./mythic-cli install github https://github.com/MythicAgents/sage

items.title: Notion Confirms AI Chat Transcripts Exposed in Fireworks AI Breach, Affecting Customer Workspaces
items.summary: Notion has confirmed that a security incident at Fireworks AI exposed Notion AI chat transcripts linked to fewer than 1% of its customer workspaces. Insights, a feature that helps teams understand their AI usage, used the affected conversations. Notion said its own systems were not breached and no other Notion features were affected. The company has contacted affected customers and provided instructions for reviewing the impacted data securely inside their workspaces. Customers who have not received a notification have not been identified as affected and need no action right now. However, Notion’s investigation remains open, and it will contact additional customers if it finds further exposure. Notion AI Chat Transcripts Exposed Fireworks first alerted Notion on the evening of November 2, 2026, after attackers accessed a small dataset. Notion’s initial review found only synthetic testing data, not customer information. By the morning of November 3, Notion had disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleted all data held there, and stopped communication with the provider. The findings changed on November 6, when Fireworks warned that attackers might have accessed customer data. Notion launched another investigation, and Fireworks confirmed the new dataset on November 8. That review identified customer chat transcripts processed for Insights, changing the company’s earlier assessment that no customer data was involved. The disclosure follows the wider Fireworks AI data breach , which involved customer records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. Those broader findings should not be confused with Notion’s confirmed exposure, which concerns Insights chat transcripts. Notion has not said that every data category affected at Fireworks was also exposed for its customers. According to Notion’s security advisory , transcripts from the vast majority of affected workspaces were “unattributable.” They lacked labels identifying the author or workspace and did not contain tool call results. Beyond the conversation text itself, Notion said there was no information linking these chats to users, workspaces, or companies. That distinction does not mean the conversations were free of sensitive details. Information typed into a chat could still identify a person or business. Separate coverage of exposed AI chat messages shows why conversation content matters even when the underlying AI model has not been compromised. These incidents have different causes, but both show the privacy risks surrounding stored chats. Notion used Fireworks for Insights classification jobs and to run open-weight models inside its product. It has disabled Insights during the investigation and stopped serving those models through Fireworks. Its AI settings documentation confirms that Insights is temporarily paused, with use cases and conversation counts unavailable. Affected customers should treat the identified transcripts as exposed. Notion recommends changing passwords, API keys, and other credentials pasted into Notion AI during the incident timeframe. Reviewing the supplied data is important because missing account labels cannot protect secrets written directly into a conversation. Further incident updates are available through Fireworks’ security bulletins . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Ivanti Patches New Security Flaws Affecting Endpoint Manager, EPMM, Sentry, CSA, and Workspace Manager
items.summary: Ivanti has released security updates for Endpoint Manager, Endpoint Manager Mobile, Sentry, Cloud Services Application, and User Workspace Manager. The November 2026 disclosures cover flaws that could allow remote code execution, changes to trusted certificates, data exposure, and service disruption. Two critical vulnerabilities in Endpoint Manager and CSA present the highest risks. Ivanti said it was not aware of customers being exploited through these vulnerabilities before public disclosure. The issues were reported through its responsible disclosure program. However, the lack of reported attacks does not remove the need to patch, particularly where attackers can reach affected services without logging in. Multiple Ivanti Security Flaws The most severe issue, CVE-2026-121653, carries a CVSS score of 9.8. This SQL injection vulnerability affects the Endpoint Manager Core before version 2024 SU8 and allows remote attackers to execute code without authentication. Earlier Endpoint Manager SQL injection flaws also exposed management servers to code execution flaws. Endpoint Manager also fixes CVE-2026-18128, rated 6.8. Sensitive information travels in cleartext through the agent, allowing an attacker positioned between communicating systems to read and change HTTP traffic. Both vulnerabilities affect EPM 2024 SU7 and earlier, with fixes available in 2024 SU8 through the Ivanti License System. CSA’s critical flaw, CVE-2026-121683, scores 9.4 and affects version 5.0.8 only. Missing authentication lets remote attackers add or delete arbitrary trusted EPM Core certificate entries. This is separate from previously reported Ivanti CSA authentication and code execution vulnerabilities , which required different updates. According to the supplied CSA advisory , version 5.0.8.1 fixes the issue. Versions 5.0.7 and earlier are not affected by this specific flaw. A dual network interface configuration following Ivanti’s guidance limits exposure to the internal interface and prevents external exploitation, but administrators should still install the update. The EPMM advisory lists six vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-105425, rated 7.2, allows remote attackers with administrator privileges to execute code through operating system command injection. The same vulnerability also affects Sentry, making it important for organizations running both products to update each deployment. Other EPMM issues allow administrators to change Linux kernel settings as root, disable Apache HTTPS services, delete arbitrary files, or expose protected personal information. These are CVE-2026-105426, CVE-2026-105427, CVE-2026-107404, and CVE-2026-83528. A separate local flaw, CVE-2026-107405, can cause denial of service. Listed fixed releases include 12.11.0.0, 12.10.0.1, and 12.9.0.3. The Sentry advisory also describes CVE-2026-105669, an argument injection flaw that lets remote administrators execute existing disk binaries. CVE-2026-123179 allows a local authenticated attacker to disrupt service through the Tomcat shutdown listener. CVE-2026-123181 lets remote administrators create arbitrary files and directories with root privileges. Fixed versions include 11.0.0, 10.8.3, and 10.7.4. User Workspace Manager addresses CVE-2026-105813, a medium-severity cleartext storage flaw. A local authenticated attacker could retrieve another local user’s session. Ivanti directs customers to install UWM 2026.4, available through its licensing system, according to the supplied Workspace Manager advisory . Security teams should prioritize the unauthenticated EPM and CSA vulnerabilities, then schedule the remaining updates based on exposure and access controls. Ivanti has not supplied vulnerability-specific indicators of compromise because no public exploitation is known. Administrators should confirm installed versions after patching and avoid treating restricted administrative access as a replacement for updates. items.title: Barracuda Confirms Active Exploitation of Email Gateway Flaws Allowing Root Access
items.summary: Barracuda has confirmed active exploitation of security flaws affecting its Email Security Gateway (ESG), warning that attackers could combine two vulnerabilities to gain root access without logging in. In a November 9, 2026, update issued at 9:00 p.m. EST, the company said exploitation had affected a small number of organizations. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, involve an authorization bypass and command injection. Successful exploitation requires access to the appliance’s administrative interface. This condition makes exposed management pages a key concern, although Barracuda says organizations with interfaces kept off the public internet are less exposed to this attack path. The confirmation changes the risk picture from the initial November 2 disclosure. Cybersecurity News previously covered the Barracuda security flaws and available patches before the vendor reported active attacks. Barracuda’s latest advisory does not identify the attackers, affected organizations, malware, or the exact number of victims. Barracuda Email Gateway Flaws CVE-2026-116606 is a pre-authentication authorization bypass affecting ESG, with a CVSS score of 9.3. On November 5, Barracuda corrected its advisory to clarify that attackers do not need valid credentials. They must, however, be able to reach the administrative user interface. Network access and authenticated access are therefore separate requirements. CVE-2026-111560 is a command injection flaw with a CVSS score of 8.6. On its own, it requires administrative access. Combining it with the authorization bypass could remove that login barrier and provide root access to the device. ESG is the only listed product affected by both vulnerabilities, so the unauthenticated chain should not be assumed to affect every listed product. According to Barracuda’s updated security advisory , both flaws carry a vendor severity rating of High. Its public guidance confirms the combined root-access risk but does not provide exploit requests or a detailed attack sequence. This limits what defenders can conclude about the methods used in the observed incidents. ESG customers need patch BNSF-40425 for versions 9.4.017 and later, or BNSF-40430 for earlier versions. The command injection flaw also affects Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller and Web Application Firewall, patched through BNADC-16586. Message Archiver requires BNMA-32468, WAF Control Center requires BNWF-60060, and Web Security Gateway requires BNYF-24789. These products serve different roles, making accurate device inventories important when checking patch coverage. For readers reviewing how mail-filtering appliances fit into their defenses, Cybersecurity News’ email security gateway guide explains their role in screening messages and attachments. That protective role makes gateway security an important part of email defense. Barracuda recommends restricting administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls. Customers should verify that the latest firmware and every applicable security patch are installed. Devices several versions behind may need multiple updates. Install missing patches manually, and enable automatic patching where it is disabled. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

CNCF Welcomes Twelve New Members as Organizations Look to Run AI Agents on Open, Sovereign Infrastructure
items.summary: Organizations join the cloud native community to strengthen security, visibility, and control for production AI Key Highlights CNCF welcomes 12 new Silver members, expanding its community across sovereign cloud, AI agent infrastructure, security and financial services. As organizations move AI agents into production, new members bring expertise in open infrastructure that supports data sovereignty, operational visibility, security and control. Enterprises, developers and platform teams gain access to a broader ecosystem of cloud native technologies and expertise to securely build, deploy and manage AI workloads across environments. KUBECON + CLOUDNATIVECON NORTH AMERICA, SALT LAKE CITY – November 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced the addition of twelve new Silver members, reinforcing the community’s focus on open, vendor-neutral infrastructure for running AI agents in production. This cohort, spanning sovereign cloud and hosting, AI agent infrastructure, container security, and financial services, broadens the ecosystem of organizations building and operating production AI. “Deploying AI agents at scale requires the same core guarantees the cloud native ecosystem has spent a decade building: choice, portability, and the ability to control your own infrastructure,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director, CNCF. “From sovereign cloud operators to specialized security and telemetry maintainers, this group of new silver members highlights how the community is expanding to support complex, autonomous AI workloads everywhere.” As organizations move AI agents from pilot to production, platform teams face rising demands for data control, operational visibility, and software supply chain trust. CNCF’s newest members reflect that shift, bringing domain expertise and technology built to run agentic workloads on open, portable infrastructure. New Silver Members The following organizations have recently joined CNCF as Silver Members: Centron is a German cloud provider on a mission to make the cloud as simple and accessible as possible – for everyone. Its ccloud³ platform offers managed Kubernetes, virtual machines, S3 object storage, and GPU compute, operated entirely from centron’s own ISO 27001- and C5-certified, GDPR-compliant data center in Germany. CIQ is the founding support and services partner for Rocky Linux and a leading provider of Enterprise Linux infrastructure. CIQ delivers secure, performant software infrastructure for the full range of modern workloads. Global enterprises, government agencies, research institutions and supercomputing centers trust CIQ to run their most advanced workloads in production, from mission-critical environments to the systems behind major scientific and AI breakthroughs. CIQ’s products include the Rocky Linux from CIQ (RLC Pro) family of operating systems, CIQ Stratum, an open source Kubernetes engine, Ascender Pro for IT automation, Fuzzball job-based container orchestration, Warewulf Pro cluster provisioning, and Apptainer, the container system built for high-performance computing, with Apptainer Pro coming soon. Cloudpunks GmbH is a cloud native IT consultancy from Germany, specializing in Kubernetes platform engineering, DevOps automation, and cloud infrastructure on AWS and Azure — covering both public cloud and on-premises environments. As a Kubernetes Certified Service Provider (KCSP) and certified AWS and Microsoft Azure partner with Kubestronaut-certified engineers, cloudpunks works embedded in customer teams to build and operate cloud native platforms, not just advise from the sideline. Emphere fixes vulnerabilities in container images at the source, inside the Dockerfiles teams already maintain. Based in Seattle, the company works to close the gap between CVE disclosure and a deployed fix across base OS packages, language runtimes, and open source libraries. FluidCloud Limited is a Cloud Cloning platform that uses proprietary Large Language Model to enable discovery, migration, and operations of entire cloud infrastructure in minutes. FluidCloud’s multi-cloud DevOps platform works across AWS, Azure, Oracle, Google Cloud, VMware, Nutanix, Vultr, and OVH to create a universally portable graph of the entire infrastructure, powering instant disaster recovery, resiliency, migration, and multi-cloud interoperability. ImageEngine Kube is a cloud native, self-hosted image optimization engine that deploys to your Kubernetes cluster via a signed Helm chart. Working alongside your existing CDN, it delivers device-aware resizing, AVIF/WebP/JPEG XL conversion, and intelligent compression—giving platform teams faster image delivery, full control over their data, security auditability, and predictable costs. Ilert GmbH is an incident management, on-call alerting, and status page platform with a built-in AI SRE, made and hosted in Germany. Paper Compute is an open intelligence platform for teams building AI agents. Its agent gateway handles model routing, inference policy, and zero-instrumentation telemetry with tapes, deployed in your own cloud. Radar is an open source Kubernetes interface for humans and AI agents that shows how everything in a live cluster connects, not just what’s in it. Teams use it through a UI built for people and an MCP server built for agents, so both can understand a cluster the way it actually works. Open-Xchange AG (OX) is the world’s largest independent email provider, and its portfolio includes ubiquitous open source software like Dovecot and PowerDNS, alongside OX App Suite and OX Cloud. OX’s philosophy is clear: keep the internet free, open, and competitive. OX achieves this by building innovative, secure, and open solutions that empower its community, partners, and customers to offer trusted alternatives to global hyperscalers. Varnish Software AB accelerates and secures the delivery of content, data, and software, from web and streaming traffic to the packages and container images that power software supply chains. About the Newest Silver End User Member CNCF also welcomes its newest Silver End User Member, an organization that actively uses cloud native technologies to drive digital transformation: Deutsche Kreditbank AG (DKB) is one of Germany’s leading digital banks, serving millions of customers as well as businesses and institutions in future-oriented industries across the country. CNCF Silver Members receive various benefits valued at over $300,000 USD, including training and educational subscriptions , event sponsorship discounts, access to The Linux Foundation’s legal resources , opportunities to join project working groups , and more . To learn more about becoming a Silver Member, visit: https://www.cncf.io/about/join/silver About Cloud Native Computing Foundation Cloud native computing empowers organizations to build and run scalable applications with an open source software stack in public, private, and hybrid clouds. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) hosts critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy. CNCF brings together the industry’s top developers, end users, and vendors and runs the largest open source developer conferences in the world. Supported by nearly 800 members, including the world’s largest cloud computing and software companies, as well as over 200 innovative startups, CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation. For more information, please visit www.cncf.io . Media Contact The Linux Foundation pr@cncf.io

items.title: CNCF Welcomes CoreWeave as a Platinum Member to Further Open Source AI Infrastructure
items.summary: Investment underscores CoreWeave’s continued push to build open, cloud native infrastructure for production AI at scale Key Highlights CoreWeave has upgraded its CNCF membership to Platinum, deepening its ongoing engagement in the open source cloud native ecosystem. CoreWeave is a participant in the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance Program and a contributor to Kubernetes, Kueue, and llm-d. CNCF Platinum membership reinforces a shared commitment to open source collaboration, vendor-neutral innovation, and long-term ecosystem sustainability. SAN FRANCISCO — November 10, 2026 — The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced that CoreWeave has upgraded to a Platinum Member, reinforcing its commitment to advancing the open source technologies that power production AI infrastructure. As generative AI moves from research labs into production environments, platform engineering teams are confronting a new frontier of infrastructure challenges. CoreWeave’s upgraded membership reflects its belief that the tools needed to meet those challenges — from distributed inference to workflow orchestration — should be built in the open, alongside the broader cloud native community. “CoreWeave’s expanded commitment as a Platinum Member reflects the growing importance of open source cloud native infrastructure to production AI,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director, CNCF. “We are proud to welcome CoreWeave as CNCF advances the open standards and technologies needed to run AI workloads reliably and efficiently at scale.” The Platinum upgrade reflects a broader pattern of contributions CoreWeave has made across the CNCF landscape. In May 2025, CoreWeave joined Red Hat, IBM, Google, and NVIDIA as a founding contributor to llm-d, believing that production inference needed to be built in the open. That project is now a CNCF Sandbox project. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America this year, CoreWeave Principal Software Engineer Rita Zhang received the Lifetime Achievement Award for her work over the past decade shaping and supporting the Kubernetes and CNCF communities. CoreWeave is also a participant in the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance Program, an initiative the company sees as an important step in aligning the community around shared standards that make deploying AI at scale more consistent and reliable. Additionally, CoreWeave is a contributor to Kubernetes and Kueue. “We built our cloud on Kubernetes to run some of the largest AI models in the world at production scale, and we learned a lot doing it,” said Shadi Saba, vice president, engineering, AI/ML at CoreWeave. “Now we are applying those lessons to large-scale training, production inference, and agentic workloads. Platinum membership is how we bring that experience back to the community, showing up in the working groups, helping define what AI on Kubernetes actually means, and making top-tier compute available to the open source projects the whole ecosystem depends on. Upgrading our membership helps us work with the community to define the standards for the next generation of AI.” To learn more about becoming a CNCF member, visit https://www.cncf.io/about/join/ . At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America this year, CoreWeave Principal Software Engineer Rita Zhang received the Lifetime Achievement Award for her work over the past decade shaping and supporting the Kubernetes and CNCF communities. Built in close alignment with Kubernetes SIG-Multicluster standards, our asynchronous pull model guarantees cluster autonomy without centralizing sensitive credentials on the hub. Just as importantly, our pluggable add-on framework turns OCM into an extensible substrate, making it effortless for other cloud-native projects to inherit multicluster capabilities without reinventing the plumbing. Klusterlet: The agent on each managed cluster that registers it with the hub and applies instructions from it. OCM joins incubating technologies Artifact Hub, Backstage, Chaos Mesh, Cloud Custodian, Container Network Interface (CNI), Contour, Cortex, Emissary-ingress, Fluid, gRPC, HAMi, k8gb, Keycloak, KServe, Kubescape, KubeVela, KubeVirt, Lima, Litmus, Longhorn, Meshery, metal3-io, Microcks, Notary Project, OpenCost, OpenFeature, OpenFGA, OpenKruise, OpenYurt, Operator Framework, Strimzi, Tekton, Thanos, Volcano, and wasmCloud. From an architecture perspective, what I’m proudest of is our commitment to a lightweight, modular foundation rather than a monolithic platform. Looking ahead, we are focused on streamlining setup and onboarding while advancing progressive rollouts for safer workload delivery, ultimately keeping distributed Kubernetes simple, secure, and composable.”

Open Cluster Management’s Milestones and Ecosystem Development

As organizations grow beyond a handful of Kubernetes clusters across clouds, regions, edge locations, and teams, they have to register and onboard clusters, distribute applications and policies, keep configuration consistent, and recover from failures without disrupting running workloads. Open Cluster Management provides these capabilities through vendor neutral, declarative Kubernetes APIs, and its hub-and-spoke model is designed to survive the failure and recovery of components without interrupting workloads.

Originally developed by IBM and Red Hat, Open Cluster Management joined the CNCF Sandbox in November 2021. Since reaching its 1.0 release in June 2025, the project has delivered four subsequent minor updates (up through 1.4 in October 2026), expanding its capabilities for multicluster management, application delivery, and observability. Key release highlights include:

  • CEL-based cluster selection and an Argo CD pull model add-on (1.0)
  • A gRPC-based hub-and-spoke connection, plus add-ons for Kueue MultiKueue and OpenTelemetry (1.1)
  • Advanced Placement configuration, automated hosting cluster resolution, and the introduction of the argocd-agent integration to provide highly scalable multi-cluster GitOps and complete application status visibility (1.2)
  • Enhancements to ManifestWork resource ordering and the graduation of the AddOnTemplate API to v1beta1 (1.3)
  • Syncing OCM PlacementDecisions to SIG Multicluster’s PlacementDecision API, ManifestWork observability, and security hardening such as network policies (1.4)

OCM works closely with the broader cloud native ecosystem. It implements and aligns with the Kubernetes SIG Multicluster APIs, supplies Argo CD with cluster decisions for GitOps deployments, and integrates with Cluster API for cluster lifecycle. KubeVela, KubeStellar, Kueue, and Meshery all document OCM integrations, and the project maintains add-ons and examples for Argo CD, Fluid, and OpenTelemetry. Twenty-seven maintainers from eight organizations, including Red Hat, Guidewire, eBay, AppsCode, and Spectro Cloud, lead the project.

OCM has demonstrated adoption across organizations including Alibaba Cloud, AppsCode, Guidewire, Red Hat, and Spectro Cloud. At eBay, OCM supports application deployment across more than 190 Kubernetes clusters through integrations with Argo CD. Groww uses OCM to support progressive application rollouts, while VESSEL AI leverages the project to manage GPU clusters and distribute AI workloads across cloud environments.

“As Kubernetes adoption expands across increasingly complex environments, organizations need open, interoperable approaches to managing clusters at scale,” said Karena Angell, CNCF Technical Oversight Committee member. “Open Cluster Management has demonstrated technical maturity, a growing contributor community, and meaningful adoption across the cloud native ecosystem. Its advancement to incubation reflects the project’s progress in helping organizations manage multicluster environments without relying on proprietary solutions.”

Main Components

Open Cluster Management’s main components consist of the following:

  • Cluster Manager: The hub side control plane that coordinates registration, work, placement, and add-ons.
  • Klusterlet: The agent on each managed cluster that registers it with the hub and applies instructions from it.
  • Cluster Inventory (registration): Registers manage clusters through a double opt-in handshake and mTLS connection, with certificate rotation and a dedicated namespace per cluster on the hub.
  • ManifestWork API: Distributes Kubernetes resources to managed clusters, with update strategies, conflict resolution, and status feedback. Agents pull work from the hub, so the hub does not store managed cluster credentials.
  • Placement API: Dynamically selects clusters using labels, resource capacity, or custom criteria and publishes the result as a PlacementDecision that any scheduler or controller can consume.
  • Add-on framework: A structure for projects to become multicluster aware, handling registration, lifecycle, configuration, and status reporting.
  • clusteradm: A command line tool to bootstrap a hub and join clusters.
  • Built-in extensions: Cluster API integration for cluster lifecycle, an Argo CD add-on for pull-based application delivery, and governance, risk, and compliance policy controllers.

Notable Milestones

  • 1,100 GitHub Stars
  • 1,370 pull requests 
  • 537 contributors from 84 organizations across 16 countries
CNCF-Hosted Projects

The CNCF Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) provides technical leadership to CNCF projects, overseeing their progression through maturity levels and supporting long-term sustainability. Projects advancing to incubation demonstrate growing adoption, technical maturity, and community development.

As a CNCF-hosted project, Open Cluster Management is part of a neutral foundation aligned with its technical interests, as well as the larger Linux Foundation, which provides governance, marketing support, and community outreach. OCM joins incubating technologies Artifact Hub, Backstage, Chaos Mesh, Cloud Custodian, Container Network Interface (CNI), Contour, Cortex, Emissary-ingress, Fluid, gRPC, HAMi, k8gb, Keycloak, KServe, Kubescape, KubeVela, KubeVirt, Lima, Litmus, Longhorn, Meshery, metal3-io, Microcks, Notary Project, OpenCost, OpenFeature, OpenFGA, OpenKruise, OpenYurt, Operator Framework, Strimzi, Tekton, Thanos, Volcano, and wasmCloud.

items.title: CNCF Welcomes Vultr as a Platinum Member to Advance Open and Sovereign Cloud Infrastructure for AI
items.summary: Upgrade extends Vultr’s 5-year history with CNCF and expands its voice in shaping open interoperability for AI factory infrastructure at global scale Key Highlights Vultr has upgraded to a CNCF Platinum membership, expanding its role in shaping open interoperability for AI infrastructure. Vultr contributed both CPU + GPU infrastructure capacity support for CNCF project testing Vultr launched the Vultr Open Source Alliance, connecting its CNCF partnership to a broader commitment across open infrastructure, cloud native technologies, and AI tooling. KUBECON + CLOUDNATIVECON NORTH AMERICA, SALT LAKE CITY – November 10, 2026– The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced that Vultr has upgraded its CNCF membership to Platinum at a critical moment when cloud native and AI infrastructure are converging on shared, open interoperability. This upgrade builds on Vultr deepening its partnerships with CNCF projects to help drive developer adoption of open, composable infrastructure through the newly launched Vultr Open Source Alliance. The alliance brings together work across open infrastructure, cloud native technologies, AI, and developer ecosystems. Together, these efforts reflect a simple principle: developers should be able to choose the infrastructure, frameworks, models, tools, and protocols that fit their workloads without being locked into a single technology stack. “AI factory infrastructure should be open and fungible, not another walled garden,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “Platinum membership in CNCF is a real commitment to help build that open future and we’re glad to have Vultr at the table as we figure out what composable AI infrastructure looks like for the next decade.” Building on a foundation started in 2021 when Vultr first joined CNCF as a Silver Member, recent milestones underscore Vultr’s growing footprint in cloud native AI infrastructure. Vultr’s engineering team has worked directly with maintainers on CNCF projects including Kubernetes and Kubeflow, contributing feedback and improvements upstream rather than only consuming the technology downstream. Its Vultr Kubernetes Engine (VKE) is a CNCF Certified Kubernetes product . Vultr runs heterogeneous GPU and CPU infrastructure that supports open source frameworks including PyTorch for model training and Kubernetes for inference, and recently contributed both CPU and GPU infrastructure capacity support for CNCF project testing. Vultr is also a member of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), a separate Linux Foundation initiative stewarding open standards for the agentic AI stack. “Open source is the foundation of modern AI infrastructure, and the developer community should be free to choose the frameworks, models, and infrastructure that fit their workloads, without being locked into a single stack or cloud,” said Kevin Cochrane, Chief Marketing Officer of Vultr. “Moving to Platinum membership builds on five years of working alongside the CNCF community. Through the Vultr Open Source Alliance and our CPU and GPU contributions to CNCF project testing, we’re helping build the open, interoperable, and sovereign AI infrastructure that the next generation of applications will depend on.” To learn more about becoming a CNCF member, visit https://www.cncf.io/about/join/ . items.title: CNCF and SlashData Report Finds Cloud Native Developers Are More AI-Ready, Global Population Surpasses 21 Million
items.summary: New research released finds 75% of cloud native developers use AI coding tools, compared to 55% of non-cloud native developer peers Key Highlights: CNCF and SlashData released the State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. The report notes that the global cloud native developer population reached an estimated 21.2 million, representing approximately 41% of developers worldwide. Cloud native developers are significantly more likely to use AI coding tools than their non-cloud native counterparts (75% vs. 55%) and integrate AI into their services (67% vs. 38%), reinforcing the relationship between cloud native maturity and AI adoption. The report finds North America is now home to approximately 4 million cloud native developers. SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America – Nov. 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today released new findings from its State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report , developed in collaboration with SlashData . As AI adoption accelerates, the report findings highlight the growing relationship between cloud native infrastructure, platform engineering and the development of production-ready AI and agentic systems. “Cloud native is foundational to how the industry builds and operates modern software, and AI is accelerating that evolution,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “This report reinforces how cloud native technologies are supporting AI workloads. As organizations move to scale AI workloads, the need for reliable, scalable and observable infrastructure will grow. Open source technologies like Kubernetes and OpenTelemetry are helping provide the foundation for that transition.” Cloud native developers lead AI adoption as agentic systems move toward production As AI becomes deeply integrated into software development, the report finds that cloud native developers are significantly more likely to adopt AI tools and integrate AI capabilities into their applications. However, the distinction is less about how developers use AI and more about whether they adopt it in the first place. 75% of cloud native developers use AI coding tools , compared to 55% of non-cloud native developers. 67% of cloud native developers are integrating AI into their services , compared to 38% of non-cloud native developers. 49% of developers integrating AI into their services report having agentic systems in production , including internal and external-facing applications. 55% of developers building agentic services are cloud native , while the remaining 45% demonstrate that developers can integrate agentic capabilities without directly managing cloud native infrastructure. These findings suggest that cloud native developers are embracing AI while maintaining established engineering practices around oversight, reliability and control. In North America, this preference for supervised AI development is pronounced. Among cloud native developers in the region, 21% use AI to draft code before reviewing and editing it themselves, while just 12% report using autonomous agents for coding tasks. “Our research shows that cloud native maturity is becoming an important indicator of how actively developers engage with AI,” said Liam Bollmann-Dodd, principal market research consultant at SlashData. “Cloud native developers are more likely to adopt AI tools and integrate AI into their services, but once developers begin using these technologies, their approaches are remarkably similar. This highlights the importance of cloud native infrastructure in supporting AI at scale, even when the developers building AI-powered applications aren’t directly interacting with the underlying infrastructure.” Global cloud native developer community surpasses 21 million The report estimates that the global cloud native developer population reached 21.2 million in Q3 2026, up from 15.6 million in Q3 2025 and 19.9 million in Q1 2026. Cloud native developers now account for approximately 41% of the global developer population, reflecting the continued expansion of cloud native technologies beyond traditional backend infrastructure and into a wider range of development disciplines. Key findings include: 21.2 million developers worldwide are cloud native , marking the first time the population has surpassed 20 million. North America is home to approximately 4 million cloud native developers , reinforcing the region’s vital role in the global cloud native ecosystem. More than 80% of professional backend services and web backend developers engage in cloud native practices and approaches. Approximately 7.5 million AI developers are cloud native , underscoring the growing intersection between AI development and cloud native technologies. While the pace of cloud native developer growth has moderated over the past six months, the report suggests that increased adoption of managed services and internal developer platforms may be making underlying cloud native technologies less visible to developers. As organizations standardize their infrastructure, developers may rely on Kubernetes and other cloud native technologies without directly interacting with or identifying the underlying platforms. Platform engineering becomes standard as AI infrastructure matures Platform engineering and DevOps standardization continue to reshape how organizations build, deploy and manage applications. The report finds that 93% of developers now work at organizations using some form of DevOps standardization or internal developer platform, up from 77% in Q3 2025. This shift reflects the growing maturity of cloud native infrastructure as organizations centralize tooling, improve developer productivity and streamline operations. At the same time, greater abstraction can make the underlying infrastructure less visible to developers, even as its importance to production applications increases. The report also examines the adoption of infrastructure technologies among backend developers: 40% use API gateways , making them the most widely adopted technology surveyed. 30% use microservices , reflecting their continued importance in modern application architectures. 21% use observability tools , highlighting the role of visibility into complex systems. 19% report using Kubernetes , although platform abstraction may contribute to underreporting of underlying infrastructure technologies. 8% use immutable infrastructure practices and 7% use chaos engineering , suggesting continued opportunities for advanced infrastructure practices to mature. As AI workloads grow in complexity, these underlying capabilities are highly relevant to production environments. AI inference and agentic systems introduce new demands around compute scheduling, resource efficiency, observability and reliable distributed operations, areas where cloud native technologies already provide established approaches. The report also identifies cost, data privacy and security as leading concerns among developers who have not yet integrated AI functionality into their services. As a result, infrastructure capable of supporting reliable operations, cost management and scalability will likely become more important. The findings reinforce cloud native’s expanding role in the AI ecosystem, not only for developers building and operating infrastructure directly, but also for the growing number of developers consuming managed AI services built on cloud native foundations. To learn more, download the full State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report . About Cloud Native Computing Foundation Cloud native computing empowers organizations to build and run scalable applications with an open source software stack in public, private and hybrid clouds. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) hosts critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus and Envoy. CNCF brings together the industry’s top developers, end users and vendors and runs the largest open source developer conferences in the world. Supported by nearly 800 members, including the world’s largest cloud computing and software companies, as well as over 200 innovative startups, CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation. For more information, please visit www.cncf.io . About SlashData SlashData helps product, platform, and engineering leaders understand how software development is changing in the AI era. For over 20 years, they have helped many of the world’s leading technology companies make sense of developers, developer ecosystems, and the tools and workflows shaping the future of software. Their work shows clients how the developer ecosystem and software engineering teams are evolving, so they can build better products, platforms, and go-to-market strategies for the AI era and make smarter decisions about the tools, practices, and investments ahead. Media Contact The Linux Foundation pr@cncf.io
