Platform engineering and DevOps standardization continue to reshape how organizations build, deploy and manage applications. The report finds that 93% of developers now work at organizations using some form of DevOps standardization or internal developer platform, up from 77% in Q3 2025.

This shift reflects the growing maturity of cloud native infrastructure as organizations centralize tooling, improve developer productivity and streamline operations. At the same time, greater abstraction can make the underlying infrastructure less visible to developers, even as its importance to production applications increases.

The report also examines the adoption of infrastructure technologies among backend developers:

  • 40% use API gateways, making them the most widely adopted technology surveyed.
  • 30% use microservices, reflecting their continued importance in modern application architectures.
  • 21% use observability tools, highlighting the role of visibility into complex systems.
  • 19% report using Kubernetes, although platform abstraction may contribute to underreporting of underlying infrastructure technologies.
  • 8% use immutable infrastructure practices and 7% use chaos engineering, suggesting continued opportunities for advanced infrastructure practices to mature.

As AI workloads grow in complexity, these underlying capabilities are highly relevant to production environments. AI inference and agentic systems introduce new demands around compute scheduling, resource efficiency, observability and reliable distributed operations, areas where cloud native technologies already provide established approaches.

The report also identifies cost, data privacy and security as leading concerns among developers who have not yet integrated AI functionality into their services. As a result, infrastructure capable of supporting reliable operations, cost management and scalability will likely become more important.

The findings reinforce cloud native’s expanding role in the AI ecosystem, not only for developers building and operating infrastructure directly, but also for the growing number of developers consuming managed AI services built on cloud native foundations.

items.title: Donating KubeRay to CNCF
items.summary: The PARK stack (PyTorch, AI models, Ray, and Kubernetes) is emerging as the de facto open source standard for production AI. Within that stack, KubeRay has become the bridge connecting scalable AI applications built on Ray with the compute orchestration of Kubernetes. Nearly every core piece of the PARK stack already lives under the Linux Foundation: PyTorch and Ray through the PyTorch Foundation, and Kubernetes through the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). KubeRay was the missing piece. Today, we’re announcing that KubeRay is joining the CNCF, bringing the entire PARK stack under Linux Foundation governance and giving teams full confidence in its neutrality and openness. Scaling Ray clusters on Kubernetes KubeRay is a powerful, open source toolkit and Kubernetes operator designed to run distributed AI, machine learning, and Python workloads powered by Ray seamlessly on cloud-native infrastructure. As distributed AI workloads become a core cloud native construct, KubeRay bridges the gap between Python-first AI frameworks and Kubernetes-native infrastructure. KubeRay provides three Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for scaling and operating Ray workloads in production: RayCluster: The foundational building block for running Ray on Kubernetes. `RayCluster` manages the full lifecycle of a Ray cluster, automating head and worker pod provisioning, health checks, Global Control Service (GCS) fault tolerance, and dynamic autoscaling in coordination with the Ray Autoscaler. RayJob: Purpose-built for batch processing, distributed training, and reinforcement learning (RL) workloads. `RayJob` automatically provisions an ephemeral `RayCluster`, submits a Ray job once the cluster is ready, and tears down the cluster upon completion to maximize compute and accelerator utilization. RayService: Designed for long-lived, high-availability online inference with Ray Serve. `RayService` manages both the underlying `RayCluster` and the Ray Serve deployment graph, enabling zero-downtime rolling upgrades, automated failover, and seamless traffic routing for production AI services. Together, these custom resources provide the foundation for enterprises to build modern machine learning platforms on top of Ray and Kubernetes. For example, end users like Spotify use KubeRay to scale their internal machine learning platform, Hendrix, which is used to train and fine-tune Spotify’s machine learning models using Ray on GKE. “Running multimodal AI workloads at scale requires a platform with tight integration between Python-first AI and Kubernetes. KubeRay is that bridge, helping us scale reliably and manage complex agentic workflows At Hark, that is why we use it, and why I contribute: I want to help more builders scale production AI with confidence.” Kai-Hsun Chen, AI Infrastructure Lead, Hark Growing the KubeRay ecosystem Beyond core cluster lifecycle management, KubeRay has seen widespread adoption because of how deeply it integrates with other CNCF projects and the broader cloud-native ecosystem. Rather than reinventing infrastructure primitives, KubeRay plugs directly into the tools platform teams already rely on: Observability with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Fluent Bit: Ray uses OpenTelemetry within its metrics pipeline and exposes metrics in Prometheus format, enabling platform teams running KubeRay to monitor cluster utilization, task execution, and Ray Serve latency alongside their existing Kubernetes infrastructure. Paired with Fluent Bit for lightweight log collection and forwarding, operators can easily aggregate distributed worker and job logs across ephemeral and long-lived Ray clusters. Batch Scheduling and Quota Management with Kueue, Volcano, and KAI: As organizations scale distributed training across scarce GPU and TPU resources, KubeRay integrates natively with different schedulers to bring Kubernetes-native job queueing to `RayJob` and `RayCluster`. This enables gang scheduling (all-or-nothing pod placement), multi-tenant resource quotas, priority preemption, and topology-aware scheduling. Workload Security and Isolation: As AI workloads scale, robust security and multi-tenancy are critical. KubeRay provides the foundation to secure Ray clusters using automated mTLS and Kubernetes network policies. What’s Next? KubeRay’s success so far has been due to its fast-growing community members — we want to give thanks to everyone who has contributed to KubeRay so far. Becoming a CNCF sandbox project is just the beginning of KubeRay’s next chapter under open, vendor-neutral governance, and we’d love for you to be part of it. If you’re at KubeCon NA 2026, come meet the KubeRay maintainers at our Birds of a Feather (BoF) session to discuss the roadmap, share production use cases, and help shape the future of Ray on Kubernetes. Hark will also be giving a talk about how they use KubeRay for multimodal AI use cases as well. You can also connect with the community in the #kuberay channel on the CNCF or Ray Slack workspaces and attend our biweekly community meetings .

items.title: CNCF and SlashData Report Finds Platform Engineering Strategies Are Shaping AI Infrastructure Adoption
items.summary: Latest research finds 54% of developers with independently managed tooling use hybrid approaches for AI workflows, compared to just 5% at organizations building custom internal platforms Key Highlights: CNCF and SlashData released the Q3 2026 CNCF Technology Radar report during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, examining developer perceptions of observability, infrastructure as code and storage technologies. Prometheus and OpenTelemetry lead observability, earning ‘Adopt’ positions based on strong developer confidence in their maturity, usefulness and reliability. OpenTofu and OpenFeature lead infrastructure as code, while Carina earns ‘Adopt’ positions in storage, highlighting developer confidence across cloud native infrastructure. Platform engineering ownership is shaping AI infrastructure strategies, with 54% of developers at organizations with independently managed tooling reporting hybrid AI workflows, compared to just 5% at organizations building custom internal developer platforms. SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America – Nov. 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today released new findings from its Q3 2026 CNCF Technology Radar report , developed in collaboration with SlashData . As organizations expand their use of artificial intelligence (AI), the report highlights how platform engineering strategies influence AI infrastructure decisions and identifies the cloud native technologies developers view as mature, useful and reliable. The research examines developer perceptions of observability, infrastructure as code (IaC) and storage technologies, identifying tools considered reliable choices for broad adoption. Findings also reveal how centralized and distributed platform engineering models influence whether organizations extend existing platforms, build dedicated AI infrastructure or adopt hybrid approaches to managing AI workflows. “Cloud native technologies are foundational to building and operating modern infrastructure, and AI is introducing new demands around scalability and reliability,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “What this research reinforces is that platform engineering is playing a critical role in how organizations approach AI infrastructure. As teams move AI workloads into production, mature CNCF projects like Backstage, Prometheus and OpenTelemetry provide the visibility and reliability needed to support complex environments.” Platform engineering ownership shapes AI infrastructure strategies As organizations integrate AI workflows into their infrastructure, the report finds that platform ownership is closely associated with how teams approach AI infrastructure. Organizations with centralized platform engineering teams tend to commit to a single strategy, while those with distributed ownership are more likely to adopt hybrid approaches. Key findings include: 54% of developers at organizations where individual teams independently manage their tooling use hybrid AI approaches , compared to 43% at organizations where multiple teams collaboratively provide platform capabilities. 38% of developers at organizations building custom internal developer platforms report using a separate, dedicated AI platform , while 33% extend their existing developer platform to support AI workflows. Only 5% of developers at organizations building custom internal platforms use a hybrid approach , compared to 18% at organizations with centralized teams curating third-party tools. 25% of developers at organizations with platform teams curating third-party tools rely primarily on AI vendor platforms , the highest proportion among the platform ownership models surveyed. These findings suggest that centralized platform teams are better positioned to establish consistent infrastructure strategies, while distributed ownership can lead to more fragmented approaches to AI deployment and management. As AI workloads move toward production, the ability to standardize infrastructure and coordinate platform capabilities will become important for managing operational complexity, resource efficiency and reliability. “The data shows that how organizations structure their platform engineering teams has a meaningful relationship with how they approach AI infrastructure,” said Liam Bollmann-Dodd, principal market research consultant at SlashData. “Centralized teams tend to make deliberate decisions about extending existing platforms or building dedicated AI environments, while distributed teams are more likely to adopt hybrid approaches. This highlights how organizational structure can influence the complexity of supporting AI workloads in production.” Prometheus and OpenTelemetry lead developer confidence in observability As cloud native environments grow more complex, observability remains an important component of reliable infrastructure. The report finds that Prometheus and OpenTelemetry lead the observability category, earning ‘Adopt’ positions based on developer perceptions of maturity, usefulness and likelihood to recommend. The report also highlights strong developer recommendations for Fluent Bit, Jaeger and Cortex, demonstrating confidence in tools supporting monitoring, logging and distributed tracing. Key findings include: Prometheus received four- or five-star maturity ratings from 80% of developers surveyed , including 38% who awarded it five stars for stability and reliability. OpenTelemetry received five-star usefulness ratings from 34% of developers , the second-highest proportion among observability technologies. Additionally, 92% of current and former users were likely or highly likely to recommend it. 99% of current and former Fluent Bit users were likely or highly likely to recommend it , making it the most recommended observability technology surveyed, despite more moderate maturity and usefulness ratings. Cortex received the highest proportion of five-star maturity ratings at 40% , while 93% of Jaeger users were likely or highly likely to recommend it. The findings reinforce the importance of established observability technologies as organizations manage distributed applications and prepare infrastructure for production AI workloads. OpenTelemetry’s strong usefulness ratings and broad developer audience underscore the value of standardized telemetry across complex environments, while Prometheus continues to demonstrate strong developer confidence as a foundational monitoring technology. Infrastructure as code and storage tools demonstrate developer confidence Beyond observability, the report highlights developer confidence in infrastructure as code and storage technologies that support cloud native operations. In infrastructure as code, OpenTofu and OpenFeature earned ‘Adopt’ positions, while Crossplane, Atlantis and cdk8s were placed in ‘Trial.’ In storage, Carina earned the ‘Adopt’ position, with established technologies such as Rook and Longhorn receiving strong developer recommendations. Key findings include: 96% of current and former OpenTofu users were likely or highly likely to recommend it , the highest recommendation rating among infrastructure as code technologies surveyed. OpenFeature received four- or five-star maturity ratings from 67% of developers , alongside 29% five-star usefulness ratings, leading the infrastructure as code category on both measures. 94% of current and former Rook users were likely or highly likely to recommend it , while 59% of Longhorn users were highly likely to recommend it. As organizations standardize their cloud native infrastructure and integrate AI workloads, these technologies provide capabilities for managing configuration, storage and operational complexity. The findings reinforce the role of cloud native platform engineering in supporting production infrastructure, with developer confidence shaped by the reliability, usefulness and operational value of the tools they adopt. To learn more, download the full Q3 2026 CNCF Technology Radar report . items.title: CNCF Hits Major Milestones with Global Community Growth, Record Industry Investment and a New Generation of Projects to Build AI Systems in Production
items.summary: New Sandbox projects, including Agent Substrate and OpenShell, expand CNCF’s portfolio to 231 projects as the community adds over 5.5 million cloud native developers in 12 months, welcomes eight Platinum memberships and brings together 82,000 attendees at events worldwide SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 – Nov. 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today highlighted a year of significant momentum, marked by new sandbox projects — including OpenShell and Agent Substrate — and milestones expanding open infrastructure for training AI models, scaling inference and securely operating autonomous agents. New Sandbox projects, including Agent Substrate and OpenShell, expand CNCF’s portfolio to 231 projects as the community adds over 5.5 million cloud native developers in 12 months, welcomes eight Platinum memberships and brings together 82,000 attendees at events worldwide

SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 – Nov. 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today highlighted a year of significant momentum, marked by new sandbox projects — including OpenShell and Agent Substrate —  and milestones expanding open infrastructure for training AI models, scaling inference and securely operating autonomous agents. The announcement builds on continued member investment, a global cloud native developer population surpassing 21 million and technical progress across a foundation now spanning 231 projects. 

In the past year, cloud native and CNCF events brought together 82,000 attendees globally at record-breaking events across more than 50 countries, while 32 new projects expanded the foundation’s technology portfolio, including exciting new Sandbox Projects Agent Substrate andllm-d, as well as OpenShell secure runtimes for AI agents. That momentum extended with new Platinum members Adyen, Broadcom, CoreWeave, CVS, HAProxy, NVIDIA, OVHcloud and Vultr representing the chipmakers, neoclouds and enterprise users underpinning the next generation of AI infrastructure.

“AI teams need control over where their models run, what their agents can do, and how their systems behave in production,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director of CNCF. “A year ago, we were talking about the opportunity in inference. Today, this community is building the infrastructure to train models, run inference and put agents to work with the security and scale production demands. We’re bringing that work together in the open so developers retain choice across models, hardware and providers. Bring your hardest problems, contribute what you’ve learned and help us build what comes next.”

OpenShell Brings Agent Runtime Security into Ecosystem Stewardship

OpenShell is joining CNCF as a Sandbox project, bringing the secure runtime for autonomous AI agents into vendor-neutral, ecosystem-led stewardship.

Spearheaded by NVIDIA, OpenShell governs how agents execute, which resources and data they can access and where inference requests are routed. It provides policy enforcement in the infrastructure surrounding an agent, helping organizations control access to files, networks, credentials and model endpoints as agents perform increasingly complex tasks and work at scale.

The contribution gives developers, platform teams and security practitioners a direct role in shaping the runtime foundation for AI and addresses the security, control and governance challenges that stand between experimentation and production.

An Expanding Foundation to Train, Infer and Act

CNCF project contributions announced today broaden the technologies available to organizations building AI infrastructure:

  • Agent Substrate provides a zero-trust runtime for executing AI agents on Kubernetes while isolating untrusted code.
  • gVisor strengthens workload isolation through a user-space kernel that limits exposure to the host operating system.
  • KubeRay supports running and managing Ray workloads on Kubernetes for distributed computing, including AI training and inference.
  • OpenRL brings Kubernetes-native orchestration to reinforcement learning, helping teams coordinate the compute required for model post-training.
  • OpenShell adds runtime governance and policy enforcement for autonomous agents.

These projects build on substantial AI progress over the last twelve months:

  • Distributed inference: llm-d joined CNCF and reached its 1.0 release, advancing an open framework for deploying and scaling distributed large language model inference.
  • AI lifecycle maturity: Kubeflow graduated, recognizing the maturity of its ecosystem for data processing, model training, fine-tuning and serving.
  • Accelerator efficiency: HAMi advanced to incubation, supporting the sharing and scheduling of heterogeneous accelerators on Kubernetes.
  • Infrastructure capabilities: Kubernetes advanced workload-aware scheduling and Dynamic Resource Allocation, improving how complex AI workloads coordinate, compute and access specialized hardware.

Together, these milestones strengthen the application delivery, orchestration, messaging, data and operational infrastructure on which production systems depend.

items.title: CNCF Launches Certified Kubernetes Network Engineer Certification (CKNE) to Advance Production Ready Networking Skills for AI Era
items.summary: New certification validates specialized expertise in Kubernetes networking, security and troubleshooting as demand for cloud native skills grows Key Highlights The Certified Kubernetes Network Engineer (CKNE) joins CNCF’s certification portfolio, validating hands-on expertise in designing, securing and troubleshooting networking across production Kubernetes environments. CKNE certification and CKNE Certification Pathway (5 modules) reinforce CNCF’s commitment to accessible, vendor-neutral education helping individuals advance their careers while enabling organizations to build and maintain secure, reliable and scalable systems. CNCF to expand its certification roadmap with two additional credentials planned for 2027: Kubernetes AI Associate (KAIA) and Certified Kubernetes Inference Engineer (CKIE). SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America – November 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation ® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced the global availability of the Certified Kubernetes Network Engineer (CKNE) certification. Developed in collaboration with Linux Foundation Education , the new exam is designed to validate hands-on expertise in designing, securing and troubleshooting networking across production Kubernetes environments. As organizations rely on Kubernetes to support all types of workloads including AI, networking has become a critical component of secure, reliable and scalable infrastructure. CKNE addresses the growing demand for specialized networking expertise, providing platform engineers, network engineers and site reliability engineers (SREs) with a vendor-neutral credential that demonstrates proficiency across the Kubernetes networking stack. “Networking is fundamental to running Kubernetes reliably at scale, yet it remains one of the most complex areas for teams operating production environments,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “As cloud native infrastructure grows to support more AI driven workloads, organizations need engineers who understand how to secure, connect and troubleshoot these systems. CKNE establishes a clear benchmark for that expertise while helping professionals build the specialized cloud native skills needed to operate modern network infrastructure.” The CKNE is a performance-based, 120-minute certification exam that evaluates candidates through practical tasks in a Linux-based remote desktop environment. The exam covers five key domains which are important for organizations operating Kubernetes across multi-cluster, hybrid and enterprise environments: Core Infrastructure and CNI (15%), Service Networking and DNS (25%), Advanced Traffic Management (20%), Network Security and Policy (25%), and Observability (15%). While no prior certifications are required, CKNE assumes Kubernetes administration knowledge comparable to the Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) certification. The credential builds on foundational Kubernetes skills while enabling professionals to demonstrate deeper specialization in networking and security. Special thanks to the following companies who contributed to the creation of CKNE: Dojobits, Ericsson, Infosys, Isovalent — now part of Cisco, Kong, Microsoft, RX-M and Solo.io Introducing the CKNE Certification Pathway To support professionals preparing for the new certification, CNCF and Linux Foundation Education are also introducing the CKNE Certification Pathway , a comprehensive training program designed to build practical Kubernetes networking expertise. “Building reliable Kubernetes infrastructure requires more than foundational knowledge, especially as organizations scale their cloud native and AI workloads,” said Clyde Seepersad, senior vice president and general manager, Linux Foundation Education. “The CKNE certification and accompanying training pathway provide a practical approach to expanding expertise that benefits both individual careers and the organizations that depend on these systems.” The pathway includes five specialized training modules aligned with the certification’s core competencies: Kubernetes Network Foundations: CNI and Pod Connectivity (LFS2015): Establishes foundational knowledge of Kubernetes networking architecture, CNI and Pod-to-Pod connectivity. Kubernetes Service Networking and DNS (LFS2016): Explores service discovery, DNS resolution and connectivity between applications running in Kubernetes environments. Advanced Kubernetes Traffic Management (LFS2017): Builds expertise in managing and routing application traffic across complex Kubernetes environments. Kubernetes Network Security and Policy (LFS2018): Focuses on securing Kubernetes network communication through traffic controls, network policies and related security mechanisms. Kubernetes Network Observability (LFS2019): Develops skills in monitoring, diagnosing and troubleshooting networking behavior across Kubernetes clusters. The five modules will be available as a bundled training pathway alongside the CKNE certification, offering candidates a structured approach to developing the practical skills required to manage production Kubernetes networking. “With CKNE and its accompanying certification pathway, we’re serving two vital audiences: helping network professionals bridge their expertise into the cloud native ecosystem, while enabling Kubernetes engineers to master advanced networking challenges,” said Christophe Sauthier, cloud native training and certification lead, CNCF. “This pathway builds confidence across both disciplines, giving organizations a trusted benchmark to identify talent ready for complex, production-grade cloud environments.” Expanding CNCF’s Cloud Native Certification Portfolio The launch of CKNE builds on CNCF’s continued investment in cloud native education and professional development, expanding a certification portfolio designed to support engineers at every stage of their careers. As Kubernetes adoption matures, more organizations require professionals with expertise beyond foundational cluster administration, including platform engineering, security, observability and networking. Certifications such as the Certified Cloud Native Platform Engineer (CNPE) and CKNE reflect this evolution, providing opportunities for professionals to validate specialized skills across production environments. Looking ahead, CNCF also plans to introduce two additional certifications in 2027: Kubernetes AI Associate (KAIA) and Certified Kubernetes Inference Engineer (CKIE) . These upcoming credentials will further expand CNCF’s training and certification portfolio as AI and cloud native technologies continue to converge. items.title: Researcher bypassed Meta smart glasses’ safeguards to run her own code
items.summary: We’ve written before about what Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses can see and hear , and who might get to use that information. Those worries focus on how the glasses handle information during normal use. A security researcher has now shown how to bypass a safeguard meant to stop unauthorized software running on them. Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. For the technical details I’ll gladly refer you to her own post about it. The glasses are controlled by the Meta AI app on the owner’s phone. Developers can add their own apps to the glasses through a developer tool, and the phone sends that software to the glasses to install. The glasses were supposed to check that the software really came from Meta. In older firmware (up to and including version 126), they didn’t check, so the researcher could swap in an app of her own. Meta introduced a check in firmware version 127 to verify the app’s digital signature to prove that it came from Meta . The researcher found the on/off switch for that signature check came from a settings file passed along by the phone. The glasses only checked the file was correctly formed, not whether it had been tampered with. Changing a single byte in the file turned the signature check off. Once her app was running, she could send commands to the glasses from the paired phone over a wireless connection. The glasses have a camera, microphones and a wireless connection, and they sit on your face all day. A wearable that can be made to run unapproved code goes beyond a privacy-policy question. It becomes a security question about who controls the device. As we’ve seen, some cheaper smart glasses already are a security disaster . In this case the person running the code would be the person that controls the phone. If malicious software running on the glasses could access the camera or stored recordings, it could potentially send footage to an attacker’s server. Pamoutaf’s research doesn’t demonstrate that scenario, but it raises questions about what that software might be able to access. In her post she promised a follow-up exploring other potential ways to attack the glasses. How to stay safe Keep the glasses’ firmware and the Meta AI app updated, and avoid unofficial apps or modifications. If smart glasses are just another gadget to you, I’d leave them on the shelf. If you rely on them as an accessibility aid, you deserve technology that helps you without putting your privacy or other people’s at risk. Scammers know more about you than you think. items.title: Huntress hands incident responders free ITDR to stop attackers walking back in
items.summary: Huntress has launched a global Incident Response (IR) Engagement Programme that gives participating IR firms 60 days of free Huntress protection for their clients, both during an active incident and in the weeks of recovery afterward. The programme goes after a familiar problem in breach recovery: re-compromise. Once the initial intrusion has been contained, attackers often come back in through whatever the clean-up missed, whether that is stolen credentials, a hijacked session, a malicious OAuth grant or an over-privileged account. To begin with, the program focuses on business email compromise (BEC) and identity-based attacks. IR partners can deploy Huntress in the middle of a breach without going through a traditional sales cycle. That gives them access to Huntress Managed ITDR, which provides 24/7 monitoring and response for suspicious logins, compromised sessions, credential theft and OAuth abuse. Looking back and checking the fix A feature called ITDR Lookback lets responders review up to six months of historical identity activity. That matters in BEC cases, where investigators often find the compromise point long after the attack began. Alongside this, Huntress Managed ISPM (identity security posture management) flags misconfigurations, excessive privileges and weak authentication policies. Responders can use it to confirm that remediation has actually held before they close an engagement. Huntress’s SOC also sets up dedicated communication channels with each IR partner during an engagement. The IR firm keeps ownership of the customer relationship and leads the remediation work. “Recovery and protection must go hand in hand, and when a business is under attack, every minute without protection matters,” said Tuan Nguyen, VP of Channels and Alliances at Huntress. “By putting the Huntress Agentic Security Platform in the hands of incident responders to immediately contain threats and prevent further damage, we’re helping businesses fight back, recover stronger, and stay protected. It’s another step in our mission to protect all businesses, especially when they need us most.” Gene Yu, CEO of incident response firm Blackpanda, argued that recovery on its own is not enough. “Across Asia, businesses are increasingly recognizing that cyber resilience requires more than responding to an attack or covering its financial fallout,” said Gene Yu, CEO of Blackpanda. “Incident response and cyber insurance are two critical pieces of the puzzle, but neither can prevent an attacker from striking again. By integrating continuous protection directly into the recovery process, we can help businesses contain threats, recover with confidence, and emerge from an incident better protected against the next attack.” When the 60 days are up, clients can choose to move on to continuous managed protection from Huntress’s 24/7 AI-centric SOC. Huntress currently protects more than 6 million endpoints and 17 million identities. The programme is available now to participating IR firms worldwide.

items.summary: TL;DR: AI agent security in banking requires controls that can deny prohibited workload actions before they complete, because an alert does not revoke an agent’s authority. An agent can use legitimate credentials to create financial exposure without exploiting a vulnerability. How to Export Cortex XDR Logs
items.summary: Use the XQL query APIs. Start a query with /public_api/v1/xql/start_xql_query, which returns an execution ID. Fetch the results with /public_api/v1/xql/get_query_results in JSON. That call returns up to 1,000 results inline; anything bigger comes back as a stream ID you pass to /public_api/v1/xql/get_query_results_stream. Authentication uses two headers: your API key in Authorization and its ID in x-xdr-auth-id. Cortex XDR collects detailed endpoint telemetry, plus network and identity data in many deployments. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API key. Create one in the Cortex XDR settings (the standard key type is simplest) with a role that can run XQL queries. Note the key and its ID. Your API URL. It’s shown when you create the key, in the form https://api- .xdr. .paloaltonetworks.com. License and quota. The XQL APIs need a Cortex XDR Pro license. Queries draw on your XQL quota, and you can run up to four API queries in parallel. The dataset. Endpoint telemetry is in xdr_data, with fields such as agent_hostname, event_type, action_process_image_command_line and actor_process_image_name. Build the query in the Query Builder first. Export with the XQL APIs XDR="https://api- .xdr. .paloaltonetworks.com" H1="Authorization: $XDR_API_KEY" H2="x-xdr-auth-id: $XDR_API_KEY_ID" # 1. start the query (timeframe in epoch milliseconds) QID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$XDR/public_api/v1/xql/start_xql_query" -H "$H1" -H "$H2" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"request_data": {"query": "dataset = xdr_data | filter agent_hostname = \"WS-042\" | fields _time, agent_hostname, event_type, action_process_image_name, action_process_image_command_line, actor_process_image_name", "timeframe": {"from": 1792368000000, "to": 1792454400000}}}' \ | jq -r '.reply') # 2. wait for the results while :; do RESP=$(curl -sS -X POST "$XDR/public_api/v1/xql/get_query_results" -H "$H1" -H "$H2" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"request_data\": {\"query_id\": \"$QID\", \"pending_flag\": true, \"format\": \"json\"}}") [ "$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.reply.status')" != "PENDING" ] && break sleep 5 done # 3. up to 1,000 results inline; more through the stream STREAM=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.reply.results.stream_id // empty') if [ -n "$STREAM" ]; then curl -sS -X POST "$XDR/public_api/v1/xql/get_query_results_stream" -H "$H1" -H "$H2" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"request_data\": {\"stream_id\": \"$STREAM\", \"is_gzip_compressed\": false}}" > xdr_ws042_1019.jsonl else echo "$RESP" | jq -c '.reply.results.data[]' > xdr_ws042_1019.jsonl fi The timeframe above is 2026-10-19 00:00 UTC to 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 Key and key ID swapped, or the key expired Key in Authorization, ID in x-xdr-auth-id License error No XDR Pro license XQL APIs need XDR Pro Quota errors XQL quota used up, or more than four parallel queries Wait; narrow the query Exactly 1,000 results Stream not used Fetch the rest with the stream ID Query errors XQL syntax Test in the Query Builder first FAQ Can I export incidents and alerts? Yes, through separate incident and alert APIs. For LogTotal, export the telemetry behind them. What about raw third-party logs? If you ingest them into Cortex, they live in their own datasets and come out the same way.

items.title: North Korean Hackers Target Drone Technology and Software Supply Chains in New Cyberespionage Campaigns
items.summary: North Korean hackers have renewed efforts to steal drone technology while expanding attacks against software developers and the projects they maintain. Activity tracked between April and September 2026 shows Lazarus returning to European defense targets, while DeceptiveDevelopment used stolen developer credentials to spread malicious code through software supply chains. The campaigns share a familiar starting point: a convincing job offer that persuades someone to run attacker-controlled software. Their goals then diverge. Lazarus seeks access to sensitive defense systems and technical knowledge, while DeceptiveDevelopment turns compromised developer accounts into distribution channels, exposing users who never interacted with the original fake recruiter. ESET researchers identified updated malware across these operations, including MortPusLoader, LightlessTeaR, OmniStealer, and DEV#POPPER RAT. Their latest APT Activity Report describes changes in delivery, persistence, and command infrastructure. The findings build on earlier European drone industry attacks , but the latest reporting shows renewed targeting and a broader software distribution risk. North Korean Hackers Target Drone Technology and Software Supply Chains Operation DreamJob resumed targeting drone technology and related supply chains around June 2026, following a quiet period after activity documented in October 2025. ESET observed attacks against defense companies, mainly in Europe, including original equipment manufacturers and important suppliers within the unmanned aircraft systems industry. In one attack against a Central European defense company, an employee received a password-protected ZIP archive containing a BAE Systems-themed job description. The PDF had an incorrect header, and the archive included a trojanized SumatraPDF viewer specifically built to open it. This made the supplied viewer appear necessary for reading the document. The approach echoes job themed manufacturing attacks , where a document viewer helped deliver malware under a recruitment pretext. In the latest campaign, Lazarus replaced previously used WinMerge plugins, tracked as BinMergeLoader, with two trojanized Notepad++ plugins collectively named MortPusLoader. Familiar software remained central to making the malicious files look credible. The main payload was either ScoringMathTea, also called ForestTiger, or LightlessTeaR, a rewritten version of LightlessCan. Execution chain using NullReceiver (Source – ESET) LightlessTeaR implements common Windows commands internally instead of launching them through the command line, reducing visible command execution. Compromised Roundcube Webmail servers belonging to academic and government institutions in South America supported command-and-control communications. ESET assesses that access to drone designs and manufacturing knowledge could help North Korea develop its own capabilities. Its earlier drone espionage research connected similar targeting with proprietary information theft. However, the precise information sought in individual intrusions remains uncertain, and the Ukraine war connection is an assessment rather than proof of direct coordination with Russia. Developer Compromises Expand Into Software Supply Chains DeceptiveDevelopment widened its reach by stealing Git credentials, SSH keys, and access tokens after developers ran malicious recruitment tasks. The attackers then used that access to inject code into public and private repositories, often rewriting commit history to hide changes. Earlier fake job interview challenges explain the recruitment setup behind this expanding threat. Affected artifacts reached npm, the Go module mirror, Packagist, PyPI, and browser extension marketplaces. Most compromised projects were small utilities maintained by individuals. ESET said this pattern suggested automated propagation rather than carefully selected targeting: each poisoned project could become another entry point for downstream users. The group also adopted NullReceiver, a blockchain-based method for locating command servers. A loader checks the latest outgoing transaction from a hardcoded Ethereum wallet and extracts the server IP from the recipient address. As previously covered in blockchain hidden malware servers , operators can change servers through another transaction without updating the malicious package. ESET also found this lookup mechanism launched through a hidden VS Code task inside a legitimate developer’s compromised repository. Payloads included OmniStealer, a cross-platform Python tool targeting credentials, wallets, password managers, and developer secrets. Updated DEV#POPPER RAT versions inserted code into VS Code, Cursor, and Discord to execute whenever those applications started. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Source-published indicator Context npm package bianira-ui@1.27.0 NullReceiver loader npm package fluid-type-ui@2.0.8 NullReceiver loader Ethereum wallet 0xa322e5f3d311d3080e6f0121063e9adc2490ef1a Attacker lookup wallet Encoded recipient 0xa658863ea658863e68656c6c6f6970626f742121 Encodes command-server address C2 endpoints 166.88.134.62:443 , 166.88.134.62:80 Published command infrastructure Code marker A10-npm3! Loader signature string Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: How to Export Cortex XSIAM Logs
items.summary: Cortex XSIAM uses the same XQL query APIs as Cortex XDR: start a query, wait for results, and use a stream for anything over 1,000 rows. What’s different is the data. Third-party logs land in raw datasets, usually named _ _raw, and the original log line sits in the _raw_log field. Select that field, and the export gives you back exactly what the source sent. XSIAM is Palo Alto Networks’ SOC platform, and it’s where many former QRadar SaaS customers ended up after the 2024 deal. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API key and URL. Create a key with a role that can run XQL queries; note the key, its ID and the API URL shown with it. Find the dataset. In the Query Builder, list datasets (dataset = offers suggestions). Raw third-party data follows the _ _raw pattern, for example fortinet_fortigate_raw. Endpoint telemetry is in xdr_data. Hot and cold storage. Recent data is in hot storage and queries quickly. Older data may be in cold storage, which needs its own query approach and costs more quota. Export with the XQL APIs To get raw lines from a FortiGate dataset: dataset = fortinet_fortigate_raw | filter _raw_log contains "web-03" | fields _time, _raw_log Run it through start_xql_query and get_query_results (plus get_query_results_stream above 1,000 rows), as in the Cortex XDR guide. Then turn the JSON into raw lines: jq -r '._raw_log' xsiam_fortigate_1019.jsonl > xsiam_fortigate_1019.log For normalized data across sources, query the data model (XDM) instead. You get consistent field names, but not the original wording. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file: raw lines from _raw_log, or the JSON rows. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Dataset not found Name differs in your tenant List datasets in the Query Builder _raw_log is empty The source was ingested as structured data Export the parsed fields instead Exactly 1,000 results Stream not used Use get_query_results_stream Quota errors XQL quota used, or cold storage queries Narrow the window; check quota Old data missing It’s in cold storage Query cold storage, or restore it FAQ Raw or XDM? Raw (_raw_log) for LogTotal, because it keeps the source’s own format. XDM when you need the same fields across many sources. I moved from QRadar SaaS. Is my old data here? That depends on your migration. Check which datasets hold the migrated history.

items.title: Set your intended architecture with your coding agent, skip the diagram
items.summary: SonarQube Cloud now lets you define your project's intended architecture by working directly with your coding agent through the SonarQube CLI or the SonarQube MCP Server . Explore your current architecture through your agent, while it proposes components and the allowed relationships for your intended architecture that you confirm before saving. Deviations then surface as maintainability issues in your existing workflow, catching architectural drift before it compounds. Architectural debt does not accumulate at the same rate as code-level debt. It compounds 2.8 times faster, because a single misplaced dependency or an improperly exposed component does not stay contained. It ripples through every module that touches it, making the whole system harder to change safely. AI coding agents make this problem more urgent, not less. An AI agent can generate functioning code at a speed no human team can match, but it does so without knowing about allowable components dependencies, or which boundaries exist to keep your system modular. The result is architectural drift: code that passes tests and does what was asked, while quietly violating the structure your team relies on to keep the codebase maintainable. Until now, fixing that gap meant building your intended architecture by hand, a process that most teams deprioritized because it competed with the time they needed to ship features. SonarQube Cloud closes that gap by putting the work where development already happens: inside a conversation with your coding agent. What does it mean to define architecture with a coding agent? Instead of opening a tool to document your architecture, you ask your coding agent questions about your codebase and let it do the analysis. Your agent reads the current architecture of your project directly from SonarQube Cloud through the SonarQube CLI or the SonarQube MCP Server, the same way it reads any other context about your code. You can ask it what you would ask a teammate who already knows the system: What are the top-level components of this project? How does the billing component use the persistence component? Which components depend on this component? Your agent starts with a focused view of the architecture and requests more detail on specific components as the conversation requires it, rather than loading the entire system at once. How do you turn current architecture into intended architecture? Exploring the current state is only half the job. You can ask your agent to help define how the project should be built going forward. Your agent proposes components and the relationships allowed between them, based on what it understands about your codebase from SonarQube. You decide what to keep and what to leave out of your intended architecture that it suggests. Before anything is saved, you can ask your agent to preview the changes, review them with you, and confirm them together. This matters for a practical reason: your agent works within your own SonarQube permissions. It can only change what you are authorized to change, so architectural authority stays with the people accountable for it, not with the agent itself. Where does the intended architecture live once it's defined? The result is stored as the intended architecture in SonarQube Cloud, structured the same way a model built through the web editor is. From that point forward, every analysis checks your code against it. If a software developer or an agent introduces a relationship that violates the intended architecture, such as an illegal dependency between components, SonarQube Cloud raises it as a maintainability issue in the same workflow your team already uses to triage other findings. You do not need a separate architecture review process. The deviation shows up where your team is already looking. You can keep refining the architecture with your agent or manually in the UI over time, one level of detail at a time, as the system evolves and new components are added. Can you automate architecture setup across many projects? For teams managing more than a handful of projects, manually repeating this process for every repository does not scale. The same capabilities used by your coding agent are available as public Web API endpoints, documented for building your own integrations. You can read the current architecture of a project or create, read, replace, and delete its intended architecture programmatically. That makes it possible to push a standardized intended architecture to many projects from a single template, or feed architecture data into internal tooling your team already relies on. Access follows the same governance model as the conversational workflow. Reading architecture data requires "Browse" permission on the project. Writing to it requires the "Administer architecture" permission, keeping that authority with the people responsible for setting the standard. Get started Install the SonarQube CLI and log in to SonarQube Cloud. If you use Claude Code or Cursor, run Sonar architecture install-skill in your terminal. This teaches your agent how to explore the architecture through a skill and how to confirm changes with you before saving. With other agents, ask them to run Sonar architecture --help to see the available commands. In your project, start a new agent session and ask "Show me the top-level architecture of this project," then "Help me define the intended architecture." If you use the SonarQube MCP Server instead, update to the latest release with architecture support, add architecture to your existing SONARQUBE_TOOLSETS configuration, and restart the SONARQUBE MCP SERVER connection. Architecture management with a coding agent is available now in SonarQube Cloud , with support for Java , C# , JavaScript , TypeScript , and Python .

items.title: Verification is the factory's feedback system
items.summary: Agents have made code abundant, but confidence is scarce, specifically confidence that the code is correct, secure, and ready to ship. Developers tell us that 5% of organizations run AI software factories today and 34% expect to within a year. As factories take on more of the work, the quality of what they ship will depend less on which model writes the code and more on how well each factory checks it. Teams have to engineer confidence into the software factory the same way they engineer reliability into any production system, and that work starts with verification. Benedikt Stemmildt, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of hackers&wizards and co-author with Alex Merced of Building the Agentic Software Factory , develops these systems with clients every day. On the latest episode of The Next Commit , he told host Tom Howlett that "ultimately this is all about trust." For Benedikt, building that trust means designing factories to run without a human in the loop and giving them checks the team can rely on in place of reading every change. Turn each failure into a check Teams improve a software factory by turning each failure into a new check that the factory applies to every change. In that sense, verification is the factory’s feedback system. Teams get the most from it when they run checks inside the development loops, starting with the agentic loop, so each check can shape a change while the agent is still writing it. Teams that build it in this way end up with clear intent, guardrails that keep agents on track, independent verification, and evidence that every check ran. A factory that falls short on any of those gives its owners little reason to trust what it ships. When Benedikt finds a problem in what a factory produced, he leaves the feature code alone and changes the factory. "I'm reviewing the artifact the factory produced," he says. "If I see something that isn't what we want, I fix the factory." He also starts clients on narrow, repeated work such as dependency updates, because the team already knows which verifications that lane needs before the factory runs. Confidence needs both kinds of verification Sonar embeds two kinds of verification at every stage. Deterministic verification is a repeatable assessment based on structural rules and known patterns, and it gives the same answer every time without changing that answer under pressure, which makes it a dependable gate for the standards a team has written down. Agentic verification applies deliberate, context-aware reasoning to verify intent and discover anomalies, covering business logic, deep semantics, and other problems no rule anticipates. Teams need both kinds, because each one checks what the other can't. Benedikt strikes the same balance in his factories, adding lint rules and ArchUnit tests "so that you can trust the non-determinism more" and handling contextual problems with skills and instructions. He warns that a factory loaded with too many hard constraints becomes "like a cage" that stalls or keeps pulling in a human, while a factory with too few gives its owners nothing to trust. Both kinds also have to run independently of the agent, model, or developer that wrote the code. Sonar verifies separately from the agents and models a team uses, so one standard holds across all of them, including code written by people. A factory that asks another model to judge its output inherits that model's inconsistency, and recent research shows frontier LLM judges change 7% to 17% of their verdicts when asked the same question again, even with their randomness setting turned all the way down. As Benedikt points out, teams trust senior engineers even though people are non-deterministic, because a senior engineer works within a known range and won't do anything wildly wrong. Agents carry no such guarantee, and he describes results that leave you asking "what on earth?" Teams need checks that stay the same no matter which agent made the change. One standard that teaches the agent in every loop A check that only reports a problem invites the agent to make the warning disappear, and Benedikt's linter example demonstrates the cost. A linter flags a 15-line method against a 10-line limit, and the agent "will just cut it in half," producing two shorter methods that pass the check and weaken the design. An experienced developer would read the warning as a reason to rethink the method's responsibilities, but that knowledge never appears in the message. Benedikt argues that most of our tooling was written for senior engineers, while agents benefit from explicit guidance the way junior developers do. Sonar issues include rule descriptions that explain why an issue matters and remediation guidance that points toward a sound correction, which gives an agent the context to fix the underlying problem rather than game the check. Sonar applies that standard wherever agents touch code. In the agentic loop, Sonar Vortex gives the agent context and constraints before it writes, verifies each change against the same SonarQube quality profile that gates merges, and prompts the agent to correct its output when a check fails. In the CI verification loop, SonarQube sets the standard through quality profiles and quality gates, and Gitar reviews each pull request for logic and intent and iterates on fixes until CI is green. SonarQube sets the standard; Gitar enforces it at merge speed. In the code maintenance loop, SonarQube Remediation Agent fixes issues in the background and rechecks each fix with the engine that found it, so only verified fixes ship. Every check leaves a consistent, auditable record, which helps a team understand a codebase it no longer reads line by line. Benedikt considers ownership of that standard the hardest part of building factories. "When we build factories with our clients, it's not a technology problem, not at all," he says. He describes the factory as an internal product, built by factory engineers and fed by product engineers who work closely with the business, and he notes that teams are still working out who owns context, skills, and verification between them. A shared verification standard gives both groups the same definition of good. Deciding what the factory treats as “good” The teams building software factories today will decide what their factories treat as “good.” Benedikt closed the episode with advice for developers adjusting to the change: "Find your new flow because this is not going away." Listen to the full episode of The Next Commit with Benedikt Stemmildt , then explore how Sonar's AI code verification fits into your software factory.

items.title: Portfolio Hierarchies arrives in SonarQube Cloud
items.summary: Enterprise organizations running dozens or hundreds of projects often manage their software projects as a hierarchical relationship. A hierarchy that exists only on paper is a hierarchy nobody can navigate, govern, or trust. This release gives that structure a visual, navigable interface. SonarQube Cloud now provides a dedicated portfolio hierarchy management in a UI that lets enterprise admins, divisional directors, and CISOs see parent-child portfolio relationships at a glance, understand exactly where they stand within a deep structure, and build or modify that structure with guardrails that prevent invalid changes before they happen. Who can use SonarQube Cloud portfolio hierarchy management? This release is built for enterprise teams managing multi-level portfolio structures across many projects and teams from a single interface. It is currently available to everyone with a SonarQube Cloud Enterprise plan. What's new in SonarQube Cloud enterprise portfolio management? Visual hierarchy at unlimited depth Organizational structures do not stop at two or three levels, so the hierarchy view does not either. The portfolio hierarchy management UI renders a full tree view of parent-child portfolio relationships, supporting unlimited nesting depth in this first version. Each level uses iconography and labeling to make the list easy to follow, no matter how many levels it has. Breadcrumb signposting at every level Losing track of your position inside a deep hierarchy is not a cosmetic inconvenience, it is a governance risk: a change made at the wrong level can misattribute metrics or break reporting for an entire division. A breadcrumb trail shows your current position in the structure at every level you navigate, so you always know exactly where a given portfolio sits relative to the rest of the organization before you act on it. Circular reference protection with plain-language messages A circular reference, a loop or self-link in the hierarchy, is not just an error state, it is a structural problem that can silently corrupt reporting if it goes undetected. SonarQube Cloud now prevents circular relationships in portfolio hierarchies, for example placing a parent portfolio under one of its own children. It blocks the change before saving and displays a plain-language message explaining why the relationship is not allowed. Guided link and unlink flows with confirmation Restructuring a portfolio hierarchy has real consequences for reporting and compliance, so making that change should never be a single accidental click. Linking a child portfolio to a parent, or unlinking one from the hierarchy, now runs through a guided flow with an explicit confirmation step before the change commits, giving admins a clear understanding of the consequences before they act. Clear level distinction at any depth Telling parent from child at a glance matters more as a hierarchy grows, not less. Each level in the tree is visually distinguished through indentation, iconography, and labeling. Therefore, the relationship between any two portfolios is clear, without requiring a user to manually trace the structure. Performance built for scale SonarQube Cloud’s portfolio hierarchy view lets users expand and collapse branches to explore nested portfolios, revealing child portfolios as branches are expanded, rather than displaying every level at once. Keyboard accessibility The hierarchy tree is fully keyboard-navigable, with appropriate ARIA roles applied to parent-child relationships, so the interface is usable for admins who rely on keyboard navigation rather than a mouse. How do I get started with portfolio hierarchy management in SonarQube Cloud? The portfolio hierarchy management feature is available now to eligible SonarQube Cloud Enterprise customers. A new portfolio hierarchy guide walks through building, navigating, and managing a hierarchy end to end, and the Enterprise admin documentation has been updated to reflect the new interface and workflows. Organizing structure is the first step. Governing it at scale is the reason that structure needs to be visible in the first place.

items.title: Weird licenses and the new open source
items.summary: Somewhere on an IRC channel, I ended up in a conversation about the The Filthy Human Hands (FHH) License . It wasn't the first time weird licenses were discussed there: Reticulum 's sparked some interesting discussions as well. Let's start from the beginning. If you don't want to read the Wikipedia article on Free Software , a couple of years ago, I gave a small presentation at school as part of the "Oral communication in English" course, which is a (shoddy) cake-based explanation of the topic. Long story short, a Free Software is a software with 4 freedoms: The freedom to run the program as you wish, for any purpose. The freedom to study how the program works, and change it to make it do what you wish. Access to the source code is a precondition for this. The freedom to redistribute copies so you can help others. The freedom to distribute copies of your modified versions to others. By doing this you can give the whole community a chance to benefit from your changes. There is also the term Open Source, which is more or less Free Software but without the sociopolitical aspect of it, which is like a pizza without olives, or art without context: something devoid of meaning, a business-oriented product instead of a creation. Like in every sociopolitical endeavour, people sometimes disagree, leading to subtle but important variations. One of the most important one in the Free Software movement has been the question of the copyleft : should derivatives of Free Software be licensed under the same license? Some licenses, like the GPL says yes and this includes everything built on top of GPL code, the LGPL says that only code under LGPL needs to be released as LGPL, and others, called permissive licenses, like the BSD and MIT don't impose such restrictions. The Free Software movement started in 1986, so we're around 40 years later now, and the picture is pretty bleak: technically, one could argue that it won, as every computer-using company in the world depends on Free Software one way or the other: Firefox, Linux, VLC, Chrome, Ubuntu, Apache, nginx, Wikipedia, Open Street Map, Open Food Facts, … as well as more fundamental software components like curl, libxml, busybox, OpenSSL, GCC, clang, … Yet virtually none of them do contribute back to those commons, some of them being thanklessly maintained by a random person in Nebraska . Worse, a handful of computer-related companies ("cloud providers") are making ungodly amount of money renting infrastructure running Free Software, most smart™ devices are running Free Software, every single software producing/selling company depends on Free Software, and again, almost none contribute back meaningfully. A small number are trying to sponsor some projects they're depending on, but it often feels like a crass move for software that are maintained as a hobby: "Could you please garden a bit more efficiently, and add 150 apple trees to your small garden? We need it for our business, here is a 1000€ one-time payment" With AI making everything worse, Free Software maintainers are now wasting their time dealing with unreviewable useless pull-requests, drowning into a sea of low-quality no-fix-provided bug reports, being demoralized by vibe-coded forks adding shiny features that are never going to be upstreamable and thus upstreamed. It really feels as if nobody is even contemplating making the pedestrian effort of trying to avoid murdering the golden goose. Copyleft does help to mitigate those behaviours a bit, as companies aren't usually big fans to having to release their secret source code. The Asahi Linux project recently re-licensed its software from MIT to LGPL, to make it, if only symbolically, harder for people to profit from the labor without giving anything back. Unfortunately, there are a handful of tricks to bypass copyleft: don't use GPL as all, use strong boundaries (like Android is doing: Linux for its kernel, but everything running on top of it can have whatever license), rent the software to the users (every Cloud is doing that, and most ISP too), provide a context-free dump of the modifications and prevent users from modifying the code their devices are running, simplify ignore the license as the odds of somebody suing you are low, … If copyleft isn't the answer, maybe it's time to find better licenses? This includes but is not limited to fascism, racism, sexism, misogyny, ableism, transphobia (including erasure and/or denial of nonbinary identities), homophobia, ageism, sane-ism (including denial of multiplicity and/or plurality), and discrimination against non-human identities. I think it's by design, and must be taken as a statement. One could use any other open-to-interpretation terms and obtain the same effects, namely that any entity with a legal department won't use it, and those small enough to not have one won't be able to sell/rent to those who do. What's beautiful about it, is that it does fit perfectly into the idea of the small web, of small communities with bespoke governance, of bricolage and of excluding authoritarianism/capitalism/morons/… by design. Given the current dire state of the world, I think it's time to realise that Free Software isn't enough, and that not wanting to have code ending up in whatever war machine bombing kids and families is less radical than the idea of Free Software at its inception 40 years ago. Somewhere on an IRC channel, I ended up in a conversation about the The Filthy Human Hands (FHH) License. It wasn't the first time weird licenses were discussed there: Reticulum's sparked some interesting discussions as well.

Let's start from the beginning.

If you don't want to read the Wikipedia article on Free Software, a couple of years ago, I gave a small presentation at school as part of the "Oral communication in English" course, which is a (shoddy) cake-based explanation of the topic. Long story short, a Free Software is a software with 4 freedoms:

  1. The freedom to run the program as you wish, for any purpose.
  2. The freedom to study how the program works, and change it to make it do what you wish. Access to the source code is a precondition for this.
  3. The freedom to redistribute copies so you can help others.
  4. The freedom to distribute copies of your modified versions to others. By doing this you can give the whole community a chance to benefit from your changes.

There is also the term Open Source, which is more or less Free Software but without the sociopolitical aspect of it, which is like a pizza without olives, or art without context: something devoid of meaning, a business-oriented product instead of a creation. Like in every sociopolitical endeavour, people sometimes disagree, leading to subtle but important variations. One of the most important one in the Free Software movement has been the question of the copyleft: should derivatives of Free Software be licensed under the same license? Some licenses, like the GPL says yes and this includes everything built on top of GPL code, the LGPL says that only code under LGPL needs to be released as LGPL, and others, called permissive licenses, like the BSD and MIT don't impose such restrictions.

Yet virtually none of them do contribute back to those commons, some of them being thanklessly maintained by a random person in Nebraska. Worse, a handful of computer-related companies ("cloud providers") are making ungodly amount of money renting infrastructure running Free Software, most smart™ devices are running Free Software, every single software producing/selling company depends on Free Software, and again, almost none contribute back meaningfully. A small number are trying to sponsor some projects they're depending on, but it often feels like a crass move for software that are maintained as a hobby: "Could you please garden a bit more efficiently, and add 150 apple trees to your small garden? We need it for our business, here is a 1000€ one-time payment"

With AI making everything worse, Free Software maintainers are now wasting their time dealing with unreviewable useless pull-requests, drowning into a sea of low-quality no-fix-provided bug reports, being demoralized by vibe-coded forks adding shiny features that are never going to be upstreamable and thus upstreamed. items.title: Now available: SonarQube plugin for Devin CLI
items.summary: What is the SonarQube plugin for Devin CLI? Devin CLI gives developers Cognition's coding agent in a local terminal. Out of the box, Devin has no view of a project's quality gate, existing issues, or coding standards, and nothing checks its output until CI runs on the pull request. The SonarQube plugin for Devin CLI gives Devin that view and brings Sonar's verification into the agent's own loop. The plugin connects Devin to three Sonar services that guide and verify its work as it writes. Sonar Vortex , the governance layer for coding agents, works inside Devin’s own loop, giving it a map of your code and your standards before it writes and checking each change against the same standard your quality gate applies at merge. SonarQube sets that standard through the quality profiles, quality gates, and rules your organization already uses to verify every change before it merges. The SonarQube CLI brings SonarQube into the terminal, handling sign-in and setup and running the checks Devin calls during a session, so Devin hands you code that has already been checked against your standards. The plugin also packages SonarQube capabilities as skills Devin can call through plain-language prompts or dedicated slash commands. Devin can list your SonarQube projects with /sonarqube:sonar-list-projects , pull open issues with /sonarqube:sonar-list-issues , and check quality gate status, coverage gaps, and duplication the same way. Teams with SonarQube Advanced Security can also check dependency risks. Every answer comes from the quality profiles and gates your organization already runs, across the 45+ languages and frameworks SonarQube supports. How the plugin works The plugin gives Devin the SonarQube skills, and the SonarQube CLI does the work underneath. When you run /sonarqube:sonar-integrate , the skill checks that the SonarQube CLI is installed and current, signs you in through your browser, stores the session in your OS keychain, and installs every component your organization has access to: Secrets scanning. A UserPromptSubmit hook blocks any prompt that contains a credential, and a PreToolUse hook scans each file before Devin reads it. An instruction in Devin's global AGENTS.md adds a second check that tells Devin to scan a file before reading it and to stop if the scan reports a secret. Treat these checks as a safeguard, since the hooks don't scan output from other tools, such as a shell command that prints a file. SonarQube MCP Server. The CLI registers the SonarQube MCP Server for every project and starts it as a container, so Devin can query SonarQube during any session. Sonar Vortex. Session-start and subagent hooks give Devin project context, a post-edit hook runs a quick check after each change, and an AGENTS.md protocol tells Devin to run a cross-file analysis over every file it changed at the end of the turn. The SonarQube CLI writes its configuration to ~/.config/devin/ , so the MCP registration, hooks, and instructions apply to every project you open in Devin. If your organization doesn't have a Vortex subscription, the CLI skips those components and still installs secrets scanning and the MCP Server. Sonar Vortex in a Devin session Sonar Vortex implements Sonar's Agent Centric Development Cycle (AC/DC) inside Devin. When a session starts, Vortex gives Devin coding guidelines drawn from your project's SonarQube rules and issue history, along with your architecture context. Devin can query the project's top-level architecture from SonarQube’s analyzed module graph, instead guessing at it through reading whatever files the agent happened to open. This helps Devin’s agent work more efficiently and write better code from the outset. When Devin finishes a set of changes, it runs Vortex analysis across every file it touched. Vortex refers to the context your CI analysis stored for the project and branch, so the check inside Devin runs against the same standard as the quality gate your organization already uses. This verification also runs deterministically, which means it works consistently every time and burns no tokens. This upfront scanning with Devin’s agentic loop helps the agent find and fix the vast majority of issues that would block the quality gate in CI, greatly streamlining the pull request review. In the setup guide , Vortex caught a security issue in code Devin wrote after its unit tests had already passed, and Devin fixed it before the code left the session instead of waiting for the CI verification loop to flag it on the PR. Why this matters Coding agents now produce changes faster than any team can read them line by line, and 94% of developers tell us they don't fully trust the code those agents write. A model that checks its own output can't settle that doubt, because it decides what to check and can reach a different answer on the next run. SonarQube verifies code independently of the agent that wrote it, and it holds human and agent contributions to the same standard every time. The SonarQube plugin puts that verification inside Devin's agentic loop, so Devin starts with your standards, works inside them, and fixes what falls short before it opens a pull request. In Sonar testing with a leading coding agent, Sonar Vortex produced up to 92% fewer issues in committed code, and Sonar research on refactoring tasks measured up to 36% lower token consumption. In Sonar's 2027 State of Code Developer Survey , SonarQube users were 81% more likely than non-users to say AI coding has had a very positive impact on code security, 34% more likely on time to market, and 76% more likely on outage frequency. Devin joins Claude Code , Codex , GitHub Copilot CLI , Cursor , and Antigravity in the set of coding agents that SonarQube plugins support. Teams that run several agents can hold all of them to one standard, defined once in SonarQube and applied wherever the code gets written. Get started now To get started, you need the Devin CLI with plugins permitted by your organization, a container runtime (Docker, Podman, or nerdctl), and the SonarQube CLI , which provides secrets scanning features out of the box. Querying SonarQube via MCP requires either SonarQube Cloud (Enterprise, or Team on an annual plan) or SonarQube Server 2026.5 or later (Enterprise or Data Center edition). The Vortex components need an active Sonar Vortex subscription. Once your SonarQube prereqs are satisfied, install the plugin from your terminal: devin plugins install SonarSource/sonarqube-agent-plugins Then open a Devin session and run the integration skill: /sonarqube:sonar-integrate Restart Devin so it loads the new hooks and MCP settings. To set the project key once, run sonar link in the repository root, and the skills will pick it up from there. The full walkthrough, including the secrets demo, the Vortex steps, and analysis across multiple files, is in the SonarQube plugin for Devin CLI setup guide . Install the plugin on your next Devin project and let SonarQube verify the code Devin writes before it reaches review. Get started with SonarQube Cloud
