items.title: Critical Apache Airflow RCE Flaw Allows Attackers to Execute Code Without Authentication
items.summary: Apache Airflow has a critical remote code execution flaw that lets anyone with write access to the Celery message broker run code on worker nodes. The attacker needs no credentials, DAG, or scheduler. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-68982 and is classified as CWE-306, missing authentication for a critical function. It affects Airflow versions before 3.4.0 that run CeleryExecutor. Airflow gives a worker three ways to receive instructions. The web UI and REST API require credentials. ExecuteTask messages on the broker carry a signed JWT, and the Execution API validates it through supervise_task() before the task runs. ExecuteCallback messages use the same execute_workload Celery task and the same broker, but nothing validates them. The execute_workload task deserializes any JSON body into a typed object based only on its declared shape. There is no signature, no HMAC, and no broker-side ACL. In version 3.2.1, execute_callback_workload() reads the path and kwargs values from the message, calls import_module and getattr, and then runs the callable with the attacker’s arguments. In 3.3.0, this moved into a forked CallbackSubprocess. It builds an httpx. Client with the token but makes no network call and checks nothing, so the callback still runs first. Because import_module can reach any module in the worker’s environment, the attacker gets full code execution. A message that names os.system with a shell command is enough. Critical Apache Airflow RCE Flaw Researcher Or Sahar of Reflectiz confirmed this on Airflow 3.2.1 and 3.3.0 in Docker Compose labs with a Redis broker and a PostgreSQL backend. The callback path was built for Deadline Alerts, which run a function when a DAG run misses its deadline. The feature is still marked experimental, but that does not limit exposure. The execute_workload task and its ExecuteCallback handler register on every CeleryExecutor worker as soon as the Celery provider loads. A deployment does not have to use Deadline Alerts to be vulnerable. The attack also leaves no trace in Airflow. The proof of concept created zero DagRuns and zero TaskInstances, and /api/v2/dags still returned total_entries as 0. A recorded demo went further and dumped the worker’s hostname and every AIRFLOW__* environment variable, including the Fernet key. Apache rates the flaw as Important and has not published a CVSS score. Reflectiz scored it 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. Reflectiz also reported that 198 of 211 reachable Redis brokers in Airflow and Celery clusters answered without authentication. The flaw echoes CVE-2020-11981, an earlier case where broker access led to code execution on Airflow 1.10.10 and earlier. Airflow 3.4.0, released November 6, 2026, fixes the flaw. The worker now redeems a single-use token with the Execution API before any callback runs. Apply the upgrade to the Execution API server and every CeleryExecutor worker. No earlier patched release exists. Until the upgrade is done, turn on Redis AUTH or a RabbitMQ username and password, and block ports 6379 and 5672 from the internet. Since Airflow’s UI will not show this activity, audit broker traffic and Celery worker process logs for unexpected execute_workload messages. Exposed Redis servers are a common target. Cyber Security News covered how hackers turned more than 3,500 Redis servers into Monero miners , and also reported on Apache Airflow flaws that expose sensitive data . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: How to Export LimaCharlie Logs
items.summary: Install the LimaCharlie CLI (pip install limacharlie), log in with your organization ID and an API key, and run an LCQL query with limacharlie search run for the time range you need, with JSON output. Events come back in LimaCharlie’s {routing, event} structure. For continuous, bulk export, configure an Output to S3, Google Cloud Storage or another destination. LimaCharlie keeps a year of telemetry in its Insight data lake by default, which makes after-the-fact investigation unusually practical. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API key and your OID. Both are in the web app under Access Management → REST API . Give the key the permissions needed to query Insight. Queries cost money. LCQL queries are billed by the data they scan. Dry runs give you an estimate first. Narrow by platform, event type and host before you widen the time range. Know the event types. LimaCharlie names events by type: NEW_PROCESS, DNS_REQUEST, NETWORK_CONNECTIONS, WEL (Windows event logs) and so on. Pick the ones that matter for your question. Export with the CLI pip install limacharlie limacharlie auth login # asks for your OID and API key limacharlie search run \ --query 'plat == windows | NEW_PROCESS DNS_REQUEST | routing/hostname == "ws-042"' \ --start $(date -d '2026-10-19T00:00:00Z' +%s) \ --end $(date -d '2026-10-20T00:00:00Z' +%s) \ --oid --output json > lc_ws042_1019.json An LCQL query has parts separated by pipes: a sensor selector (plat == windows), the event types, a filter, and optionally a projection of fields. If the output is an array, flatten it with jq -c ‘.[]’. The CLI can also generate an LCQL query from a plain-language description (limacharlie ai generate-query), which helps when you don’t remember the field paths. Bulk: Outputs For ongoing export, add an Output in the web app that sends events (and detections or audit logs, if you want them) to S3, Google Cloud Storage, a SIEM or a webhook. Outputs send data from the moment they’re created. For history, query Insight as above. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. Install the LimaCharlie CLI (pip install limacharlie), log in with your organization ID and an API key, and run an LCQL query with limacharlie search run for the time range you need, with JSON output. Events come back in LimaCharlie’s {routing, event} structure. For continuous, bulk export, configure an Output to S3, Google Cloud Storage or another destination.

LimaCharlie keeps a year of telemetry in its Insight data lake by default, which makes after-the-fact investigation unusually practical. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

An API key and your OID. Both are in the web app under Access Management → REST API. Give the key the permissions needed to query Insight.

Queries cost money. LCQL queries are billed by the data they scan. Dry runs give you an estimate first. Narrow by platform, event type and host before you widen the time range.

Know the event types. LimaCharlie names events by type: NEW_PROCESS, DNS_REQUEST, NETWORK_CONNECTIONS, WEL (Windows event logs) and so on. Pick the ones that matter for your question.

Export with the CLI 
pip install limacharlie
limacharlie auth login        # asks for your OID and API key

limacharlie search run \
  --query 'plat == windows | NEW_PROCESS DNS_REQUEST | routing/hostname == "ws-042"' \
  --start $(date -d '2026-10-19T00:00:00Z' +%s) \
  --end $(date -d '2026-10-20T00:00:00Z' +%s) \
  --oid  --output json > lc_ws042_1019.json

An LCQL query has parts separated by pipes: a sensor selector (plat == windows), the event types, a filter, and optionally a projection of fields. If the output is an array, flatten it with jq -c ‘.[]’.

The CLI can also generate an LCQL query from a plain-language description (limacharlie ai generate-query), which helps when you don’t remember the field paths.

For ongoing export, add an Output in the web app that sends events (and detections or audit logs, if you want them) to S3, Google Cloud Storage, a SIEM or a webhook. Outputs send data from the moment they’re created. For history, query Insight as above.

Yes, as artifacts collected from the sensor, and Windows event logs also stream in as WEL events.

items.title: 10 Best Adversarial Exposure Validation (AEV) Platforms in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
items.summary: Adversarial exposure validation (AEV) is the category that happened when breach-and-attack simulation tools and autonomous penetration testing stopped pretending to be different markets: both exist to replace “we believe our controls work” with “we attacked ourselves and here is what happened.” Analysts formalized the merger; buyers feel it as one question which platform proves, continuously and safely, what an adversary could actually do in my estate this week? The distinction that still matters inside the category is evidence class. Simulation platforms run attacker techniques with safe payloads and grade whether controls caught them; exploitation platforms execute the real thing under guardrails and come back holding domain admin. Both produce truth; they produce different truths, and this ranking scores ten platforms on proof quality, production safety, continuity, and the remediation payoff that justifies the line item. One exclusion to note: Picus Security is not evaluated in this roundup. Key Takeaways 1 overall: Pentera — proof-grade findings from real exploitation, safely orchestrated. Podium: Pentera, Cymulate (the broadest usable validation sweep), Horizon3.ai (autonomous pentesting at subscription cadence). Evidence classes: exploitation platforms (Pentera, Horizon3.ai, RidgeBot) return proof; simulation platforms (Cymulate, AttackIQ, SafeBreach, SCYTHE) return coverage mature programs run one of each. 2026 theme: AEV results now feed exposure-management prioritization directly validation as the truth filter on the CTEM pipeline rather than a standalone scorecard. Quick Capability Check A fast Yes/No pass before the countdown the five questions that sort the field: Platform Real exploit execution? Production-safe simulation? Continuous scheduling? AD/credential attack depth? Control-tuning output? Pentera Yes Guardrailed Yes Yes Partial Cymulate No Yes Yes Yes Yes Horizon3.ai Yes Guardrailed Yes Yes Partial AttackIQ No Yes Yes Partial Partial SafeBreach No Yes Yes Partial Partial XM Cyber No (modeled) Yes Yes Yes Partial SCYTHE Yes (operator-run) Controllable Partial Yes Partial Mandiant Validation No Yes Yes Partial Partial IBM (Randori) Yes Guardrailed Yes Partial Partial Ridge Security Yes Guardrailed Yes Yes Partial How We Scored (Methodology) Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: evidence quality (proof versus coverage, and how defensible either is), production-safety engineering, attack-content currency, continuity (always-on versus episodic), and remediation specificity. Weights: evidence quality 25% , safety engineering 20%, content currency 20%, continuity 20%, remediation payoff 15%. The 2026 AEV Power Rankings 1. Pentera — Best Proof-Grade Validation Pentera — Best Proof-Grade Validation Snapshot: Per-scope licensing | Autonomous real exploitation with guardrails | Credential/AD chain depth Why it earns #1: Pentera ended the argument simulations sometimes lose: its findings arrive as accomplished facts credentials harvested, relays executed, a domain-admin chain documented hop by hop because the platform ran the actual attack under production guardrails. That evidence class changes remediation politics permanently; nobody files “we obtained domain admin” under accepted risk. Continuous scheduling turns the annual pentest’s snapshot into a standing capability. Feeding these exploits into a broader cybersecurity risk assessment program ensures leadership views remediation items through an accurate risk lens. Pros: Unarguable evidence; AD/credential depth; automation scale; remediation chains mapped. Cons: Change-control culture must bless live exploitation; scope discipline required. Bottom line: The platform that returns holding the keys. 2. Cymulate — Best Full-Surface Validation Sweep Cymulate — Best Full-Surface Validation Sweep Snapshot: Module-based SaaS | Email/web/WAF/endpoint/lateral/exfil modules | Exposure-management convergence Why it ranks here: Cymulate validates more of the estate per analyst-hour than anything else in the field: safe simulations across the email gateway, web gateway, WAF, endpoint stack, lateral movement, and exfiltration paths, runnable weekly by lean teams and scored in language executives accept without translation. Its convergence into exposure management makes validation the standing truth layer rather than a quarterly report, aligning smoothly with cloud security posture management (CSPM) tools to uncover underlying misconfigurations. Pros: Surface breadth; lean-team ergonomics; kill-chain scenarios; exposure integration. Cons: Proof-class evidence belongs to the exploitation lane. Bottom line: The widest honest sweep in the category. 3. Horizon3.ai — Best Autonomous Pentest Cadence Horizon3.ai — Best Autonomous Pentest Cadence Snapshot: Subscription (NodeZero)| Self-service autonomous pentesting | Attack-path proof with fix verification Why it ranks here: Horizon3.ai’s NodeZero made the real pentest a button: autonomous operations that chain misconfigurations, credentials, and exposures exactly as an operator would, documented with proof, then re-run after remediation to verify the fix actually closed the path. The verify-the-fix loop attack, fix, re-attack is the discipline annual testing never delivered, making it an essential companion to structured incident response playbooks . Pros: Self-service autonomy; fix-verification loop; attack-path proof; subscription cadence. Cons: Same live-exploitation governance conversation as its lane. Bottom line: The pentest that re-runs itself after you patch. 4. AttackIQ — Best Framework-Anchored Validation AttackIQ — Best Framework-Anchored Validation Snapshot: Platform subscription | ATT&CK-aligned scenario library | Flexible delivery tiers Why it ranks here: AttackIQ anchors validation to the MITRE ATT&CK canon: scenarios mapped tightly to the framework, gap reporting that names precisely which techniques slipped past which control, and delivery options from self-serve to fully managed. For programs that report coverage to boards and regulators in MITRE ATT&CK framework language, the alignment is the product. Pros: Framework rigor; detection-gap precision; managed options. Cons: Framework-first lens rewards mature programs most. Bottom line: Coverage claims, graded against the canon. 5. SafeBreach — Best Attack-Playbook Arsenal SafeBreach — Best Attack-Playbook Arsenal Snapshot: Platform subscription| Thousands of curated attack methods | Rapid headline-threat coverage Why it ranks here: SafeBreach competes on arsenal: a playbook corpus curated across a decade, headline ransomware TTPs operationalized within days of disclosure, and a breach studio for teams that compose custom attacks. Depth of method rewards programs with dedicated owners who exploit it; the library is the ultimate tool for verifying continuous endpoint security management posture. Pros: Playbook depth; new-threat velocity; customization studio. Cons: Arsenal breadth needs an owner to exploit it. Bottom line: The deepest safe-attack library on the board. 6. XM Cyber — Best Modeled-Path Validation XM Cyber — Best Modeled-Path Validation Snapshot: SaaS platform | Continuous attack-path computation | Choke-point remediation math Why it ranks here: XM Cyber validates by graph rather than payload: continuously computing how an attacker would chain exposures from breach points to crown jewels, then ranking the choke-point fixes that sever the most paths at once. The remediation economics one fix, fifty paths are the argument, and the always-on model makes drift visible the week it opens, strengthening compliance workflows across data security posture management initiatives. Pros: Path-chaining insight; choke-point ranking; hybrid/cloud graphing. Cons: Modeled evidence persuades differently than executed proof. Bottom line: Validates the routes before anyone walks them. 7. SCYTHE — Best Adversary-Emulation Craft SCYTHE — Best Adversary-Emulation Craft Snapshot: Platform licensing | Emulation authoring with real, controllable payloads | Purple-team workflow Why it ranks here: SCYTHE serves the teams who write their own adversaries: emulation plans mapped to named actors, real payloads under operator control, and purple-team workflow that turns each campaign into detection improvements. It multiplies offensive skill already on staff rather than replacing it the craftsman’s platform in an automation market that works hand-in-hand with threat hunting platforms . Pros: Campaign authoring; payload control; actor-mapped plans. Cons: Rewards offensive expertise; not push-button validation. Bottom line: The red team’s force multiplier. 8. Mandiant Validation — Best Frontline-Intel Content Mandiant Validation — Best Frontline-Intel Content Snapshot: Platform + intel pairing | Verodin lineage | Breach-floor TTPs as test content Why it ranks here: Google’s Mandiant Validation answers the content-provenance question no rival can: test your controls against what Mandiant’s responders met on breach floors this quarter. Actor-specific validation with incident-grade sourcing strongest for estates already inside the Google/Mandiant intelligence orbit, where fresh tradecraft flows straight into test content to evaluate existing managed SIEM services . Pros: Frontline TTP provenance; actor-specific tests; intel fusion. Cons: Standalone momentum versus the pure-play leaders. Bottom line: Validate against last month’s real adversaries. 9. IBM (Randori) — Best Outside-In Attack Pipeline IBM (Randori) — Best Outside-In Attack Pipeline Snapshot: IBM portfolio packaging | Attacker’s-eye recon into continuous red teaming | Temptation-ranked targeting Why it ranks here: The Randori lineage runs validation from where attackers start: external reconnaissance ranking your assets by adversary temptation, flowing into continuous automated red teaming against what it found. The recon-to-attack pipeline remains distinctive inside IBM’s portfolio; packaging and roadmap deserve written confirmation in procurement, especially when integrated with enterprise external attack surface management frameworks. Pros: Attacker’s-eye targeting; recon-to-attack pipeline; continuous model. Cons: Portfolio-era packaging clarity. Bottom line: Validation that begins at the adversary’s start line. 10. Ridge Security — Best Value Autonomous Attacker Ridge Security — Best Value Autonomous Attacker Snapshot: Platform licensing (RidgeBot) | Automated exploitation with risk scoring | Accessible economics Why it ranks here: RidgeBot brings the exploitation class down-market: automated attack and exploitation runs with documented proof, risk-scored findings, and economics that put real validation inside budgets the premium platforms ignore. Ecosystem gravity trails the leaders; the alternative at this spend is validation theater or nothing, complementing standard deployments of vulnerability scanner software . Pros: Exploitation-class evidence at value pricing; automation simplicity. Cons: Content depth and ecosystem versus the anchors. Bottom line: Real attacks, mid-market invoice. Buying Advice: Match the Evidence Class to the Audience The architecture question is who must be convinced. Boards and auditors accept coverage scorecards (simulation class); patch-owner standoffs and budget fights end faster with executed proof (exploitation class) which is why mature programs run one of each: a Cymulate/AttackIQ-class sweep for continuous breadth, and a Pentera/Horizon3-class engine for the arguments worth ending. Structure the pilot as a remediation test, not a demo: same three control sets for every finalist, graded on failures fixed within thirty days using each platform’s guidance. Gate exploitation-class tools through change control with scope discipline in writing, measure content velocity against headline threats (days from disclosure to runnable test), and wire results into the exposure-management queue so validated gaps age visibly the half-life of a proven finding is the program’s real KPI. Your BAS stack and CTEM program decide where these results land; your SIEM detections are what half these tests are actually grading. Pentera leads on proof-grade exploitation, Cymulate on validation breadth, Horizon3.ai on autonomous pentest cadence, with AttackIQ, SafeBreach, XM Cyber, SCYTHE, Mandiant Validation, IBM’s Randori lineage, and Ridge Security completing the field. Picus Security was excluded from this evaluation. What is adversarial exposure validation? The category merging breach-and-attack simulation and autonomous penetration testing: platforms that continuously prove by simulation or real execution what an attacker could accomplish against your actual estate. Simulation or exploitation — which class do we need? Simulation runs weekly without governance drama and grades control coverage; exploitation produces unarguable proof but needs change-control blessing. Mature programs run one of each for different audiences. Is it safe to attack production? Simulation classes are engineered production-safe; exploitation platforms run real techniques under guardrails and deserve explicit change-control governance, scope discipline, and lab-first trials. Pentera and Horizon3.ai and RidgeBot come back holding credentials, Cymulate and AttackIQ and SafeBreach grade the whole surface safely, XM Cyber ranks the routes, SCYTHE arms the purple team, Mandiant tests against last month’s adversaries, Randori starts where attackers start match the evidence to the audience, pilot on fixes shipped, and let the half-life of proven findings tell you whether the program works.

items.title: New Mirax Android Malware Uses Accessibility Services to Remotely Control Phones and Steal Bank Funds
items.summary: An Android banking malware campaign is using advertisements inside streaming apps to turn everyday phones into tools for financial theft. Mirax, the malware abuses Accessibility Services to watch screens, capture passwords, intercept verification codes, and let criminals operate banking apps directly on infected devices. Thousands of Android phones belonging to retail banking customers across the Middle East, Türkiye, and Africa were confirmed infected between March and September 2026. Reported fraud cases point to losses reaching millions of US dollars, although the confirmed figures cover only infections and transactions visible to investigators and affected banks. Researchers from Group-IB identified the campaign in a technical investigation published November 5, noting sharp increases in activity around Eid and late July. The operation remained active when the report appeared, with its operators changing application names and infrastructure to complicate detection. New Mirax Android Malware Uses Accessibility Services Evidence suggests the infection begins with advertisements or video links inside low-reputation streaming apps available through Google Play. Those links direct users to a separate installer outside the official store. Similar fake streaming app campaigns have used entertainment offers to persuade victims to install remote-control malware and approve dangerous permissions. One confirmed Mirax installer pretended to be “TikTok 18+,” an imitation unrelated to TikTok or ByteDance. It retrieved the second-stage payload, which disguised itself as Google Play Services. Its displayed name substituted a Cyrillic “о” for the Latin letter, making the fraudulent system component harder to distinguish at a glance. The crucial step is persuading victims to enable Accessibility access. Mirax actively guides users toward granting this permission rather than simply displaying a request. ‘Google Play Services’ Interface prompts displayed to targets leading to Accessibility Service authorization (Source – Group-IB) Once enabled, the malware can observe the interface and perform actions on the victim’s behalf, giving operators an interactive route into banking sessions. Mirax, the malware abuses Accessibility Services to watch screens, capture passwords, intercept verification codes, and let criminals operate banking apps directly on infected devices.

Thousands of Android phones belonging to retail banking customers across the Middle East, Türkiye, and Africa were confirmed infected between March and September 2026.

Researchers from Group-IB identified the campaign in a technical investigation published November 5, noting sharp increases in activity around Eid and late July.

The operation remained active when the report appeared, with its operators changing application names and infrastructure to complicate detection.

items.title: CISA Confirms Hackers are Exploiting SSHole, the OpenSSH Vulnerability
items.summary: CISA has flagged active exploitation of SSHole, an OpenSSH authentication bypass (CVE-2026-123158) that lets remote attackers access certain Linux accounts without a valid password or SSH key. The OpenSSH flaw affects specific server configurations, carries a CVSS score of 8.1, and was added to CISA’s KEV catalog on November 9, 2026, with a November 12 remediation deadline. The entry requires forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 and lists ransomware use as unknown. Organizations should assess exposed systems and follow vendor guidance. SSHole affects OpenSSH on Linux when the server uses musl libc, a system software library, and checks passwords without PAM, the Linux authentication framework. Alpine Linux is one affected platform. OpenSSH versions before 10.6p2 need the upstream fix or a patched distribution package. As explained in Cybersecurity News’s earlier OpenSSH analysis , several conditions must exist together. Password authentication must be enabled, the target account’s stored password field must contain *, and another local account must hold a valid SHA-crypt password hash. Simply running an Alpine container does not establish exposure. The failure occurs when musl’s crypt() function receives an overly long password. For the affected hashing path, input exceeding 256 bytes can make the function return * as an error marker. OpenSSH may compare that marker with the target account’s stored * and accept the login. The documented trigger range is 257 to 1,024 bytes. Active Exploitation of OpenSSH SSHole Flaw Accounts with valid password hashes are not bypassed through this mechanism. The risk concerns accounts whose password fields contain the matching marker, even when administrators intended those accounts to use SSH keys. The official CVE record identifies the underlying problem as a password hash interpretation error. The supplied SANS Internet Storm Center findings describe deliberate attempts using passwords filled with repeated “A” characters. Researcher Johannes Ullrich recorded 232 long-password requests on November 5 and 713 on November 6. These totals represent suspicious requests, not confirmed breaches or separate attackers. Cowrie honeypots record only the first 255 password characters, limiting analysis of longer inputs. Ullrich suspected some logins succeeded, but the supplied account does not confirm successful sessions. CISA’s listing provides the broader exploitation warning. Administrators should install patched packages and restart sshd. OpenSSH 10.6p2 contains the upstream workaround, while distribution fixes may keep older version banners. Where updates must wait, setting PasswordAuthentication no blocks this path; confirm working key access before changing settings. Investigation should cover successful password logins to accounts without usable passwords, unexpected privilege changes, and newly added authorized keys. Earlier SSH honeypot research shows why monitoring must include non-interactive commands after login. Updating closes the flaw, but teams must also check whether attackers already used the affected account to run commands, change files, or establish continued access before the fix was applied. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: How to Export Amazon Security Lake Logs
items.summary: Amazon Security Lake stores your data in S3 as Parquet files in the OCSF schema, so you don’t download it directly. You query it. Use Amazon Athena with an UNLOAD statement and format = ‘JSON’: Athena writes the results as JSON lines to an S3 prefix you choose, and you download that. Security Lake tables live in a Glue database named amazon_security_lake_glue_db_ , one table per source. Security Lake centralizes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53, Security Hub findings, EKS audit logs and third-party sources in one normalized format. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Query access. Use the Security Lake delegated administrator account, or a subscriber with query access. Access is governed by Lake Formation, so you need SELECT on the tables, plus Athena permissions and write access to an S3 bucket for the export. Find the tables. In Athena, open the database for your region. Table names follow the pattern amazon_security_lake_table_ _ _ , for example amazon_security_lake_table_eu_west_1_cloud_trail_mgmt_2_0. The region uses underscores. Partitions keep costs down. Tables are partitioned by region, accountid and eventday (YYYYMMDD). Athena bills by data scanned, so always filter on eventday. Export with Athena UNLOAD In the Athena console, or with aws athena start-query-execution: UNLOAD ( SELECT * FROM amazon_security_lake_glue_db_eu_west_1.amazon_security_lake_table_eu_west_1_cloud_trail_mgmt_2_0 WHERE eventday = '20261019' AND accountid = '123456789012' ) TO 's3://my-athena-exports/security-lake/ct-20261019/' WITH (format = 'JSON', compression = 'NONE') The target prefix must be empty. When the query succeeds, download and combine the files: aws s3 cp s3://my-athena-exports/security-lake/ct-20261019/ ./ct-20261019/ --recursive cat ./ct-20261019/* > securitylake_ct_20261019.jsonl Each line is one OCSF event. To narrow it further, filter on OCSF fields such as api.operation, actor.user.uid or src_endpoint.ip. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Insufficient Lake Formation permissions No SELECT grant on the table Ask the Security Lake admin for a Lake Formation grant Table not found Wrong region in the database or table name Use underscores: eu_west_1 HIVE_PATH_ALREADY_EXISTS or similar Target prefix isn’t empty Use a new, empty prefix Huge scan cost No eventday filter Always filter on partitions Files are gzipped Compression left at the default Set compression = ‘NONE’, or use zcat FAQ Can I read the Parquet files directly? You can, with tools that read Parquet, but Athena handles the schema and partitions for you. For LogTotal, JSON lines from UNLOAD is the simplest route. Is OCSF the same as raw CloudTrail? No. Security Lake normalizes events into OCSF, so field names differ from the original source.

items.title: Hackers Exploit IBM Aspera Faspex Vulnerability, Granting Admin Access to Any User
items.summary: IBM has released a security update for a critical IBM Aspera Faspex vulnerability that lets a signed-in user bypass access checks and gain full administrative privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-123218, the flaw affects versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 and carries a CVSS severity score of 9.8. IBM published its security bulletin on November 7, 2026. The supplied CISA catalog entry lists the vulnerability as exploited , with an addition date of November 9 and a remediation deadline of November 12, 2026. It also marks forensic triage as required and ransomware use as unknown. However, we could not independently retrieve the specific entry during verification. IBM’s bulletin does not describe attack campaigns, victims, or exploitation methods beyond a specially crafted message. According to IBM’s security bulletin, an authenticated user can craft a specific message that bypasses user authorization. Successful exploitation gives that user full administrative privileges within Faspex. The advisory does not identify the affected endpoint, message fields, or exact request needed to trigger the flaw. The weakness falls under CWE-863, or incorrect authorization . In simple terms, the software fails to check whether a user has permission to act. Logging in proves who someone is, but authorization should still prevent a standard account from performing tasks reserved for administrators. Hackers Exploit IBM Aspera Faspex Vulnerability IBM’s published details show an important mismatch. Its description says the attacker must already be an authorized user. At the same time, its CVSS vector includes “PR: N,” which means no prior privileges are required. Until IBM clarifies this difference, the stated signed-in requirement should guide descriptions of the attack rather than claims that anyone can exploit it without an account. The published score rates potential effects on data privacy, data integrity, and service availability as high. However, the bulletin does not establish that attackers can execute operating system commands or obtain root access. Full Faspex administration and control of the underlying Linux host are different outcomes. Cyber Security News previously covered a separate IBM Aspera Shares vulnerability involving sessions that remained valid after password changes. That issue affected another Aspera product and should not be confused with this Faspex authorization bypass. IBM strongly recommends upgrading affected Linux deployments to Aspera Faspex 5.0.19 PL1. Administrators must then verify that the faspex-core container image reports version 5.0.19 with build identifier “1ce4b13” and “Fix Pack: 1.” Checking only the main version number could miss whether the required fix is installed. IBM lists no workarounds or alternative mitigations. Teams should follow the patch instructions linked in the bulletin and confirm the running container contains the corrected image. A deployment still showing version 5.0.19 without the required fix-pack details should not be treated as patched. For defenders following vulnerability news , this case highlights why patch verification matters. Confirming the exact fixed build is essential when vulnerable and corrected releases share the same main version number. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.summary: Google has released an emergency security update addressing CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity zero-day vulnerability in the XML component of Google Chrome that is already being exploited in real-world attacks. The issue is classified as a use-after-free memory-safety flaw and was reported anonymously to Google on November 6, 2026. Google confirmed on November 9 that an exploit for the vulnerability exists in the wild. However, the company has not disclosed how attackers are delivering the exploit, which organizations or individuals are being targeted, or whether the vulnerability is being chained with additional browser or sandbox escape flaws. Access to the underlying Chromium bug remains restricted while users deploy the security update. The fix is included in Chrome Stable 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. Google also released Extended Stable 156.0.8078.96 for Windows and macOS with a fix for the same vulnerability. Contact Sales CVE-2026-125350 is the eighth Chrome zero-day known to have been exploited in the wild during 2026, following CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491. As of November 10, SecurityWeek reports that CISA has not yet added the newly disclosed flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Use-after-free vulnerabilities occur when software continues referencing memory after that memory has been released. Depending on the affected code and exploitation technique, such memory corruption can potentially result in browser crashes, data corruption, or attacker-controlled code execution. Google has not disclosed the exact impact achieved in the observed attacks, so defenders should avoid assuming that a publicly documented full system compromise chain already exists. Security teams can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to strengthen detection coverage against browser exploitation, suspicious child processes, payload execution, and follow-on attacker behavior across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Detect CVE-2026-125350 by combining browser version inventory with endpoint and network telemetry, monitoring for suspicious processes launched by Chrome, abnormal browser crashes, unexpected payload downloads, and post-exploitation behavior occurring after visits to potentially malicious websites. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. CVE-2026-125350 analysis CVE-2026-125350 affects vulnerable Google Chrome releases containing the use-after-free condition in the browser’s XML component. Google rates the vulnerability High severity but has not published a CVSS score or vector in its November 9 advisory. A use-after-free occurs when memory is released but software later attempts to access the same memory location. If an attacker can influence the contents subsequently placed in that memory, the stale reference can potentially be manipulated to alter program behavior. In a web browser, memory-safety vulnerabilities are particularly important because attacker-controlled content is routinely processed by complex browser components. However, Google has not yet disclosed the exact XML object involved, the sequence required to trigger the bug, or the specific web content used by attackers. The Chromium issue associated with the vulnerability is currently restricted. Google routinely limits access to technical bug details until a majority of users have received the patch, and restrictions can remain longer when a flaw also exists in third-party software. As a result, several important technical details remain unknown. The available sources do not establish whether exploitation requires simply visiting a malicious page, opening specially crafted XML content, interacting with a page, or another delivery mechanism. They also do not confirm whether attackers are achieving code execution inside a Chrome renderer, escaping the browser sandbox, or combining the vulnerability with another flaw. The Hacker News notes that use-after-free bugs can potentially lead to data corruption, crashes, or arbitrary code execution. This describes the general security impact of this vulnerability class rather than a Google-confirmed description of the exact exploitation chain used against CVE-2026-125350. Google’s statement is nevertheless significant because the company explicitly confirms that an exploit exists in the wild. This means the vulnerability should be treated as an immediate patching priority even though technical information about the attacks remains limited. The vulnerability was anonymously reported to Google on November 6, 2026. Only three days later, on November 9, Google released patched Stable builds for Windows, macOS, and Linux and acknowledged active exploitation. The update containing the zero-day fix addresses nine security issues in total. Other high-severity flaws include an uninitialized resource issue in WebGL, incorrect authorization in FileSystem, a buffer overflow in Compositing, an out-of-bounds write in GPU, a type confusion vulnerability in V8, and another use-after-free issue in XML tracked as CVE-2026-125346. Two medium-severity GPU vulnerabilities were also patched. The presence of CVE-2026-125346 in the same release is worth distinguishing from the actively exploited vulnerability. Both issues involve use-after-free conditions in Chrome’s XML functionality, but Google has only stated that CVE-2026-125350 is being exploited in the wild. Google released the following fixed Stable versions: Platform Fixed Chrome Stable version Windows 157.0.8103.50/.51 macOS 157.0.8103.50/.51 Linux 157.0.8103.50 Extended Stable users on Windows and macOS should move to version 156.0.8078.96 or later. Because Chrome updates roll out progressively, an installed browser may not immediately receive the patched version. Users and administrators should therefore verify the actual running build instead of assuming that automatic updates have already remediated the issue. The CVE-2026-125350 PoC situation also requires caution. Google confirms that attackers possess a working exploit, but neither Google nor the two supplied reports identifies a publicly released proof-of-concept reproducing the exploit. The Chromium bug details remain restricted, which limits defenders’ ability to reproduce the vulnerability or identify exploit-specific artifacts. For CVE-2026-125350 detection, organizations should begin with exposure management. Security teams should inventory Chrome versions across endpoints and identify systems running builds older than the fixed releases. Internet-facing servers are not the primary concern here; employee workstations and other systems used for web browsing deserve immediate attention. Endpoint telemetry can provide additional hunting opportunities. Defenders should investigate unusual processes originating from Chrome, particularly command interpreters, scripting engines, system utilities, or newly downloaded executables that appear immediately following browser activity. Suspicious behavior can include unexpected execution of PowerShell, cmd.exe, Windows Script Host, mshta.exe, rundll32.exe, or other utilities from a Chrome-related process tree. Such activity is not specific to this vulnerability and should not by itself be treated as proof of exploitation, but it can provide a useful behavioral signal when combined with vulnerable browser versions and suspicious browsing activity. Security teams should also examine endpoint telemetry for unusual Chrome crashes or renderer failures followed by new process execution, file creation, credential access, persistence, or network connections. Browser crashes alone are common and therefore require correlation with other evidence. Web proxy, DNS, secure web gateway, and endpoint browser telemetry can help reconstruct user activity immediately before suspicious execution. Organizations should preserve relevant browsing history and network logs if exploitation is suspected, particularly because Google has not published information about the websites or infrastructure used in the observed attacks. There are currently no vendor-published CVE-2026-125350 IOCs such as malicious domains, IP addresses, payload hashes, or attacker infrastructure. Google has also not disclosed the threat actors responsible, affected organizations, campaign scope, or geographic targeting. This lack of static indicators makes behavior-based monitoring and rapid browser version management especially important. A hunt based exclusively on hashes or known domains cannot reliably determine whether an environment has encountered exploitation when the public attack infrastructure remains unknown. Organizations using Chromium-based browsers such as Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi should monitor their respective vendor advisories and deploy relevant security updates as they become available. The Hacker News specifically recommends that users of these browsers apply fixes when their vendors release them. CVE-2026-125350 Mitigation The primary remediation is to update Google Chrome immediately to a fixed version and restart the browser so the corrected build is running. Google has released: Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for macOS Chrome 157.0.8103.50 for Linux Chrome Extended Stable 156.0.8078.96 for Windows and macOS Chrome normally downloads updates automatically, but users must relaunch the browser for the updated build to replace the vulnerable running process. The Hacker News recommends opening More → Help → About Google Chrome and relaunching after the update is installed. Enterprise security teams should take the following actions: Inventory Chrome versions across managed endpoints. Prioritize systems still running versions older than the fixed Stable or Extended Stable builds. Force or accelerate Chrome updates through enterprise browser-management tooling. Verify that browsers have actually restarted after receiving the patch. Monitor endpoints that cannot be updated immediately for suspicious browser-originated processes. Restrict access to known malicious or newly registered web infrastructure through existing web security controls. Review security telemetry for suspicious Chrome activity that occurred before patch deployment. Monitor vendor advisories for Chromium-based browsers and update those products when fixes become available. Because exploitation has already occurred in the wild, patching should not be the only response for systems that may have been exposed. Administrators should consider reviewing recent endpoint activity on vulnerable machines, especially where security tools recorded unusual Chrome crashes, browser-spawned command execution, suspicious downloads, or connections to untrusted infrastructure. If suspicious activity is discovered, isolate the affected endpoint and preserve browser, EDR, DNS, proxy, and network telemetry before remediation. Investigators should reconstruct the browser activity preceding the event and determine whether any follow-on payloads, credential theft, persistence, or lateral movement occurred. Organizations should also verify whether the browser was running under an account with access to sensitive web sessions, enterprise applications, cloud consoles, or privileged credentials. Depending on evidence of compromise, session revocation and credential rotation may be appropriate. Google’s restricted disclosure means defenders do not currently have enough public information to build a signature for the actual exploit. This reinforces the importance of patch management and generic exploitation detection rather than waiting for a reliable network or file signature. FAQ What is CVE-2026-125350 and how does it work? CVE-2026-125350 is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Google Chrome’s XML component. Use-after-free flaws occur when software accesses memory after it has been released, potentially leading to crashes, memory corruption, or attacker-controlled code execution. Google has not disclosed the exact trigger or exploit chain because technical bug details remain restricted. When was CVE-2026-125350 first discovered? An anonymous security researcher reported the vulnerability to Google on November 6, 2026. Google released the patched Chrome Stable channel update on November 9 and simultaneously confirmed that an exploit exists in the wild. What is the impact of CVE-2026-125350 on systems? The flaw can cause memory-safety violations in Chrome’s XML component. Use-after-free vulnerabilities can potentially result in browser crashes, data corruption, or code execution, but Google has not disclosed the exact capabilities achieved by attackers exploiting this zero-day or whether another vulnerability is required for sandbox escape or broader system compromise. Can CVE-2026-125350 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Google has confirmed active exploitation, so Chrome installations that have not reached the corrected Stable or Extended Stable versions should be considered at elevated risk. As of November 10, 2026, Google has not disclosed the actors, targets, or scale of the attacks, and SecurityWeek reports that CISA has not yet added the vulnerability to KEV. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-125350? Update Chrome to 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Windows or macOS, 157.0.8103.50 on Linux, or Extended Stable 156.0.8078.96 where applicable, and restart the browser. Enterprise defenders should verify deployment across endpoints, investigate suspicious activity on systems that remained vulnerable, and follow Google’s release notes for updated details for CVE-2026-125350 as technical information becomes available.

items.title: Turla Hackers Use Cereal Malware Toolset to Exploit Microsoft Exchange Servers for Email Theft
items.summary: Russia-aligned hacking group Turla is using a newly documented malware toolset called Cereal to turn compromised Microsoft Exchange servers into email collection systems and command centers. ESET Research disclosed the findings on November 10, 2026, describing attacks against government organizations in Kazakhstan and Romania. The malware copies selected emails while allowing normal delivery to continue, helping the attackers collect sensitive information without causing an obvious service failure. Turla Hackers Attacking Exchange Servers Researchers first detected the toolset at a Kazakh government organization on November 28, 2025. After improving their detection rules, they identified another compromised government organization in Romania, where activity dated to December 23, 2025. In Romania, the attackers configured the malware to identify messages involving NATO and European Union addresses, including nato.int and europa.eu. These filters point to targeted intelligence collection rather than broad, random email theft. ESET attributed Cereal to Turla with high confidence, citing its use alongside a previously attributed Turla component and similarities to older malware. The group has targeted governments and diplomatic organizations for years. Earlier Cybersecuritynews.com coverage of Turla’s cooperation with Gamaredon described another route to long-term spying, with Gamaredon providing access before Turla deployed its Kazuar backdoor. The researchers could not determine how the attackers initially entered either organization. Although the Exchange servers were internet-facing, exploitation of a software flaw remains only a possibility. The findings do not establish a particular vulnerability, phishing campaign, or stolen account as the entry point. That distinction matters because Cereal describes activity after compromise, not a confirmed new method for breaking into Exchange. Cereal Architecture Overview Diagram (Image Source: ESET Static) Cereal takes its name from serialization, a process for packaging program data so it can later be rebuilt. Its components use this approach to carry encrypted .NET programs, unpack them, and run them in memory. CerealLoader is the only component stored as a recognizable, unencrypted .NET file. Other components arrive inside encrypted containers, reducing the amount of readable malware available for investigators to examine on disk. Exchange Becomes the Command Center According to ESET’s technical white paper , CerealNeuron serves as a passive backdoor. Instead of regularly contacting an outside command server, it waits for incoming requests on the compromised Exchange server. Observed paths include /owa/sdds/ , /AUTODISCOVER/PROXYSERVICE/ , and /MICROSOFT-SERVER-ACTIVESYNC/INTEGRATED/API/ . Their resemblance to normal Exchange services helps malicious requests blend into traffic that organizations need for everyday email access. Requests that pass encryption and integrity checks deliver programs for execution. Invalid requests receive redirects to an Exchange error page. ESET observed no dedicated external command infrastructure and could not identify the operators’ incoming IP addresses. This does not mean the malware has no network activity. Rather, the victim’s server becomes the reachable control point, removing a separate attacker-controlled server that defenders might otherwise identify and block. CerealRunner packages individual tasks as encrypted .NET programs. Observed commands retrieved mail through Exchange Web Services, queried Active Directory, checked processes and connections, extracted locally stored credentials, and managed files. A second backdoor, CerealHermit, reads encrypted commands from disk instead of the network. This use of compromised systems also echoes earlier reporting on Turla’s STOCKSTAY operations , although those attacks involved a different backdoor. CerealBox Delivery Execution Chain (Image Source: ESET Static) The email collection component, CerealBox, runs inside EdgeTransport.exe, which handles Exchange mail flow. Rather than register a new transport agent, it wraps handlers belonging to existing agents in memory. Its code examines messages before returning control to the original handlers. Mail delivery continues, while Exchange’s configuration does not show a newly installed agent. ESET describes this approach to hooking the transport pipeline as previously undocumented in malware. Collection follows specific rules. A message must contain a .doc, .docx, or .pdf attachment and match configured sender, recipient, subject, or attachment-name criteria, while avoiding ignore lists. Selected messages are compressed, encrypted, and stored on disk. Operators then retrieve and delete the staged files using other Cereal commands. The design separates continuous email monitoring from later data removal, allowing the attackers to choose when they collect the results. CerealLoader uses native entry points and VTable Fixups to reach malicious .NET code through execution paths that managed-code inspection can miss. Operators also planted loaders in the .NET native image cache and used DLL search-order hijacking. Together, these techniques show why checking only transport-agent settings or outbound connections would leave important parts of this intrusion unseen during an investigation of compromised Exchange infrastructure and its surrounding Windows systems. items.title: Hackers Exploit Trusted Qubole IAM Roles to Access AWS Accounts and Download Entire S3 Buckets
items.summary: Hackers abused trusted Qubole integrations to enter customer AWS accounts, steal secrets, and download data from Amazon S3, sometimes taking entire buckets in one session. The activity ran from October 14 through October 26, 2026, using IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with Qubole rather than exploiting a software vulnerability. The attackers relied on permissions customers had granted to the data processing platform. Roles created for legitimate business needs remained accessible even when integrations were no longer active. The case highlights why cloud identity access management requires regular reviews of both permissions and external trust relationships, not simply checks on whether an integration still works. Researchers from Wiz.io, working with Sentra and Mandiant, investigated the campaign after Sentra detected suspicious activity across customer environments. Wiz also identified a malicious bootable Linux image hosted on attacker infrastructure, but could not confirm its deployment or use. Its published technical investigation separates that discovery from the confirmed cloud intrusions. Hackers Exploit Trusted Qubole IAM Roles Qubole integrations use cross-account IAM roles to operate inside customer environments. A customer creates a role whose trust policy permits the vendor’s AWS account to assume it, typically with an External ID. AWS Security Token Service then issues temporary credentials limited to that role’s permissions. The attacker followed this legitimate access path. Initial requests came through Mullvad VPN, followed by activity mainly from an OVH-hosted server. Every role-assumption request attributed to the attacker included an External ID and succeeded. Most compromised roles were otherwise unused, yet their trust policies continued accepting requests. After gaining access, the attacker mapped storage, compute, databases, identities, and encryption keys. It inspected Lambda function configurations for environment variables, retrieved Secrets Manager values, and read Systems Manager Parameter Store entries. These locations can hold credentials that extend access beyond the original integration role. The attacker then used TruffleHog to validate discovered credentials across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and Okta. Similar AWS credential validation techniques have appeared in other cloud intrusions, although Wiz found no established connection between this campaign and previously reported activity. TruffleHog itself is a legitimate security tool. S3 theft followed a repeatable sequence: list available buckets, enumerate objects, inspect object metadata, and download files. The attacker appeared opportunistic, reading whichever buckets each role could reach rather than pursuing a clearly defined dataset. In some environments, this meant downloading complete buckets during a single session. Detection, Containment, and Third-Party Trust Hardening Wiz recommends reviewing CloudTrail records from October 1, 2026, onward across every account holding a Qubole integration role. Investigators should correlate role assumptions with source networks, principal identities, and subsequent secret or storage access. Legitimate Qubole traffic observed during the investigation originated from AWS infrastructure, making unexpected external networks especially useful hunting signals. Logging coverage matters. CloudTrail management events show role assumptions and bucket listings, but not the object reads responsible for data theft. Sensitive buckets therefore need S3 data events or server access logs. Separately reported rapid AWS account compromises reinforce the importance of investigating credential abuse before attackers expand access. If an integration role was abused, revoke its active sessions and rotate every accessible secret, parameter, and credential-bearing Lambda variable. Credential rotation alone does not invalidate temporary sessions already issued. Remove unused integrations, restrict trusted principals and source networks, and reduce permissions to the resources each vendor actually needs. External IDs should not be treated as passwords: they appear in plaintext logs and may exist in vendor systems or infrastructure code. Wiz also reported separate customer-owned key abuse during October 8–11, but could not link it to this campaign. Neither the attacker’s identity nor its plans for stolen data were established. items.title: Update Chrome now to fix a flaw attackers are exploiting
items.summary: On November 9, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux . It includes nine security fixes, including one for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability. A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available. Hong Kong’s Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) rates the overall risk as “Extremely High.” Its bulletin says some of the vulnerabilities address in the update could allow denial of service, security restriction bypass, and remote code execution. How to update Chrome The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update. If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it. Chrome 157.0.8103.51 is up to date You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system . Google also released Chrome 157.0.8103.50 for Android on November 9. Google says it includes the same security fixes as the desktop release unless otherwise noted. Android users should check Google Play for the update. Technical details Let’s take a closer look at that zero-day vulnerability. Google says it was notified about a vulnerability by an unnamed third party on November 6. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated as a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome’s XML component. XML is a data format Chrome uses to read and process certain kinds of structured web content. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language: it labels information with tags, rather like HTML, but allows authors to define their own tags to describe their data. A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code. Google only says that it is “aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” It has not named the attackers, the targets, the delivery method, or what the exploit can do. The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

Technical details

Let’s take a closer look at that zero-day vulnerability.

Google says it was notified about a vulnerability by an unnamed third party on November 6. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated as a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome’s XML component.

XML is a data format Chrome uses to read and process certain kinds of structured web content. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language: it labels information with tags, rather like HTML, but allows authors to define their own tags to describe their data.

items.title: Dark Storm Team Expands DDoS-for-Hire Operations, Demands $5,000 to Stop Alleged Amino Attack
items.summary: Dark Storm Team is combining political attack claims with a growing cybercrime business, advertising distributed denial-of-service services and demanding money to stop alleged disruption. A November 6, 2026, investigation documents its Telegram activity, including a $5,000 cryptocurrency demand linked to the Amino social app. The demand dates to October 2025, rather than a newly confirmed incident. First observed in late 2023, the group gained attention after claiming responsibility for the March 2025 outage affecting X. Its later posts describe attacks against government websites, banks, airports, and online platforms. However, the available evidence does not independently confirm every attack, its duration, or the damage claimed. Researchers from StealthMole identified the commercial operation by tracking Telegram channels, account changes, and messages associated with the persona GLITCH. Their investigation into Dark Storm describes DDoS services and extortion activity, not a newly identified malware family. That distinction matters because the report does not establish which attack software Dark Storm itself deployed. Dark Storm Team Expands DDoS-for-Hire Operations, Demands $5,000 On October 19, 2025, GLITCH posted that the alleged DDoS activity against Amino would stop in exchange for $5,000 in cryptocurrency. A formal attack claim followed on October 22, and the group returned to the target in October 2026. The report does not establish whether Amino paid or independently verify the claimed disruption. The message shows a move beyond selling attacks to customers: the operator publicly used an alleged attack to pressure a target for payment. This sits within the market illustrated by the NightmareStresser DDoS service takedown , where customers could purchase disruptive traffic without building their own attack infrastructure. Dark Storm’s frequently reposted price list offered three hours of DDoS activity for $20, eight hours for $50, one day for $100, one week for $350, and one month for $600. Cryptocurrency was the only advertised payment method. Promotions included an eight-hour service for $25 in late October 2026. The catalogue extended beyond DDoS. A June 2026 menu advertised access to social media accounts starting at $250 and website database dumps from $300. Other advertisements listed database dumping from $50, showing that prices varied between menus. Posts also offered payment card data, CCTV access, and paid channel advertising; these advertisements do not prove successful delivery. GLITCH acted as owner, spokesperson, and sales contact across several accounts. Researchers linked renamed sales handles through a persistent Telegram user ID, allowing them to follow the commercial operation despite changes in its public presentation. This continuity provides stronger evidence of account relationships than matching display names alone. Telegram Resilience, Alliances, and Limits of the Evidence Repeated platform bans did not remove Dark Storm’s presence. Replacement channels appeared throughout 2025 and 2026, while backups and allied communities circulated fresh links. In September 2026, Team1914 helped promote a replacement channel. The pattern adds detail to earlier reporting on pro-Russian hacktivist group alliances involving Dark Storm and other groups. The relationship with Team1914 included reciprocal promotion and joint attack claims. Dark Storm also regularly forwarded NoName057(16) posts and adopted its campaign tags. However, researchers distinguished this amplification from a proven operational partnership. Shared targets, forwarded messages, and overlapping hashtags cannot establish that groups share infrastructure or jointly execute attacks. GLITCH also appeared in a DDoSia Project chat in October 2026 and identified himself as Dark Storm’s owner. Previous reporting on NoName057(16)’s DDoSia attack tool explains its volunteer-driven model, but that appearance does not demonstrate that Dark Storm used the tool. The report leaves the group’s underlying attack infrastructure unresolved. Many attack posts relied on Check-Host availability reports. These show whether selected probes can reach a website, not why access failed. Geographic restrictions, unrelated outages, or defensive filtering may produce similar results. items.title: Before you buy an advent calendar, check these warning signs
items.summary: .kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.85);}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Store-added reviews and countdowns that keep resetting make products look popular and deals urgent Missing contact details can make it harder to resolve a problem with an order AI-generated images and unverified brand partnerships promote products with no licensing information Learn how to check an online seller before you buy Advent calendar buying guides are already appearing across the holiday shopping coverage this year. Social media can also put unfamiliar sellers directly in shoppers’ feeds. We found several stores using the same website template, product images with an AI-generated content watermark, and a TikTok account using one store’s branding to link straight to its product page. We examined stores selling a Legend of Zelda music calendar, a Michael Jackson music calendar, a Lord of the Rings figure calendar, and Harry Potter character plant pots. Other stores, including one selling a Metallica calendar, use the same layout, low-stock warning, and recycled marketing lines. We found no licensing information on the stores, which is reason enough to avoid them. Fake reviews and countdowns create a false sense of demand Each store sells a single product. Its page surrounds polished product images with urgency cues: a sale that ends today, a low-stock warning, a five-minute cart reservation timer, a count of orders placed in the last day, and star ratings with thousands of reviews. Testimonials appear underneath, with “verified buyer” badges and timestamps such as “three hours ago.” None of it is connected to anything. The ratings, review counts, and testimonials are entered into the site theme manually, rather than generated by a review system. The timestamps don’t change, and countdowns reset and run again—on some stores, every day. Checkout runs through Shopify. That doesn’t establish whether orders will arrive or match their descriptions, and our investigation found no evidence that these pages were designed to steal card details. The risks we can support are misleading sales claims and the possibility of paying for something that never arrives or is very different from what was advertised. Several stores also offer optional checkout add-ons, including shipping protection, a queue-skip fee, and a mystery gift. On one store, these add-ons total nearly $35. The Zelda calendar’s description contradicts itself The clearest finding needs no technical analysis. The listing says each of the 25 discs holds a small chip storing your track data, and that the included player reads it and plays music through a built-in speaker with no app, no subscription and no Wi-Fi. Elsewhere on the same page it says the discs work with Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube, and that you can re-link any disc to a new song using a chip-writing app on your phone. These claims cannot all be true. A device without a network connection can’t stream music from those services. And the instructions for linking discs to new songs suggest that each chip stores a link to a track, rather than the track itself. That’s how the legitimate version of this product works, according to our research: the chip holds a link, and a phone plays the music. Someone appears to have copied that mechanism and bolted a fictional standalone speaker onto it. The bundle pricing also doesn’t add up. Two bundles claim savings of $15 and $33, but the prices shown below them work out to about $19 and $43 in savings. The stores are copies of one another Despite their different names, the stores we examined are nearly identical. They use the same commercial theme version and share an internal fingerprint indicating that their theme files are copies of one another. They also block right-clicking and access to developer tools. The most direct link was left behind by accident, in that one store’s theme is still named after the file it was exported from, and that filename includes the web address of another store in the group. Other pages contain leftover text from a previous shop, including a warranty promising to replace costumes that don’t inflate properly and a scrolling banner with the unedited placeholder “use code X for X percent off.” The stores’ files are timestamped from mid-July to the second week of September, with the newest store only days old when we examined it. Most merchant accounts are registered in Romania, while prices are shown in dollars. None of the calendar stores we examined listed a business address or phone number. The pattern runs well past unlicensed character merchandise. We found advent calendars for fishing lures, squishy toys, charm bracelets, and wearable jumpers, with the same countdowns, stock warnings, and paid add-ons. Most appear to sell real, inexpensive goods at a steep markup. Their add-on prices differ, so we can’t conclude that the same person runs all of them. The evidence points to a shared sales playbook, not necessarily a shared owner. What the evidence shows, and what it doesn’t Product images from two of the calendar stores triggered a provenance checker for a watermark, indicating they were produced with OpenAI tools. The filenames agree: across three stores every product image follows the same automated naming pattern, and one store’s entire photography set is timestamped to a single afternoon. A TikTok account uses one store’s name and branding and links directly to its product page. Several videos claim the store is collaborating with Walmart. They show retail scenes, including an oversized character figure outside a store and pallets of branded boxes. We found no evidence of such a partnership.
