In this article
  • Store-added reviews and countdowns that keep resetting make products look popular and deals urgent
  • Missing contact details can make it harder to resolve a problem with an order
  • AI-generated images and unverified brand partnerships promote products with no licensing information
  • Learn how to check an online seller before you buy

Advent calendar buying guides are already appearing across the holiday shopping coverage this year. Social media can also put unfamiliar sellers directly in shoppers’ feeds. We found several stores using the same website template, product images with an AI-generated content watermark, and a TikTok account using one store’s branding to link straight to its product page.

We examined stores selling a Legend of Zelda music calendar, a Michael Jackson music calendar, a Lord of the Rings figure calendar, and Harry Potter character plant pots. Other stores, including one selling a Metallica calendar, use the same layout, low-stock warning, and recycled marketing lines. We found no licensing information on the stores, which is reason enough to avoid them.

Fake reviews and countdowns create a false sense of demand

Each store sells a single product. Its page surrounds polished product images with urgency cues: a sale that ends today, a low-stock warning, a five-minute cart reservation timer, a count of orders placed in the last day, and star ratings with thousands of reviews. Testimonials appear underneath, with “verified buyer” badges and timestamps such as “three hours ago.”

None of it is connected to anything. The ratings, review counts, and testimonials are entered into the site theme manually, rather than generated by a review system. The timestamps don’t change, and countdowns reset and run again—on some stores, every day.

Checkout runs through Shopify. That doesn’t establish whether orders will arrive or match their descriptions, and our investigation found no evidence that these pages were designed to steal card details. The risks we can support are misleading sales claims and the possibility of paying for something that never arrives or is very different from what was advertised. Several stores also offer optional checkout add-ons, including shipping protection, a queue-skip fee, and a mystery gift. On one store, these add-ons total nearly $35.

The Zelda calendar’s description contradicts itself

The clearest finding needs no technical analysis. The listing says each of the 25 discs holds a small chip storing your track data, and that the included player reads it and plays music through a built-in speaker with no app, no subscription and no Wi-Fi. Elsewhere on the same page it says the discs work with Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube, and that you can re-link any disc to a new song using a chip-writing app on your phone.

These claims cannot all be true. A device without a network connection can’t stream music from those services. And the instructions for linking discs to new songs suggest that each chip stores a link to a track, rather than the track itself. That’s how the legitimate version of this product works, according to our research: the chip holds a link, and a phone plays the music. Someone appears to have copied that mechanism and bolted a fictional standalone speaker onto it.

The bundle pricing also doesn’t add up. Two bundles claim savings of $15 and $33, but the prices shown below them work out to about $19 and $43 in savings.

The stores are copies of one another

Despite their different names, the stores we examined are nearly identical. They use the same commercial theme version and share an internal fingerprint indicating that their theme files are copies of one another. They also block right-clicking and access to developer tools.

The most direct link was left behind by accident, in that one store’s theme is still named after the file it was exported from, and that filename includes the web address of another store in the group. Other pages contain leftover text from a previous shop, including a warranty promising to replace costumes that don’t inflate properly and a scrolling banner with the unedited placeholder “use code X for X percent off.”

The stores’ files are timestamped from mid-July to the second week of September, with the newest store only days old when we examined it. Most merchant accounts are registered in Romania, while prices are shown in dollars. None of the calendar stores we examined listed a business address or phone number.

The pattern runs well past unlicensed character merchandise. We found advent calendars for fishing lures, squishy toys, charm bracelets, and wearable jumpers, with the same countdowns, stock warnings, and paid add-ons. Most appear to sell real, inexpensive goods at a steep markup. Their add-on prices differ, so we can’t conclude that the same person runs all of them. The evidence points to a shared sales playbook, not necessarily a shared owner.

What the evidence shows, and what it doesn’t

Product images from two of the calendar stores triggered a provenance checker for a watermark, indicating they were produced with OpenAI tools. The filenames agree: across three stores every product image follows the same automated naming pattern, and one store’s entire photography set is timestamped to a single afternoon.

A TikTok account uses one store’s name and branding and links directly to its product page. Several videos claim the store is collaborating with Walmart. They show retail scenes, including an oversized character figure outside a store and pallets of branded boxes. We found no evidence of such a partnership. The videos also depict scenes that don’t appear to be real. Combined with the shared website template and the filename linking two stores, this suggests that one operator or a closely connected group may be involved. It doesn’t establish who is behind the stores.

How to spot a questionable store before you pay

In our survey earlier this year, 22% of respondents said they had been “misled by AI-generated photos or product reviews.”
Here are some checks that can help you spot warning signs.

  • Be wary of endless urgency. If a sale keeps “ending today” or low-stock warnings never change, don’t treat them as proof of a genuine deal.
  • Check that the product could exist. Search the product type and read how the real version works. If the listing claims something the technology can’t do, stop there.
  • Don’t arrive through a link. These stores sell largely through social video. Search the brand name separately and look for history, press, or customers outside its own website.
  • Treat partnership claims as claims. A video saying a brand is stocked by a retailer isn’t evidence that it is. Partnerships are announced by the retailer too, not only by the seller.
  • Look for a real business. A postal address, company registration and working phone number are easy for a legitimate seller to provide and were absent from these.
  • Reverse-image search the photos. Generated images usually have no history anywhere else online. A complete absence of results is itself informative.
  • Read the small print against itself. If a calendar’s warranty talks about inflatable costumes, the page wasn’t written for the product you’re buying.
  • Check the spelling, including on the box. We found a misspelled artist name in a product title, a mangled savings line, and a calendar with the word spelled “calindar” on the packaging artwork itself. A real manufacturer proofreads its own box.
  • Pay with a method that offers buyer protection. A credit card or payment service with buyer protection gives you a route to a refund. Bank transfers can be harder to reverse.

Details . Slashdot thread . And another news article .

10 Ways Cybersecurity Vendors Can Stand Out in a Crowded Market
items.summary: The cybersecurity industry is more competitive than ever, with new vendors, technologies and solutions constantly entering the market. As a result of sophisticated cyber threats, organisations are investing in tools to protect their systems, data and employees. However, with so many cybersecurity companies competing for attention, standing out from the crowd can be a challenge. For cybersecurity vendors, having an innovative product or service is only one piece of the puzzle. Building brand awareness, establishing credibility and reaching the right audience are equally important when it comes to attracting customers and growing a business. Here are 10 ways cybersecurity vendors can get noticed in an increasingly crowded market. Invest in Cybersecurity PR One of the most effective ways for cybersecurity vendors to increase their visibility is through public relations (PR). A strong PR strategy can help companies build brand awareness, establish credibility and secure coverage in publications read by potential customers and industry decision-makers. Working with a specialist cybersecurity PR agency, such as Eskenzi PR , can be particularly valuable. Agencies with experience in the cybersecurity sector understand the industry, its key publications and the challenges vendors face when trying to communicate complex technologies to different audiences. From securing media interviews and arranging thought leadership opportunities to promoting company announcements and providing expert commentary on breaking cyber incidents, PR can help vendors become recognised voices in their industry. Importantly, a good PR agency can also help support many of the other activities on this list, from promoting original research and securing speaking opportunities to raising awareness of industry awards, organising events and amplifying customer success stories. This makes PR a valuable part of a wider marketing and communications strategy. Attend Cybersecurity Conferences and Industry Events Industry events provide cybersecurity vendors with an opportunity to showcase their solutions, meet potential customers and build relationships with other professionals in the sector. Conferences such as Infosecurity Europe , RSA and Black Hat bring together security practitioners, business leaders, researchers and technology providers, making them useful platforms for companies looking to increase their exposure. However, simply attending an event is not always enough to stand out. Vendors can maximise their presence by hosting demonstrations, participating in panel discussions, arranging meetings with journalists or securing speaking opportunities. Events can also provide valuable opportunities to network with potential partners, investors and more. Establish Thought Leadership Becoming a recognised industry expert can help cybersecurity vendors build trust and credibility with their target audiences. Rather than focusing exclusively on promoting products and services, companies should encourage their spokespeople to share their knowledge of emerging threats, industry developments and best practices. This could involve contributing guest articles to industry publications, participating in podcasts, commenting on breaking cybersecurity news or sharing insights on LinkedIn. By consistently contributing valuable insights to industry conversations, cybersecurity companies can position themselves as trusted sources of information rather than simply another vendor trying to sell a solution. Publish Original Cybersecurity Research Original research is another way cybersecurity vendors can attract attention and demonstrate their expertise. Cybersecurity journalists and industry professionals are constantly looking for new information about emerging threats, attack techniques and security trends. Companies that can provide credible, original data are therefore well placed to contribute to these conversations. This might involve publishing threat intelligence reports, conducting surveys of IT and security professionals, analysing cyberattack trends or sharing findings from internal security research. Original research can also be repurposed into blog posts, webinars, infographics and social media content, helping vendors reach wider audiences and get more value from their findings. Enter Cybersecurity Industry Awards Industry awards provide cybersecurity vendors with an opportunity to gain recognition for their products, services, innovations and achievements. Being shortlisted for or winning a respected award can help companies build credibility and differentiate themselves from competitors, particularly when potential customers are comparing multiple solutions. There are numerous cybersecurity awards programmes that recognise everything from emerging startups and innovative technologies to established industry leaders and individual achievements. Vendors should focus on entering awards that are relevant to their business and target audience, ensuring their submissions clearly demonstrate the value and impact of their technology. Build a Strong Online Presence Having a strong digital presence is essential for cybersecurity vendors looking to reach potential customers and establish themselves within the industry. A company’s website is often one of the first places prospective customers visit when researching a solution, making it important that information is clear, accessible and regularly updated. Search engine optimisation (SEO) can help vendors improve their visibility when potential buyers search for cybersecurity solutions, while informative blogs, educational resources and technical guides can demonstrate expertise. Social media platforms such as LinkedIn also provide opportunities for cybersecurity companies to engage with industry professionals, share research findings and contribute to relevant discussions. As more people turn to AI-powered tools to research products and services, AEO and GEO have become vital. Vendors should also ensure their content is accurate, well structured and supported by credible sources, making it easier for prospective customers to discover and understand their offerings. Host Webinars and Educational Workshops Webinars and workshops can help cybersecurity vendors demonstrate their expertise while providing practical value to potential customers. Rather than relying solely on traditional sales presentations, vendors can organise educational sessions covering relevant cybersecurity challenges, emerging threats and industry developments. Inviting guest speakers, customers or independent industry experts can also help make these sessions more engaging and attract a broader audience. In addition to generating interest in a company’s expertise, webinars provide opportunities to build relationships with potential customers, answer questions and better understand the challenges organisations are facing. Showcase Customer Success Stories For cybersecurity buyers, understanding how a product performs in real-world environments can be just as important as knowing its technical capabilities. Customer testimonials, case studies and success stories can provide valuable evidence of how a vendor’s technology helps organisations overcome specific security challenges. Where possible, vendors should include measurable results and real customer experiences to make these stories more credible and engaging. Success stories can be shared through company websites, industry publications, social media and marketing campaigns, helping prospective customers understand the practical benefits of a solution. Engage With Cybersecurity Communities Building relationships within the wider cybersecurity community can help vendors increase brand awareness and establish credibility among security professionals. There are numerous online and offline communities where cybersecurity practitioners share knowledge, discuss emerging threats and exchange advice. These include LinkedIn groups, Reddit communities, technical forums, open-source projects and local security meetups. By participating in relevant conversations, answering questions and sharing useful information, vendors can build recognition among the people who may eventually recommend, evaluate or purchase their solutions. Offer Free Tools, Trials and Product Demonstrations One of the best ways for cybersecurity vendors to demonstrate the value of their technology is to let potential customers experience it for themselves. Offering free trials, product demonstrations, interactive assessments or useful security tools can help organisations understand how a solution works and whether it addresses their needs. Providing access to practical resources can also help companies reach new audiences, particularly when users share tools they find useful with colleagues and peers. For vendors entering a competitive market, a memorable product experience can help build trust, encourage word-of-mouth recommendations and create opportunities for future customer relationships. Standing Out in Cybersecurity Takes More Than a Good Product With so many cybersecurity companies competing for attention, vendors need to think beyond the technical capabilities of their solutions when building their brands. Ultimately, the companies that stand out are not necessarily those making the most noise, but those that consistently demonstrate expertise, communicate their value and build trust with the people they are trying to reach.

items.title: Hackers Breach Fireworks AI Through Third-Party Cloud Provider to Steal Customer Data
items.summary: Fireworks AI has disclosed a wider security breach involving customer account details, billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. In a November 9, 2026 update, the company said attackers reached its development machines through a third-party cloud provider, expanding the impact beyond the exposed credentials reported in October. The findings change the picture presented in its first disclosure. Fireworks initially reported unauthorized access to secrets used in evaluation jobs across a limited number of accounts. Its latest investigation confirms access to additional customer information, including portions of unfinished models and datasets belonging to certain customers. Fireworks AI Data Breach The newly disclosed attack path began on October 23, when a cloud provider hosting Fireworks research and development machines experienced a security incident. On October 24, an unauthorized party used that opening to access Fireworks development machines and run an unauthorized workload, causing further customer data exposure. Fireworks said it detected the activity that day, took immediate response measures, and closed known critical vulnerabilities. The company has not named the cloud provider or disclosed specific vulnerabilities. It reported no further detected successful access by the attacker on its customer platform as of October 25. The earlier incident began on October 6, when Fireworks detected misuse of internal credentials. Attackers accessed environment variables used by evaluation jobs, potentially capturing API keys and tokens. Fireworks began customer notifications on October 7 and later revoked affected keys, employee credentials, and service-account tokens. According to the updated security bulletin , the affected internal application exposed resource identifiers, names, descriptions, and creation times. Billing information included billing and shipping addresses, invoices, payment history, balances, and credit usage. Fireworks does not store payment card numbers and said those numbers were unaffected. For certain customers, attackers accessed a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets. The disclosure does not establish theft of complete production models. Fireworks also reported no detected impact to Inference, Training SDK, or Nexus, which operate with zero data retention by default. Its investigation remains ongoing. Fireworks said evidence points to a financially motivated cybercriminal group seeking to sell unauthorized access to large language models through illicit routing gateways, known as LLMJacking. Cybersecurity News previously covered LLMHijacking attacks and large cloud bills , explaining how stolen cloud credentials enable resale of paid AI services. The company has notified law enforcement and brought in Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for forensic support. Its response includes replacing credentials, reducing elevated permissions, isolating affected systems, and tightening storage access. Related reporting on cloud credential theft using autonomous AI agents highlights the broader risk around compromised cloud accounts. Fireworks has disabled self-service dataset uploads and downloads for Batch Inference and dataset-based training during the investigation. Training SDK remains available, while Fireworks Lab-based training runs in an isolated environment with added network and storage protection. The company is directly notifying customers whose data was affected. Its original customer guidance advises affected users to replace revoked Fireworks keys and rotate exposed third-party credentials with their issuing providers. Deleting a stored secret does not invalidate the underlying credential. Customers should also review access logs, unfamiliar users, API keys, training jobs, and datasets for unauthorized activity. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

Fireworks does not store payment card numbers and said those numbers were unaffected.

For certain customers, attackers accessed a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets. The disclosure does not establish theft of complete production models. Fireworks also reported no detected impact to Inference, Training SDK, or Nexus, which operate with zero data retention by default. Its investigation remains ongoing.

Fireworks said evidence points to a financially motivated cybercriminal group seeking to sell unauthorized access to large language models through illicit routing gateways, known as LLMJacking. Cybersecurity News previously covered LLMHijacking attacks and large cloud bills, explaining how stolen cloud credentials enable resale of paid AI services.

The company has notified law enforcement and brought in Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for forensic support. Its response includes replacing credentials, reducing elevated permissions, isolating affected systems, and tightening storage access. Related reporting on cloud credential theft using autonomous AI agents highlights the broader risk around compromised cloud accounts.

Fireworks has disabled self-service dataset uploads and downloads for Batch Inference and dataset-based training during the investigation. Training SDK remains available, while Fireworks Lab-based training runs in an isolated environment with added network and storage protection. The company is directly notifying customers whose data was affected.

Its original customer guidance advises affected users to replace revoked Fireworks keys and rotate exposed third-party credentials with their issuing providers. Deleting a stored secret does not invalidate the underlying credential. Customers should also review access logs, unfamiliar users, API keys, training jobs, and datasets for unauthorized activity.

items.title: Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely
items.summary: Google has fixed a Chrome zero-day that attackers are already using. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-125350, and it lets a remote attacker run malicious code in the browser. Google’s Stable channel update moves Chrome to version 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The rollout will reach users over the coming days and weeks. The Chrome Security team explains that bug details stay locked until most users have the fix. CVE-2026-125350 is a high-severity use-after-free bug in Chrome’s XML component. Google says it is aware that an exploit for this flaw exists in the wild. An anonymous researcher reported it on November 6, 2026, only three days before the patch shipped. Google has not said who is using the exploit or how many people were targeted. A use-after-free flaw happens when a program keeps using memory after it has been released. Attackers can sometimes use this to crash the browser or run their own code, often through a booby-trapped web page. Eight More Flaws Fixed in the Same Update The release carries nine security fixes in total, and seven of them are rated High. Google’s list includes an uninitialized resource in WebGL (CVE-2026-125345), incorrect authorization in FileSystem (CVE-2026-125347), a buffer overflow in Compositing (CVE-2026-125343), an out-of-bounds write in GPU (CVE-2026-125348), and type confusion in V8 (CVE-2026-125344). A second use-after-free in XML, CVE-2026-125346, came from Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security. Two Medium flaws were also fixed. These are CVE-2026-125349 and CVE-2026-125342, and both are uninitialized resource bugs in the GPU. Vo Duc Thang reported the second one. Google’s own team found most of the rest. The full issue tracker list will open up once most users are updated. CVE ID Component Flaw Type Report Date CVE-2026-125350 XML Use after free (exploited in the wild) 2026-11-06 CVE-2026-125346 XML Use after free 2026-10-12 CVE-2026-125344 V8 Type confusion 2026-10-02 CVE-2026-125348 GPU Out-of-bounds write 2026-09-18 CVE-2026-125347 FileSystem Incorrect authorization 2026-09-15 CVE-2026-125343 Compositing Buffer overflow 2026-09-15 CVE-2026-125345 WebGL Uninitialized resource 2026-08-21 CVE-2026-125342 GPU Uninitialized resource 2026-09-26 CVE-2026-125349 GPU Uninitialized resource 2026-07-20 Browsers read untrusted content all day, so memory bugs in parts like XML are a favorite target. A victim may only need to open a bad link. Attackers can send that link through phishing emails, ads, or hacked sites. We saw the same pattern when Google patched an earlier Chrome zero-day in June , which also allowed remote code execution through a crafted page. The newest fix also reaches enterprise users. The Extended Stable channel gets the same zero-day patch in version 156.0.8078.96. This patch arrives just days after Chrome 157 launched. That release fixed 213 security issues, including seven rated Critical, as our earlier report on the Chrome 157 update covered. Google says many of its security bugs are caught by tools such as AddressSanitizer , MemorySanitizer , Control Flow Integrity and libFuzzer . These tools help find memory errors before they reach the stable channel. Zero-days like this one show that some still slip through. You can read the full list of code changes in this build . Chrome downloads updates in the background, but the fix only works after a restart. Open the menu, choose Help, then About Google Chrome, and select Relaunch when it appears. Linux users should update through their package manager. People who use Chromium-based browsers should watch for vendor patches, because they often share the same engine code. items.title: Terminal2Shell: 55-Year-Old ‘Zero-Day’ Dating Back to 1971 Claims to Affect Billions of Devices
items.summary: Terminal2Shell claims a critical flaw dating back to 1971 affects more than two billion devices, allowing anyone who opens a terminal to gain an interactive shell. However, the website is satire, not a confirmed vulnerability disclosure. Its “exploit” describes normal terminal use, making it a joke about security marketing rather than a newly discovered threat. The page calls the issue “TermGeddon,” lists its CVE as pending, and claims a CVSS score of 11.0 out of 10. That score is an immediate warning sign because the official CVSS scale stops at 10.0. Claims about billions of affected devices should therefore not be treated as verified findings. Terminal2Shell 55-Year-Old ‘Zero-Day’ The supposed attack requires local access, a keyboard, and the ability to open a terminal. It then gives the person the permissions of the account already signed in. Nothing in this description demonstrates an authentication bypass, remote compromise, or access to another user’s account. The claimed attack simply starts with access the person already has. This distinction matters. A shell provides a way to enter commands. A security flaw must do more than show that commands run when an authorized user types them. Terminal2Shell presents expected behavior as a critical discovery, using alarming labels and a branded website to make an ordinary feature sound dangerous. For readers, the useful question is not whether a demonstration opens a shell. It is who controls that shell, what access they needed beforehand, and whether the attack crosses a security boundary. Terminal2Shell’s own description fails that test because the user already has the access being “obtained.” How Real Shell Exploits Differ The Terminal2Shell website contrasts sharply with Able2Shell . N-able took hosted N-central servers offline after reports of 33 alleged vulnerabilities and published exploit code. Huntress identified four exploit chains, including three leading to remote code execution. Unlike opening your own terminal, these chains involve attackers gaining control through weaknesses in management software. Plex2Shell shows why that difference matters. Attackers reportedly used a chain of Plex flaws to install cryptocurrency miners shortly after exploit code became public. The reported fixed release is Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861. Users should check their installed version rather than assume an exposed server remains safe because it works normally. PHP2Shell involved another important distinction: gaining an initial foothold is not always the final step. Researchers reported attackers combining it with a Linux kernel flaw to obtain root access on 25 servers. Updating an application alone would not address a separate weakness in the underlying operating system. HTTP2Shell and Node2Shell concern a Brotli decoding flaw, not ordinary command entry. Reported effects differ across affected software, including crashes and demonstrated code execution. Node.js users should check the fixed releases listed in the coverage: 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. A shared component does not mean every affected product has an identical attack path. WP2Shell reportedly allows attackers to create WordPress administrator accounts and install web shells without signing in. That missing login requirement marks a real security boundary being crossed. The coverage identifies WordPress 6.8.6, 6.9.5, and 7.0.2 as fixed releases. Terminal2Shell needs no emergency patch based on its stated behavior. Its practical lesson is to separate dramatic branding from evidence: identify the affected product, required access, demonstrated impact, and available fix before treating a claim as an incident. items.title: N-able Takes N-central Servers Offline Worldwide After 33 0-Day Vulnerabilities and Able2Shell Exploits
items.summary: N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline on November 9, 2026, after an independent researcher published details of 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities and exploit code. The company also told customers running N-central on their own servers to take them offline until further notice, creating an outage for users of its remote monitoring and management platform. The shutdown covers hosted services across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. N-able said the move was a precaution while its teams worked on a hotfix. As of November 9 at 15:15 UTC, the company said it had not seen active exploitation. Customers were told not to restore servers until N-able confirms they can safely return online. The public release, called Able2Shell, contains technical writeups and proof-of-concept code. Huntress reported that the 33 disclosed issues can form four separate exploit chains. Three lead to remote code execution, allowing commands to run on a vulnerable server. The fourth enables privilege escalation to root, the most powerful account on the underlying operating system. The research targets N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, with earlier versions also potentially affected. However, the full scope remains unconfirmed. Censys noted that N-able had not published an affected-version list, fixed versions, CVE identifiers, or severity scores for these newly disclosed issues as of November 9. The reported count should therefore remain distinct from a vendor-validated vulnerability list. N-central gives managed service providers a central place to monitor devices, install patches, run scripts, and support customer systems. That access makes a server compromise especially serious. Earlier N-central authentication bypass attacks showed how attackers could use the platform’s Take Control feature to reach managed devices. Those previous incidents are separate from Able2Shell. Able2Shell Exploit Chains Allow Server Takeover According to Field Effect’s analysis , the disclosure includes both authenticated and unauthenticated weaknesses. Claimed impacts include command execution, credential exposure, administrator account creation, configuration changes, and audit record manipulation. One published Python proof of concept describes an XML External Entity, or XXE, flaw that can be chained into remote code execution without a login. An XXE flaw occurs when an application processes unsafe references inside XML data. In this case, researchers describe it as an entry point into a broader server takeover chain. However, the public release should not be treated as proof that every claimed issue works across every installation. Censys cautioned that N-able’s notice did not confirm the individual mechanisms or impacts. The incident follows earlier N-central security problems, including an actively exploited remote code execution vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-86218. That flaw received a September hotfix. It is not an Able2Shell identifier, and installing an earlier security update does not establish protection against this new disclosure. Customers need guidance specific to the current incident. Some management functions remain available despite the classic N-central outage. N-able’s notice directs eligible customers to its separate application portal using N-able Login. The application documentation describes asset views, patch management, vulnerability management, scripts, policies, and tags. Availability depends on permissions, licensing, and configuration. Take Control through this portal currently supports Windows devices, not macOS. For defenders, Huntress recommends reviewing login and authentication activity from November 8 onward. Teams should investigate unexpected administrator accounts, unusual remote access sessions, and newly deployed scripts. Suspicious activity should trigger an incident response review that includes customer networks managed through the affected server, rather than stopping at the N-central appliance itself. Recovery should follow N-able’s instructions, not simply the appearance of an update. Huntress noted that live hotfixes may not change the displayed version number. Administrators should keep servers offline, confirm that the required fix has been applied, and wait for explicit clearance before restoring access to production management services.

Weekly Update 529: Kids Social Media Bans (and Everything Else)
items.summary: The kids-and-social-media discussion is just dumb. It's not the premise of delaying their access until 16, but the inability of those who should know better to grasp where the responsibility for enforcement lies. Here's our PM's explainer after the laws passed down here a couple of years ago: The onus won't be on parents or young people. There will be no penalties for users. And it's been expressed many times since, in similar terms, always to the effect of placing responsibility for implementation and enforcement on the social media platforms. Inevitably, there are some massive holes in their implementation, along with major privacy and social concerns. But as I say this week (and have said on many previous occasions), it doesn't have to be perfect; over the long run, it will gradually change social norms, and the kids in that shoulder age bracket right now will have a different set of expectations than those who come after them. But hopefully, in the interim, the whole "onus won't be on parents" mantra will be respected more than it has been to date.

items.title: Go Turns 17
items.summary: The Go Blog Go Turns 17 Austin Clements, for the Go team 10 November 2026 Today, November 10th, we celebrate the 17th anniversary of Go’s open source release ! Over the past year, we released Go 1.26 in February and Go 1.27 in August , alongside a steady stream of releases across our golang.org/x libraries and developer tools. Meanwhile, the pace of change across the software industry continues to accelerate, driven by shifting hardware, evolving security threats, and the rapid rise of AI-assisted development and agentic systems. In a tumultuous time for the industry, Go aims to be a steady hand on the tiller. Our goal is to keep Go grounded in its foundational principles of simplicity, reliability, efficiency, and an unwavering commitment to compatibility , while adapting to modern hardware, production workloads, and developer workflows. Increasingly, our investments serve a dual purpose : what helps human engineers write, understand, and maintain reliable Go code at scale also provides the guardrails and authoritative context that AI coding assistants and agents need to be effective. Core language and library improvements In the language itself, Go 1.26 and 1.27 addressed several long-standing restrictions in generics and everyday Go syntax, guided by years of real-world experience. When generics first landed in Go 1.18, methods could not declare their own type parameters, which sometimes forced awkward package-level functions and “inside-out” nested calls. Go 1.27 introduced generic methods on non-interface types (such as the new Rand.N method in math/rand/v2 ), allowing APIs to stay naturally organized on types and enabling readable method chaining. Together with support for self-referential type constraints in Go 1.26 and broader type inference for generic function values in Go 1.27, generics in Go feel more complete and natural than ever. Alongside generics, two refinements to value construction make everyday Go code cleaner and more concise. Go 1.26 extended the built-in new function to accept an initial value expression , allowing new(42) or new("go1.26") without the ubiquitous newInt -style helper functions used to populate optional pointer fields in JSON and protocol buffer structs. And in Go 1.27, struct literal keys can refer directly to fields of embedded or nested structs , reducing boilerplate in composite literals. In the standard library, our focus has been on evolving Go’s “production stack” and eliminating subtle operational traps. Few packages are as central to that as encoding/json , which has been a mainstay of Go since before Go 1.0. While its core model has held up remarkably well for over 15 years, tighter JSON standards and security expectations have turned some of its original defaults into interoperability and security hazards, such as silently accepting invalid UTF-8 or duplicate object keys and matching struct fields case-insensitively. At the same time, its buffered design prevented true streaming and limited performance. Addressing these issues while upholding Go’s compatibility promise for the millions of existing programs that depend on encoding/json meant designing a new major version of the package. Six years in the making, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages reached general availability in Go 1.27. Driven by Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, and contributors from across the Go community, this modern JSON API brings safer, stricter defaults, flexible caller- and type-specified customization, and up to 10× faster unmarshaling, while cleanly separating high-level semantic marshaling ( json/v2 ) from low-level, reflection-free syntactic streaming ( jsontext ). Crucially, we didn’t leave existing code behind: the original encoding/json package is now implemented entirely in terms of v2 under the hood. Existing v1 callers get faster unmarshaling simply by upgrading, and packages using v1 and v2 interoperate seamlessly so that the ecosystem can migrate gradually without flag days. We’ve also brought new production diagnostics to Go’s concurrency primitives. Concurrency is one of Go’s greatest strengths, but goroutines accidentally left blocked on abandoned channels or locks can silently leak memory and CPU in long-running services, and traditional goroutine profiles cannot distinguish leaked goroutines from ones legitimately waiting for work. First previewed in Go 1.26 and now generally available in Go 1.27, the new goroutine leak profiler ( goroutineleak in runtime/pprof and /debug/pprof/goroutineleak in net/http/pprof ) solves this for production services. Contributed by Vlad Saioc and Uber’s Programming Systems team, building on academic research with Aarhus University and Washington University in St. Louis, the profiler repurposes the garbage collector’s reachability phase to identify goroutines blocked on concurrency primitives that no runnable goroutine can ever reach. That allows it to pinpoint leaks in production with near-zero false positives and zero overhead when not in use. Bespoke modernizers work well for the language and standard library, but a centralized team can never write them for every third-party module in the ecosystem. Today, November 10th, we celebrate the 17th anniversary of Go’s open source release!

Over the past year, we released Go 1.26 in February and Go 1.27 in August, alongside a steady stream of releases across our golang.org/x libraries and developer tools. Meanwhile, the pace of change across the software industry continues to accelerate, driven by shifting hardware, evolving security threats, and the rapid rise of AI-assisted development and agentic systems.

items.title: Proudly nonprofit
items.summary: A few times a year, Signal broadcasts in-app fundraising messages, inviting everyone who uses Signal to make a donation. You may have seen these messages and maybe even made a gift yourself. (If so, thank you, generous friend!) These fundraising “megaphones” help us raise the critical funds we need to operate Signal and continuously improve the app. They also help us raise awareness about the fact that Signal is a 501c3 nonprofit public charity . Those words are not casual descriptions but formal, legal designations that are made by the US Internal Revenue Service. To become a 501c3 nonprofit , an organization must prove that it exists exclusively for charitable purposes, and to become a public charity , the organization must provide a direct public benefit and have broad public funding. The Signal app is the direct benefit we provide, and our broad public funding comes primarily from user donations.
